News.title: Heartbroken dad of daughter who died after Turkey op urges Brits to avoid surgery abroad
News.content:
Heartbroken dad of daughter who died after Turkey op urges Brits to avoid surgery abroad

EXCLUSIVE: Morgan travelled to Turkey for life-changing surgery, but came home in a coffin. Her grieving dad speaks out to deter others from taking the same risk

My daughter passed away from gastric sleeve complications

Broken by grief, Ricardo Ribeiro has a question for anyone thinking of cut-price surgery abroad.

‌



“Is it worth taking a risk to possibly come back in a brown box?”, he asks.

‌



He was speaking just days after an inquest heard how his beloved daughter Morgan died aged just 20 after jetting to Turkey for a weight loss operation.

‌



Having struggled with her weight from a young age, she could barely wait to jet to Turkey for gastric sleeve surgery.

The nursery worker had counted the days until her surgery, hoping it would change her life. Instead, it ended it.

Just three days after going under the knife in January 2024, Morgan collapsed on a flight back to the UK, forcing the plane to make an emergency landing in the Serbian capital Belgrade.

‌



View 6 Images Morgan was excited about having gastric sleeve surgery (Image: Philip Coburn/Daily Mirror)

Turkey surgeon still dodging questions over British woman who died after gastric band operation READ MORE :

She died in a hospital there five days later. Last week an inquest concluded Morgan perished as a result of ­complications from the op.

Today, her heartbroken dad, Ricardo, is sharing his precious girl’s story in a bid to deter others from travelling abroad for cosmetic procedures.

‌



Speaking to people considering surgery overseas, he said: “You’re putting your life in the hands of someone you can’t guarantee will do the job correctly.

“Yes, 80% may come out with a perfect result, and everyone says ‘it’s my body, my choice,’ but you’ve still got family who’ve got to deal with the agony if you pass away – you have to realise the effect is wider than that.

“Part of me died that day – it’s a gut punch I wouldn’t wish on my worst enemy. I don’t want any other family to suffer what I’ve suffered.”

‌



View 6 Images Ricardo says part of him died the day Morgan passed away (Image: Philip Coburn/Daily Mirror)

A post mortem examination found Morgan’s intestinal wall had ruptured during the procedure, which triggered deadly peritonitis.

Ricardo, 46, told how Morgan spent hours choosing a reputable-looking surgeon with glowing reviews.

‌



But when she arrived in Istanbul on January 5, 2024, the hospital replaced her chosen doctor with someone else.

He fears the new medic may have lacked experience and proper checks were not conducted.

Ricardo said: “If they have to replace a surgeon with somebody else, they should ensure they’re capable of doing the job.

‌



“It feels like many doctors there [in Turkey] are not held to the same high standards as British surgeons. It doesn’t make sense.”

View 6 Images Morgan was bullied for her weight at school (Image: Philip Coburn/Daily Mirror)

Morgan, from Croydon, South London, was scheduled to stay in hospital for two nights, but she was kept in for an extra day because of swelling, stomach pains and a fever.

‌



Yet in discharge notes obtained by the coroner, hospital staff claim Morgan was recovering and signed her off as medically fit to fly.

Ricardo said: “You cannot have kept her in for an extra day due to concerns, and on the discharge sheet have no concerns written ­whatsoever – it’s rubbish.

“It was blatantly just a form that you reuse and change the pieces to suit your needs. All they’ve done is cover ­themselves. To me, it just doesn’t ring true.”

‌



View 6 Images Morgan fell unconscious on her way back to the UK

In 2024, the Mirror tracked down Morgan’s surgeon, who was named by the coroner as Dr Serkan Bayil, and he denied any wrongdoing, claiming that Ms Ribeiro died of an embolism. But the coroner couldn’t get hold of him, and the hospital in Istanbul, ­Medivita Incirli Hastanesi, is listed online as permanently closed.

Ricardo says Global Medical Care – the firm that organised the trip and introduced Morgan to the hospital – also has ­questions to answer.

‌



He said: “They put the [team] together, so some of that ­responsibility has to lie with them.

“If you’re going to provide a service to someone, you make sure that their best interests are at the forefront.”

Ricardo thinks Global Medical Care and other similar companies should be barred from plugging surgery through social media ads. He added: “These companies are targeting the British public with ­fairytales – no matter what social media you go on, you’re bombarded with everything from gastric bands to Turkey teeth.

‌



“The UK government should be banning [the ads].

“If people were more aware they probably wouldn’t go, because who is going to risk their life for a BBL, breast implant or a gastric sleeve? It feels like money is more motivational to these ­companies than human life.”

View 6 Images Morgan's surgeon Dr Serjan Bayil denies any wrongdoing (Image: Humphrey Nemar)

‌



For Ricardo, most agonising of all is just how much his girl had to live for. “Morgan did have a stage where she was crying out for help,” her dad said. “She was dealing with bullying due to her weight, and she wasn’t in the best of places. But at the time of her death, she was blossoming.

“She knew she wanted to work with young people, because she ­understood what it was like to get bullied.

“She’d overcome all those problems, and wanted to help others do the same.

‌



“She went from trying to do so much good to having her life end in the blink of an eye.” And he has vowed never to give up on his fight for justice.

View 6 Images Morgan was counting down the days until her surgery

He said: “Someone, somewhere, has got to take accountability for what happened. Because if that doesn’t happen, how many more people are going to be burying their children?” Global Medical Care Turkey said: “We were saddened by Morgan’s death. We understand why her father is asking these questions.

Article continues below

“When a patient approaches us, we present more than one doctor and hospital option. The patient makes their own choice. Before a patient travels, a live consultation is arranged directly between the patient and the treating doctor, in which... the risks are explained and set out in writing.

“The decision to proceed remains the patient’s. The ­clinical assessment, consent process, the surgery and post-operative care are carried out by the hospital

A UK government spokesperson said: “We would urge anyone ­considering medical procedures abroad to review guidance from the NHS and other bodies.”

News.title: Putin makes chilling warning of 'war' over peacekeeping force in Ukraine
News.content:
Putin makes chilling warning of 'war' over peacekeeping force in Ukraine

Vladimir Putin made it clear that Russia would see the sending of a peacekeeping force to Ukraine as meaning war, with some European leaders pledging their commitment to the plan

View 2 Images Vladimir Putin has threatened Europe with war over a peacekeeping force (Image: Alexander Kazakov/Pool Sputnik K)

Vladimir Putin made a chilling warning to Europe of "war" over a peacekeeping force as Russian strikes killed eight people and injured dozens more in Ukraine.

‌



The Russian leader did not mince his words when speaking at a summit of the BRICS group of emerging economies in India, when asked about the involvement of western European countries in Ukraine.

‌



He said: “Now they’re talking about how they’re considering sending troops into Ukraine. That means a war with Russia."

‌



Some European leaders have pledged their commitment to a potential peacekeeping force, a prospect that Moscow has repeatedly described as unacceptable.

View 2 Images Putin with the Russian delegation at the BRICS summit (Image: Kristina Solovyova/Pool Sputnik)

UK temperatures to soar to 25C on Monday as another heatwave on the cards READ MORE :

NATO military aircraft scrambled over Europe as urgent warning issued in Poland READ MORE :

At the same time, Putin also denied Russia posed any threat to Europe, saying “there is no such threat and never has been. We do not threaten, nor do we intend to threaten, European countries."

‌



Overnight Russian strikes killed eight civilians and wounded dozens of other people in Ukraine, local officials said today.

Ukraine is under mounting pressure from Russia’s intensifying air campaign that uses ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones to pierce defences. Moscow’s attacks have targeted Ukraine’s power grid ahead of winter in what officials say is meant to demoralise civilians.

Two people were killed and one wounded when Russian drones struck a residential area in the city of Zaporizhzhia, regional head Ivan Fedorov said. One person also died and three others were wounded in strikes on Kryvyi Rih.

‌



In the Black Sea port of Odesa and the surrounding area, 35 people were wounded overnight in what regional head Oleh Kiper called a “massive attack.” Among the buildings hit was a residential high-rise, whose upper floors were completely destroyed.

Three people were killed on Saturday when cars were hit by drones in Kramatorsk in Ukraine’s partially occupied Donetsk region, along with a further two people in a Russian attack on a grocery store in the Zhytomyr region, local officials said.

Separately, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukrainian forces struck two chemical industry facilities in Russia, one in Samara and one in Perm. The governors of the regions did not immediately comment, but Russian independent online news outlet Astra reported drone attacks on chemical plants in both regions.

‌



Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk has said that two incidents along Ukraine’s borders with Poland and Moldova this week were a preview of potential intensified Russian provocations at Ukraine’s border crossing points with Europe.

Two people died when Russian drones hit the Starokozache border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova on Tuesday night, while a “direct threat” to a Polish-Ukrainian crossing point on Wednesday night was only avoided thanks to cooperation between Warsaw and Kyiv, he said.

In an interview with Deutsche Welle today, Zelensky said he would meet Putin if both leaders were invited to the Group of 20 summit of rich and developing nations in December in Miami.

Article continues below

Putin’s foreign policy adviser, Yuri Ushakov, said the possibility of Putin attending the summit had not yet been discussed. The Kremlin in the past has said that Zelenskyy can come to Moscow if he wants a meeting with Putin, a proposal Kyiv has rejected.

“If he really wants to meet with Putin, Putin has already said that he could fly to Moscow,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Saturday. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov affirmed Saturday that Russia is “ready for negotiations,” but that the so-called “special military operation,” as Moscow refers to its war in Ukraine, “will not be suspended during this period of negotiations.”

News.title: Professor Tim Spector's 'harmless daily habit' warning - eat these 6 things instead
News.content:
Professor Tim Spector's 'harmless daily habit' warning - eat these 6 things instead

Professor Tim Spector, co-founder of the Zoe app and well-known for his TV appearances on the BBC and ITV, has warned against the seemingly 'harmless daily habit'

View 2 Images Professor Tim Spector (Image: ITV)

A UK professor has issued a warning over a 'harmless daily habit'. Professor Tim Spector, co-founder of the Zoe app, and Professor of Genetic Epidemiology at King's College London and Honorary Consultant Physician at Guy's and St Thomas' NHS Foundation Trust, is a familiar face on BBC and ITV.

‌



He also regularly features on the Zoe health podcast. In a recent Instagram post, he revealed he had decided to "have a closer look at some of the world's most popular snack bars."

‌



The clip shows him adding ingredients to a jar relating to an unnamed snack. He said: "I don't know about you, but seeing all the ingredients laid out like this doesn't make me want to reach for one."

‌



He admitted that during his time as a hospital doctor, he would routinely reach for a chocolate bar or chocolate digestive most afternoons. He added: "I thought it was a harmless daily habit, but in the short-term, snacks like these will leave you hungrier due to spikes and crashes in blood sugar, and in the long-term, can lead to problems like inflammation."

View 2 Images The professor says fruit is a much better simple snack than the snack he examined (Image: fcafotodigital via Getty Images)

He then went on to list six healthier alternatives, saying: "Nuts, fruit, vegetables, yoghurt, cheese or a couple squares of dark chocolate are all simple snacks that can keep you satisfied and support your health. If you get into the habit of reaching for basic whole foods, you really can't go wrong."

‌



His followers were quick to respond, though not everyone was ready to ditch their favourite treats. One commented: "I'm sticking to all things in moderation I think - some a bit more moderate than others."

Another asked: "But healthy eating IS eating a treat and not denying and restricting any food. Is this post saying not to eat any treats?"

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



In the video, he adds a series of ingredients to the jar, starting with oats before including others.

"Let's see what's in the UK's leading snack bar," he says. The other ingredients are sunflower oil, sugar, honey, molasses, sunflower lecithin and sodium bicarbonate.

He concludes: "So there you have it. That's what's in your average healthy snack bar. Now the oats might have some health benefits. The rest of the ingredients none at all."

‌



NHS advice on what to eat each day for a healthy diet

The NHS website encourages people to look at The Eatwell Guide. It shows that to have a healthy, balanced diet, people should try to:

drink at least 6 to 8 glasses of fluids a day – this can include tap and bottled water, tea, coffee and fruit juice.

eat some beans, pulses, fish, eggs, meat and other protein.

have some dairy or dairy alternatives (such as soya drinks).

eat at least 5 portions of a variety of fruit and vegetables every day (see 5 A Day).

base meals on higher-fibre starchy foods like potatoes, bread, rice or pasta.

choose unsaturated oils and spreads, and eat them in small amounts.

The NHS says: "If you're having foods and drinks that are high in fat, salt and sugar, have these less often and in small amounts. Try to choose a variety of different foods from the 5 main food groups to get a wide range of nutrients."

Article continues below

The site warns that most people in t Britons are consuming far too many calories, along with excessive amounts of saturated fat, sugar and salt, while falling short on fruit, vegetables, oily fish and fibre, according to the health service.

It does point out, however, that The Eatwell Guide does not apply to children under the age of 2, as they have distinct nutritional requirements. The NHS advises that once children reach the age of 2, they should gradually transition to eating the same foods as the rest of the family, in the proportions outlined in the Eatwell Guide.

You can find out more about the Zoe science and nutrition podcast here.

News.title: Captain's four-word take on boy, 15, found clinging to upturned boat in freezing sea for days
News.content:
Captain's four-word take on boy, 15, found clinging to upturned boat in freezing sea for days

A 15-year-old boy survived for days clinging to an overturned boar in Alaska's freezing Bering Sea after a fishing trip with his brother and cousin ended in tragedy

View 3 Images Derek was rescued after days stranded at sea (Image: CARLOS ALEXIS ESCARTIN)

A fishing boat captain has described his reaction after a teenage boy was found alive on an overturned boat following days in freezing waters.

‌



Captain Adam White and the crew of the Northwest Explorer helped bring 15-year-old Derek Parker Aghnaanga to safety after he was spotted stranded in Alaska’s Bering Sea. The youngster had been clinging to the upturned skiff after setting out on a fishing trip with his older brother and cousin, who both died following the tragedy.

‌



The trio had left Savoonga, a small village on St Lawrence Island, on Friday morning to catch halibut and were expected back early on Sunday. But their boat capsized on Saturday night far out at sea, Derek’s aunt Collen Walker was later told, leaving the teenager battling to survive in waters of around 10C.

‌



When they failed to return, relatives raised the alarm and US Coast Guard planes and helicopters launched a search on Monday morning. One air crew spotted Derek at around 10.30am and dropped a raft and supplies before contacting the Northwest Explorer.

View 3 Images Derek was found alive on the overturned skiff (Image: CARLOS ALEXIS ESCARTIN)

Stalking charges reach record high after UK harassment hotspots revealed READ MORE :

Footage of the dramatic rescue showed Derek in a luminous yellow jacket crouched on top of the overturned boat as the crew threw him a rope, pulled the skiff closer and hauled him aboard in a rescue basket.

‌



Captain White believed the teenager had been holding on for nearly three days before his crew reached him. Speaking after the rescue, he said: “That’s one tough kid.”

Derek was showing signs of hypothermia when he was brought aboard, with the crew using blankets and hot packs to warm him.

Captain White added: “Through the teeth chattering, he had mentioned that his brother was still under the skiff. And then he said that, in the previous night, before our rescue, that his cousin had slipped away.”

‌



Their bodies were recovered after the youngster was winched to safety near St Lawrence Island - an isolated Alaskan outpost that lies nearer to Russia than mainland America. Derek said his cousin had also managed to cling to the overturned boat before dying prior to rescuers reaching them.

View 3 Images Captain Adam White described Derek as "one tough kid" (Image: CARLOS ALEXIS ESCARTIN)

His mum Vina Kulowiyi listened to radio transmissions of the rescue as other relatives huddled around a speakerphone. His aunt added: “We all cried and jumped for joy when the captain announced on the radio, ‘We found a kid, he’s alive, he’s alive,’”

Article continues below

“Then we asked, ‘Where’s the rest of them?’”

Following the rescue, Vina shared her relief in a Facebook post. She wrote: “My survivor. His story is amazing. He was never afraid the whole time. He knew he would be OK knowing his big brother was under the boat.

“He lived on prayer with no food and water. Love you son.”

News.title: Labour under Andy Burnham given 'second hearing', union boss Sharon Graham says
News.content:
Labour under Andy Burnham given 'second hearing', union boss Sharon Graham says

EXCLUSIVE: Unite general secretary Sharon Graham - one of Labour's most powerful union backers - tells The Mirror the Budget must end freeze on income tax thresholds

View 3 Images Unite general secretary Sharon Graham is urging Andy Burnham to end Tory 'stealth tax' (Image: Getty Images)

Labour is being given a "second hearing" under Andy Burnham, according to one of the party's most powerful union backers.

‌



General Secretary of Unite union, Sharon Graham, told The Mirror the party now had a shot at leaving a legacy similar to the transformational post-war 1945 Labour government.

‌



In an interview she also called on the Prime Minister and Chancellor John Healey to use October's crunch Budget to help struggling families and end the freeze on income tax thresholds.

‌



The leader of the country's second biggest union said it would show workers and pensioners hit by the ‘stealth tax’ that the government is on their side. And the union chief reiterated her call for a wealth tax on the super-rich and a levy on the bumper profits of banks.

Ms Graham - a frequent critic of Keir Starmer's government - said: "I do think there is an absolute chance - I haven't said this for a long time - but I do think there is a chance that Labour could get this right.

"But they also could absolutely get it wrong if they get caught by the 'computer says no brigade'".

‌



Ms Graham said she had no doubts that Unite - which slashed £580,000 in funding to the Labour party earlier this year - would have voted to cut ties with the party without a change in direction.

She said: "I have to say that had it continued in the way that it was, I have no doubt in my mind that we would have that our members would have asked us to disaffiliate. No doubt in my mind at all. It was absolutely there and it was real.

View 3 Images Labour is being given a 'second hearing' says Unite union chief Sharon Graham (Image: Ian Davidson/SOPA Images/Shutterstock)

‌



"What I think now is that Labour have been given a second hearing. I definitely think they've been given a second hearing, and that's why I say they get one shot.

"But if they get it right, it could almost be a 1945 NHS moment."

"If they do it right it could be a legacy that could last, if they do it right. We're talking about, you know, a long-term vision for Britain. We're in a fourth industrial revolution - we led the first, we're nowhere in the fourth let me tell you.

‌



"If we do it right we could have the jobs of the future, we could reindustrialise where these communities have been just left abandoned, quite frankly.

"To get there will take trust and people to believe, and on the way to that, you have to show why that trust is warranted. And that means you're going to have to take some of the burden off everyday people in the short term as well.

"That will give him the trust for the long term. I suppose the ball's in his court, is what I'd say."

‌



On the eve of the TUC's annual gathering of the union movement in Brighton this weekend, Ms Graham urged the government to end the freeze on income tax thresholds.

The £12,570 tax-free personal allowance threshold was first frozen by the Tories in 2021 and it was announced at last year's Budget it would continue until the end of the decade.

The policy results in more and more people being dragged into paying income tax as earnings increase.

‌



Unite argues workers would be able to enjoy around £3,500 extra tax free of their earnings if the threshold had risen with inflation since 2021. Some nurses and teachers are also being dragged into paying the 40% tax band, with the higher threshold also froze at £50,270.

Ms Graham said: "I see it as a stealth tax. I see it as completely unfair. I see it as an attack on workers. It is completely and utterly unfair."

The day before entering Downing Street, Mr Burnham said he had heard the "frustration about personal allowance" on the campaign trail in the Makerfield by-election and was "lodged in my mind".

‌



Andy Burnham rules out Tory benefit cut plan to fund extra defence spending READ MORE :

View 3 Images Chancellor John Healey will deliver the first Budget of Andy Burnham's premiership on October 28 (Image: Getty Images)

He later dismissed the prospect of any immediate changes to the income tax threshold freeze, saying: "There is no commitment at this point to change, but we will look at that at the Budget."

Experts estimate unfreezing the threshold could cost up to £8billion-per-year.

‌



But Ms Graham highlighted Unite's campaign to introduce a wealth tax on the super-rich. The union has previously said a one-off 1% emergency wealth tax on the assets of the super-rich could raise £25bn.

The union chief added equalising capital gains tax with income tax - something the Trades Union Congress (TUC) has also highlighted - could bring in £12billion-per-year.

She said funds could also be raised through a windfall tax on the big banks after bumper profits.

‌



Ms Graham added: "No one blinks an eyelid when it's the working class getting taxed pretty much through every sort of avenue possible.

"Why is taxing wealth so much worse than what we've done with austerity, freezing tax thresholds, the public sector decimation? I mean, that side of the equation looks far worse to me."

Ms Graham also said she agreed with the PM's analysis of the state of the country after he declared the country had taken a "series of wrong turns" since the 1980s with privatisation of key industries.

‌



She said: "I do agree with his analysis that actually from the '80s when we privatized everything within an inch of its life - I mean, I've often said, if they could have privatised air at that time, we would have probably been having to pay for breathing the air that we breathe."

But the Unite general secretary added: "He does have to now move into the action part of what is required."

She said she had told Mr Burnham recently "we almost need winter fuel in reverse".

Article continues below

"What I mean by that is that when Labour went in and made the absolute diabolical decision to cut pensioners' heating allowance, we need something that is equally important as that the other way round in terms of saying 'we back workers, we back communities, this is Labour now in'.

"That shows that in a way is clear, crystal clear and not be embarrassed about wealth tax, not be embarrassed about unfreezing tax thresholds, not be embarrassed to say to the banks you've had a good run, you do need to pay back a little bit here."

She added: "The Budget I do think has to show a good direction of travel."

News.title: Teen killed in motorbike crash was 'beautiful young soul' says family
News.content:
Teen killed in motorbike crash was 'beautiful young soul' says family

Harry Douglas, 19, from Liverpool, suffered multiple injuries when his Lexmoto bike was involved in a collision on the East Lancashire Road in St Helens and died later in hospital

View 2 Images Harry Douglas died in a motorbike crash (Image: MEN/HANDOUT)

A 19-year-old who tragically died in a motorbike crash was a "beautiful young soul" said his heartbroken family.

‌



Harry Douglas, 19, from Liverpool, suffered fatal injuries when his Lexmoto bike was involved in a collision on the East Lancashire Road in St Helens last Sunday evening, September 6.

‌



Emergency services raced to the scene and he was taken to hospital with multiple injuries but died later.

‌



A statement from Merseyside Police confirmed the death today as his distraught family told how he had a "one-of-a-kind personality". They told how he showed "compassion and care" to everyone he met and also revealed that his organs would be donated.

View 2 Images Harry's heartbroken family have paid tribute (Image: MEN/HANDOUT)

UK temperatures to soar to 25C on Monday as another heatwave on the cards READ MORE :

His family said in a tribute: "Harry was such a kind hearted lad, devoted to his mum, sister and partner. Everything he did in life was for their benefit. He was truly the best, most generous big brother, son and partner. He shown compassion and care to everyone that he met.

‌



"Harry was a beautiful young soul who loved hard and during his 19 short years blessed everybody around him with his one-of-a-kind personality.

"Harry understood the importance of organ donation, something he had spoken about with his family previously. His wish to help others will save and improve the lives of people he never met, a perfect example of Harry's personality."

Merseyside Police said in a statement how they received reports of a crash involving a Lexmoto motorcycle on the East Lancashire Road shortly before 9pm last Sunday and that Harry was taken to hospital with multiple injuries from which he died on Thursday, reported the Manchester Evening News.

Article continues below

It read: "We can sadly confirm that a man has died following a collision on the East Lancashire Road, in St Helens, on Sunday 6 September.

"Just before 9pm we received a report of a collision involving a Lexmoto motorcycle. The rider of the motorcycle was taken to hospital with multiple injuries.

"Harry Douglas, 19, from Liverpool, tragically died on Thursday 10 September. Our condolences and thoughts are with Harry's family and friends."

News.title: Trump Ireland visit live: No 10 responds to Trump's support for united Ireland
News.content:
Donald Trump declared his support for a united Ireland while taking questions alongside Taoiseach Micheál Martin this morning.

The US President is visiting Ireland for two days, and has said he would "love to see" the unification of the Republic of Ireland with Northern Ireland. "The UK would have something to say about it but I think it would be a great thing," he said. There were gasps in the room as he said it.

In response, Downing Street referred to what Andy Burnham said in the House of Commons on Wednesday - that he "will stick to [the Good Friday Agreement] 100%".

Trump also weighed in on the Falklands, saying he did not know if the UK is “going to be willing to travel that far” should there be a dispute with Argentina, adding he was “sure I’ll be called into that potential disaster” and would be able to “settle it out”.

Meanwhile, controversial aide Natalie Harp has been spotted among the US delegation in Ireland. Questions have been swirling about her personal relationship with the US President as she is reported to have frequently left "intimate" letters for him, saying things like "You are all that matters to me," and "I don't ever want to let you down...I want to bring you joy."

News.title: BBC TV Licence refund on £180 payment - full list of people entitled
News.content:
BBC TV Licence refund on £180 payment - full list of people entitled

TV Licensing outlines the specific circumstances in which you can claim a refund on your £180 TV Licence payment

View 2 Images TV Licensing rules show people could get a TV Licence refund in some circumstances (Image: courtneyk via Getty Images)

People with a TV Licence could get a refund if they meet the criteria. TV Licensing rules outline specific circumstances under which a repayment can be claimed.

‌



You can request a refund if you no longer require your licence before it runs out, provided you have at least one full month remaining on it. If you qualify for an over-75 or blind concession, you can apply for a refund at any point and for however long is left on your licence.

‌



Their website says: "Working out precise refund amounts can be complicated. But we will do it for you. We'll look carefully at the information you give us and let you know if we can offer you a refund, and how much it will be."

‌



A standard TV Licence costs £180. Most households spread the payments via Direct Debit, from £15 per month, with concessions and alternative licence types also available. Should you no longer require your licence and are eligible for a refund, officials say their calculations will be based on when your licence was issued and its expiry date.

View 2 Images You may be entitled for a refund if you meet the criteria (Image: aquaArts studio via Getty Images)

They say that all this data is used to determine whether you're entitled to a refund and, if so, the amount owed. Any refund is worked out in unused months. You must have at least one complete month remaining on your licence that you won't need before it expires - meaning you could receive a refund for anywhere between one and 11 months, officials say.

‌



You won't qualify for a refund if less than one month remains between the cancellation date and the expiry date, TV Licensing notes. If you haven't paid for your licence in full, its expiry date may be adjusted to reflect what you've paid. You can check your licence expiry date by signing in with your licence number, name and postcode.

TV Licensing says that if your refund is approved, your licence will be cancelled automatically. If you're not entitled to a refund, you can still cancel your licence online. Another section of their website addresses what happens if you've received a refund but wish to claim the difference. It says this isn't possible, adding: "We do not reconsider claims or change refund amounts once a refund has been applied for and processed."

The full list of people who could be entitled to a refund on their TV Licence includes:

‌



TV receiving equipment is no longer in use

The address is covered by another licence

TV Licence is bought in error

A replacement TV Licence has been bought

Refunds in consequence of a free TV Licence application - payments are made for each complete month remaining on the current licence.

Refunds due to the death of the licence holder

refunds for those who do not need it before it runs out and there is at least one month left on it

refunds for those who qualify for over-75 concession

refunds for those who qualify for a blind concession

For more details on the refund process and who qualifies, visit the the TV Licensing website.

How to get a free TV Licence

According to the gov.uk website, if you're aged 75 or over and receive DWP Pension Credit, you're entitled to a free TV licence. Those who are blind or residing in residential care can obtain a discounted TV licence.

‌



If you're 75 or over, you qualify for a free TV licence if you either: receive Pension Credit, or live with a partner who receives Pension Credit. Officials confirm the licence covers all residents at your address. The website notes: "You can apply when you're 74 if you already get Pension Credit. You'll still need to pay for your licence until the end of the month before your 75th birthday. After that you'll be covered by your free licence."

Applications for a free licence can be made online or by telephone. Telephone: 0300 790 6071, or Minicom: 0300 709 6050. If you live in an eligible residential care home, supported housing or sheltered accommodation, you can obtain a TV Licence for just £7.50.

To qualify, you must be either: retired and over 60 or disabled. Your housing manager is able to verify your eligibility and submit the application on your behalf. A 50% discount is available if you are registered blind or share your home with someone who is. TV Licensing stipulate that the licence must be held in the blind person's name - if this isn't the case, a fresh application can be made to transfer it accordingly.

Article continues below

You'll be required to supply your current TV licence number upon application. Apply for a licence if you're registered blind on the TV Licensing website.

News.title: Reform receives second £36m donation in two days as crypto investor matches record
News.content:
Harborne has already donated millions to Reform and Farage, who is currently under investigation by the parliamentary standards commissioner over whether he should have declared a Â£5m cash gift from Harborne ahead of the 2024 election.

Farage has argued that he was under no obligation to register the "purely private" gift, as it was unrelated to his parliamentary or political activities.

The party is also facing scrutiny after a broadcast by Channel 4 News last week showed two senior Reform aides apparently suggesting a way around electoral law to secure foreign party donations.

The Metropolitan Police has said it is investigating, while the party denies any wrongdoing.

The force is also looking into donations given to the party by Fiona Cottrell, mother of longstanding Farage ally George Cottrell, as well as a company controlled by Tice.

Harborne wrote on Saturday that he had "already accumulated enough wealth for the rest of my life", while Reform was a "start-up party" that lacked "the benefit of hundreds of years of patronage".

"A start-up party needs more money than can be provided by membership fees alone, to build and sustain itself and be ready for government," he said.

Harborne and Delo's donations mark the largest sums received by a UK political party since they had to begin declaring them in 2001.

Delo, who also announced his donation in a Telegraph op-ed, said he was giving the money away because he wanted a "fair fight and a level playing field". He said in April he was moving back to Britain from Hong Kong.

Addressing the recent scrutiny of Reform's finances, he said: "My conclusion from Reform's recent troubles is that they should spend less time trying to raise funds to compete on equal terms and more time preparing for government."

Last year, he was given an unconditional pardon by US President Donald Trump over a breach of anti-money laundering laws at his crypto trading platform, BitMEX, to which he had pleaded guilty in 2022.

There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties.

However, the Labour government has introduced a Â£100,000 cap on donations from British citizens living overseas, and plans to introduce a similar one for those who have recently returned to the UK.

There were nine donations of Â£1m or more to political parties in 2025. The largest was Â£9m given to Reform UK by Harborne.

Labour had five donations of Â£1m or more - totalling nearly Â£10m - and the Conservatives had three of Â£1m each.

Labour said Reform and Farage still had "serious questions" to answer about their finances.

Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson said Reform were "drowning" in "sleaze and scandal".

She added: "It's time Farage and Reform came clean with the public, fully co-operated with the ongoing police investigations and prove they're not just in it for themselves."

Rachel Millward, deputy leader of the Green Party, told BBC News it wanted a cap on donations from individuals of Â£500,000.

She said the donations to Reform were "absolutely staggering amounts", adding: "What I am very frustrated about is the influence of extreme wealth and the super rich. What I want to see is people in politics representing the needs of their communities and ordinary people."

Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart called for the government to introduce emergency legislation to cap donations.

She said: "These are eye-watering amounts of money. This is real emergency for our democracy. It presents a very clear and present threat."

Duncan Hames, Director of Policy and Programmes at campaigning charity Transparency International UK, said: "This is a watershed moment, with two billionaires pledging Â£72m to one political party in less than 48 hours.

"This situation is now completely out of control, and makes an irrefutable case for government to bring forward an annual cap on political donations, and fast."

News.title: Burnham and Badenoch revive red versus blue politics as Reform land 'gobsmacking' donations
News.content:
Look closely at the posters, placards and online posts. Your eyes aren't deceiving you if Labour's red seems a little deeper and the Conservatives' blue a little truer.

Politics seems to have found a new rhythm, one that feels a little familiar, despite Reform's jaw-dropping new donations putting it back in the headlines today.

For the avoidance of doubt, the scale of that initial Â£36m gift to Nigel Farage's party alone is like something from a different political universe.

"It's a gobsmacking sum," a senior figure involved in running successive election campaigns for one of the big parties tells me.

That was even before another Reform donor pledged to match that astonishing sum with another Â£36m, saying the first donation had provoked his "competitive spirit".

But one cabinet minister is enjoying what they see as a newly obvious difference between Labour and the Tories. "It's clarifying," they say, a clear gap between Labour and the Tories' "sense of purpose and values".

A member of Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch's top team tells me, "normal jogging is reasserting itself", hopeful they're at the start of a more straightforward, routine moment in politics after years of craziness, with smaller parties vying to shove the traditional tribes out of the way.

The standout moment was at the despatch box this week when Prime Minister Andy Burnham declared that national security couldn't come at the expense of social security - a phrase immediately seized on by the Tories, interpreting it as the PM saying he'd never cut welfare spending to pay for defence.

News.title: Oscar-winning film producer Jeremy Thomas dies aged 77
News.content:
Oscar-winning producer Jeremy Thomas, whose films included The Last Emperor and Sexy Beast, has died aged 77.

The British filmmaker "passed away peacefully" surrounded by family and loved ones at his home in Oxfordshire on Friday, his publicist said in a statement.

Thomas built an international reputation over a career spanning five decades, working with directors including David Cronenberg, Nagisa Oshima, Julian Temple and Nicolas Roeg and backing independent films alongside mainstream successes.

He best known work, Bernardo Bertolucci's The Last Emperor, won nine Academy Awards, including best picture, and earned Thomas an Oscar as producer.

The critically-acclaimed 1987 biographical drama about the final monarch of China's Qing dynasty starred Joan Chen, Peter O'Toole and Vivian Wu.

Thomas repeatedly collaborated with Bertolucci, also producing The Sheltering Sky, Little Buddha, Stealing Beauty and The Dreamers.

He has also worked with several British directors at the start of their careers including Ben Wheatley, Jonathan Glazer, Stephen Frears and David Mackenzie.

Thomas's other credits include Oshima's Merry Christmas, Mr Lawrence, starring David Bowie, Cronenberg's A Dangerous Method, Roeg's Bad Timing and Eureka, Fast Food Nation, the Great Rock 'n' Roll Swindle, and the film adaptations of the JG Ballard books Crash and High-Rise.

After beginning his career in the cutting room, London-based Thomas landed his first production role on the 1976 Australian film Mad Dog Morgan.

In 2006 he received the European Film Academy's award for Outstanding European Achievement in World Cinema and in 2009 was made a CBE in the New Year Honours.

Thomas's latest collaboration with Japanese director Takashi Miike, Bad Lieutenant:Tokyo, is due to premiere at the Toronto Film Festival on Monday.

News.title: I never got to experience my baby's scan, but blind parents like me can now feel them
News.content:
When I attended pregnancy scans a decade ago, the best the sonographer could do to involve this blind expectant mum was to turn up the volume on the heartbeat.

But now, parents like me can receive tactile 3D models created from their scans, allowing them to have a special moment with their unborn baby.

Reece Finnegan-Knight, who has been blind since his teens, is one of the first people to experience a 3D-printed model of his baby's scan with his wife, Sophy, as part of a new pilot scheme.

At their routine 12-week scan, Sophy had attempted to describe what she was seeing for Reece, but he struggled to feel involved in the moment.

Afterwards, when the couple showed the sonogram to their loved ones, Reece said it felt like "friends and family knew more about my baby than I did".

But he said the 20-week scan was more positive.

"The sonographer described everything to me, and explained why what she was seeing meant that everything looked good," he says.

News.title: Hardened activists are changing tactics and mobilising the anti-migrant vote
News.content:
At around seven o'clock last Saturday morning, dozens of men dressed in black climbed into the backs of lorries in a quiet Kent village called Preston-next-Wingham.

The men had arrived under cover of darkness the night before, leaving their cars everywhere: in the village hall car park and on the recreation ground.

In an operation with a degree of military precision, the small fleet of lorries departed for Dover just after sunrise, where the men staged an intimidating show of strength near the port.

In disciplined, serried ranks, they wore paramilitary-style balaclavas as they blocked roads around the port. There were at least three waves of arrivals, including the men who had spent the night in Preston-next-Wingham. Glaring ominously at motorists and police officers, they stood their ground.

Hardened anti-immigration campaigners were using their newly developed tactics for the first time.

It bore little resemblance to the running battles seen in cities in the Midlands in the days of Tommy Robinson's original vehicle, the anti-Muslim English Defence League (EDL).

"I seriously thought we'd been invaded by Russians," a Dover resident, Robin Burkhardt, told the BBC.

The main organiser Danny Thomas, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, said on Instagram afterwards: "This is our warning."

The style of protest is a new development in the crowded world of British hard-right and far-right politics. It was visually striking, and the men - who were part of a new group called Patriot Platform - chanted "Christ is King" as well as "Stop the Boats".

On Sunday, using a social media live stream, Thomas was able to organise a second, more impromptu protest of a few hundred people in his home city of Portsmouth.

His activists tried to block coaches that had come to collect migrants, who had arrived illegally, brought ashore after making the long journey from Normandy in France.

On Thursday, Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood met senior police officers and urged them to make full use of their powers to stop activists wearing face coverings.

"These scenes have caused disruption for people and, given that people are dressed in black wearing balaclavas, there is a fear factor and obvious malign intent being communicated to our residents," she said.

"This makes it different from other protests, so we need to make sure we are learning lessons."

Some of Patriot Platform's disruptive, eye-catching tactics seem to have been borrowed from environmental groups like Just Stop Oil. But its leaders are also getting ideas and funding from the growing "Christian nationalism" seen in the United States.

Its organisers say they are building a working-class "voting bloc" to persuade political parties on the right to adopt their agenda.

News.title: 'Every museum in the world is stressing': Did the Louvre heist embolden thieves?
News.content:
Museums are vulnerable and easy to burgle, Brand says, compared with well-secured jewellery shops and banks - which these days hold less cash.

Directors historically "never have enough money for security" or prefer to spend it on the next exhibition, and museums are often housed in old buildings that are difficult to protect, he adds.

For example, the Denis Diderot Maison des LumiÃ¨res (House of Enlightenment) - burgled hours after the Louvre - is housed in two 18th-Century mansions in Langres.

"We therefore have to reconcile modern security requirements with the need to preserve historic buildings and comply with France's heritage regulations," local mayor ThÃ©o Caviezel explains.

Museums are also open public spaces that have less access control and perpetrators can come in as visitors, says Kumar Sokka, CEO of Acre Security which works with some museums in Europe.

And even if a museum is secured well, thieves could still come in armed, Brand says, adding that it would be impractical to put police in galleries.

Many of these burglaries are over in minutes and the thieves have long gone by the time police show up - the Renoir case happened within five minutes.

Heists used to depend on deception, but burglaries are now becoming increasingly violent, Europol's report last month, external points out. Offenders are using tools such as sledgehammers, axes, crowbars and, in some instances, explosives, to get inside.

In the Louvre, the thieves used a mechanical lift to gain access, cut through the window with power tools and then threatened guards, who left, before forcing their way inside displays and grabbing the jewels. In the Renoir case, the perpetrators used an electric knife to cut through a fence before sawing through structures holding the paintings' frames in place.

The increased aggression creates new security concerns.

"An armed incident during opening hours, like the one we experienced, creates a situation in which the immediate priority is to keep our audience and staff safe," says Lilli Hollein, the director of the Museum of Applied Arts (MAK) in Vienna, which was burgled last month.

News.title: When an avalanche killed climber Nirmal Purja, his friends faced the hardest mission of all
News.content:
As he picked his way past the frozen slope towards two bodies, Mingma Gyalje Sherpa knew his friends were gone.

Together, the three of them had climbed the world's highest peaks, under crisp mountain skies and in treacherous snowstorms. Nirmal Purja and Kili Pemba Sherpa were two of the strongest climbers Mingma G had ever known.

But this July, an avalanche swept through Pakistan's Broad Peak while the two were on their way up, engulfing everything in its path.

The drone images seemed clear: no-one had survived.

And yet, as Mingma G came closer to the fluorescent down suits, sharp against the snow, he couldn't shake the idea they were waiting for him.

"I told them: 'It's ok. You don't have to be here in the cold anymore.'"

Speaking to the BBC in Islamabad, he recalls the terrible moment he reached for their bodies.

Holding one of them, he promised: "I'm here to take you guys home."

News.title: We've followed their lives for six decades - now the stars of 7 Up are bowing out
News.content:
Six decades have passed since Jackie Bassett first appeared on TV aged seven, skipping down the road with her little sister.

It was 1964 and she had been selected by teachers at her east London primary school to appear in a documentary called 7 Up.

The show interviewed 14 seven-year-olds from vastly different socioeconomic backgrounds. Inspired by the Jesuit saying: "Give me the child until he is seven and I will show you the man", it was intended as a one-off - a snapshot of Britain's class system and how it shapes us from a young age.

"They only picked me because I never stopped talking," Jackie told the BBC, with an infectious giggle that hasn't changed since childhood.

Little did she know then, but Jackie was being filmed for a show that would go on to be the longest-running documentary series ever made. In 2024, it was voted the most influential TV show of the past 50 years.

Now the curtain is falling, with the final instalment - 70 Up - airing on ITV this Tuesday.

News.title: Three arrests at rival protests in Portsmouth
News.content:
The new powers came into effect at 10:00 BST. Participants on both sides were not seen to be wearing any face coverings when the marches started.

The city centre protests follow disorder on 6 September, when police attended Eastney Marina as hundreds of demonstrators blocked roads in an attempt to stop coaches carrying 120 migrants, who had crossed the Channel in a dinghy, from leaving the city.

On Saturday, up to 500 anti-migrant protesters held Union and St George flags while some wearing Portsmouth Patriot branded clothing gathered outside All Saints Church on Commercial Road shortly before midday on Saturday.

The crowd chanted "stop the boats" as they marched to Guidhall Square.

About 300 people joined the counter-protest.

Both sets of demonstrators were kept apart by police when they arrived at the square.

Speaking before the march, Simon Magorian, of Stand up to Racism Portsmouth, described the demonstrations in Eastney as a "horrible spectacle".

He said: "Portsmouth is actually a good functioning multi-cultural city.

"We are now organising to have the broadest possible opposition to what we see as a fascist street movement and we're not going to allow them to get a grip on Portsmouth or any other town - this is quite terrifying."

Among the anti-migration protesters, Pete Davies, from Portsmouth, said he had also taken part in the demonstrations at Eastney.

"They should be having them turned back to France again. It's a safe country, there's no war in France.

"They want to stop the benefits, stop the free housing... they don't give nothing back to the people of the country."

Hampshire Police and Crime Commissioner Donna Jones said: "I'm pleased that today's protests in Portsmouth took place without major issue.

"Thankfully, we didn't see repeated scenes of Sunday night with assaults on police officers and criminal damage to police vehicles and people's property."

She thanked the officers for their work and their impartial use of the power to ask people to remove face coverings.

News.title: England survive scare to sweep Pakistan series
News.content:
Third Rothesay Test, Edgbaston (day four of five)

Pakistan 133 (Tongue 4-42) & 449 (Masood 95, Razaullah 81, Babar 76, Awais 59)

England 453 (Brook 75, Smith 69, Lawrence 65, Gay 60, Robinson 50; Razaullah 4-148) & 130-2 (Root 62*, Cox 59*)

England won by eight wickets, won series 3-0

Scorecard

England survived an almighty scare to eventually win the third Test against Pakistan by eight wickets and complete a 3-0 clean sweep.

The home side were already facing an unexpected chase of 130 on the fourth day after being frazzled by the hitting of Pakistan debutant Razaullah on Friday evening.

And the prospect of one of Test cricket's greatest turnarounds was raised when England were reduced to 2-2 in the opening over. Ben Duckett edged Muhammad Abbas' first ball behind and Emilio Gay was palpably leg before.

England could have been 35-3 after Joe Root rashly dragged on to his own stumps off Mohammad Ali. Ali was found to have overstepped and Root was reprieved on 23.

While Root needed fortune, Jordan Cox once again impressed with a composed 59, a further claim for the Essex man to be in the XI for the first Test against South Africa in December.

Cox and Root shared an unbroken stand of 128, Root unbeaten on 62 when victory was sealed just before lunch.

For Root, this completes a successful return to the captaincy he resumed when Ben Stokes retired in June, while England end one of their most turbulent summers in history in a positive fashion.

They switch formats to begin a white-ball series against Sri Lanka in Southampton on Tuesday, with Brendon McCullum back in charge and Kevin Pietersen as part of the coaching staff.

News.title: Battle to save the tiny, gooey snail only found in one lake in the UK
News.content:
A tiny snail found in only one lake in the UK has been dubbed as precious as an Egyptian artefact as conservationists bid to save it.

Several British zoos are setting up so-called ark populations of the glutinous snail, one of Europe's rarest species, using creatures bred in a back garden in Ceredigion.

"Beguiled by their cuteness," conservationist Ian Hughes has made it his "life-defining" mission to protect the threatened mollusc, which was once widespread in UK waters.

"There was a point where we'd got more snails in our garden than have ever been seen in the wild," he said.

News.title: Six people rescued after yacht gets tangled in fish farm
News.content:
Six people have been rescued after a 46ft yacht got into difficulty off the coast of Northern Ireland.

Red Bay Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI) spent seven hours at sea in the early hours of Saturday morning off Cushendall, County Antrim.

Belfast Coastguard received a distress call from the boat, which had been travelling from Oban in Scotland to Portugal.

The yacht lost all power and steering after making contact with a fish farm in Red Bay, in 60 knots of wind, causing it to become trapped.

A lifeboat was launched at 03:22 BST, with an inshore lifeboat also launched.

In a statement Red Bay RNLI described the weather conditions as "difficult" due to "Force 9 gusting winds, driving rain and the darkness of night".

The RNLI crew observed that those on the yacht were safe and, given the difficult weather and sea conditions, the decision was made "for the sailors to remain onboard the yacht and for the lifeboat to standby until daylight broke" at 07:30.

At 09.30 the lifeboat crew "successfully freed the yacht from the fish farm and brought the sailors safely to Glenarm".

Those on the yacht stayed onboard the vessel while it was towed by the RNLI, who said there were no injuries.

The yacht is now receiving repairs.

Speaking following the call out, Paddy McLaughlin, Red Bay RNLI Coxswain said: "This was a challenging call out in difficult weather conditions, but we were delighted to bring the sailors to safety, and we would like to wish them well.

"We would also like to commend our colleagues in the Coastguard and thank our crew who responded quickly in the middle of the night, launched our lifeboats in darkness and made their way to the scene in what were gale force conditions, and for then spending seven hours at sea."

News.title: Four arrested during gangland violence 'day of action'
News.content:
Police have arrested four men during a pre-planned "day of action" as part of an ongoing investigation into gangland violence.

Police executed warrants at addresses in Bellshill and Motherwell on Friday and also recovered four stolen vehicles.

One of the men arrested, a 29-year-old, was charged after a car crashed into a house in Eaglesham on Friday 21 August. There were no reports of any injuries. He is due to appear in court on Monday.

It brings the total number of arrests as part of Operation Portaledge to 81.

News.title: Driver threatened with knife as bus hijacked and chased in police pursuit
News.content:
A man has been arrested after a hijacked bus was brought to a stop after a police chase.

The driver of the bus was threatened at knife point by a man, who then allowed passengers to leave the bus. However, the bus driver was kept on board.

Videos circulating on social media appear to show a Translink Goldliner coach being driven at speed through residential streets while being chased by a Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) patrol car.

Police said the bus was hijacked in the Beltany Road area of Omagh, Co Tyrone, shortly before 13:00 BST on Saturday.

The man who hijacked the bus then made off in the direction of Newtownstewart and a pursuit ensued along the A5 through Victoria Bridge and Sion Mills. The pursuit lasted nearly 20 miles.

"The bus was eventually stopped in the Head of the Town area of Strabane and a man, aged in his 30s was removed from the bus and subsequently arrested," said a PSNI spokesperson.

The police said one man has been taken to hospital for treatment for his injuries.

A number of reports of collisions involving the stolen bus and other vehicles, including a police car and damage to property have been received by police, who are appealing for information.

The Fountain Street and Drumallagh areas in Strabane remain closed at this time and the public are asked to avoid the area.

Sinn FÃ©in councillor Brian Barney Harte said a wall was damaged at the side of a house in Strabane during the pursuit.

He said people were shocked and distressed, adding that his thoughts were with those involved.

"How there has not been a fatality is only by a miracle," he said.

"Numerous cars and properties have been damaged and people have told me of near misses of pedestrians, some pushing prams."

Barney said the bus came to a stop right beside a children's play park and that a police helicopter was involved in the chase.

A spokesperson for public transport operator Translink NI said: "We can confirm an incident occurred involving a Goldliner coach travelling on the Beltany Road in Omagh this afternoon.

"We are assisting the PSNI with their investigation including use of onboard CCTV and would ask anyone with information relating to the incident to contact the police."

News.title: MPs vote against fresh attempt to legalise assisted dying
News.content:
MPs have voted against proposals to legalise assisted dying in England and Wales, bringing the latest effort to change the law to an end.

Following a debate in which both sides made emotional speeches, the House of Commons voted 286 to 270 - a majority of 16 - against the proposed legislation.

The Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill would have allowed adults with fewer than six months to live to apply to be given help to end their own life, subject to certain safeguards.

A similar bill in the last parliamentary session was supported by MPs before stalling in the House of Lords. The decision from MPs on Friday rules out the prospect of changes to the law on assisted dying in the short term.

The bill tabled by Labour MP Lauren Edwards will make no further progress, although MPs and peers could make another attempt in the next parliamentary session.

Assisted dying is an issue that has been debated for hundreds of hours in Parliament over the last two years and would have represented one of the biggest societal changes in recent years had it been approved.

MPs were given a free vote, meaning they were not required to vote along party lines.

Safeguards within the bill included a requirement that a person applying for an assisted death had the approval of two doctors and an expert panel.

But critics said it included too few measures to protect vulnerable people from being coerced into ending their lives, while some say improving palliative care should be the priority.

News.title: Watch: Is the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition worth the hype?
News.content:
Visitors flocked to the British Museum in London on Thursday as the Bayeux Tapestry exhibition opened its doors to the general public.

The Bayeux Tapestry is an embroidery almost 70m (230ft) in length and nearly 1,000 years old. It tells the story of the Norman conquest of England and the Battle of Hastings in 1066.

Adult tickets to see the tapestry are priced at Â£33 during peak times and Â£27 at off-peak times, with an additional Â£3.50 donation.

The BBC's Katie Razzall asked the first visitors if it was worth the price.

News.title: George Osborne is right – we need a closer bond with the rest of Europe
News.content:

George Osborne suffers from being too clever for his own good, from his superior analysis of the political game to his reputation as the “austerity chancellor” of the first half of the 2010s.

But he is entitled to point out that his partnership with David Cameron in government was a period of relative economic stability that contrasts with the “utter chaos” that followed. And he remains one of the sharpest observers of British politics, even as he devotes himself to the day job of running the British Museum and organising the exhibition in London of the Bayeux Tapestry.

We should listen, therefore, when he supports The Independent’s campaign to move beyond Brexit to rebuild closer ties with the European Union. He is right to repeat what has now become widely accepted: “Brexit has been a mess. Britain has basically gone off a cliff. It has had a huge impact on the British economy. It is clearly poorer than it would otherwise be.”

He is also right to observe that political, business and union leaders are “frightened” to reopen the Brexit controversy. “There’s been a kind of conspiracy of silence about it,” he said, in an exclusive interview with Geordie Greig, editor-in-chief of The Independent.

But, he added, “People now realise you can’t look at Britain’s growth problem without beginning to think, ‘How can we revive trade with the continent, how can we get investment?’”

Rightly, in our view, he wants to push at the softest of Labour’s “red lines” drawn against reversing Brexit. He accepts that rejoining the EU is “hard”, politically, even though that would be most in Britain’s economic interest. He realises that joining the single market, like Norway and Iceland, or large parts of it, like Switzerland, is off the table for the time being because it would mean accepting the free movement of people between Britain and the EU.

But there is one form of economic integration with the EU that would not involve free movement and which would make trade significantly easier. It would therefore have an effect in mitigating the damage done by Brexit to our prosperity. That is a customs union.

“I would rejoin the customs union,” Mr Osborne said. “It’s a quite simple thing to do. That was never part of the Brexit debate. No one knew we were leaving it and it has had a devastating impact on trade.”

It may not be quite as simple as he suggests; Britain could not join “the” EU customs union, as that is an integral part of the single market, but we could negotiate a bespoke customs union that would remove checks on goods flowing between Britain and the EU.

We know that this is possible because such a deal was negotiated by Mr Osborne’s nemesis, Theresa May. Her Brexit deal was essentially a customs union that did not require free movement. It was an excellent deal and many Labour MPs regretted not voting for it and paving the way for Boris Johnson’s harder Brexit.

The argument against a customs union is that it would not allow Britain to negotiate its own trade deals with other countries. “The reason we weren’t supposed to be in the customs union – according to the Brexiteers – was these great trade deals we were going to strike with America,” said Mr Osborne. “That all looks pretty fanciful now.”

He is right again. British trade deals with America, India, South Korea and the Gulf states are together worth a small fraction of the value of a customs deal with the EU.

A customs union is the pinkest of Labour’s red lines. Mr Osborne should be congratulated for breaking the conspiracy of silence about it. Mr Burnham – and indeed any politician who is serious about promoting growth – should listen to him.

Lando Norris hailed one of the laps of his life after he came from nowhere to take pole position for the Spanish Grand Prix in Madrid.

World champion Norris had not troubled the top of the timesheets at any stage across the weekend before he delivered a magical lap to see off Kimi Antonelli by just 0.011 seconds.

Max Verstappen will start from third place for the inaugural event at the Madring, a spot ahead of Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton, who at one stage looked set to land his first pole in Ferrari colours, only to fall down the order in the closing moments. George Russell, the nearest title challenger to Antonelli, will start a disappointing sixth.

open image in gallery World champion Lando Norris saw off Kimi Antonelli to land pole position for Sunday’s Spanish Grand Prix (David Davies/PA) ( PA Wire )

Norris raised hope of defending his world crown with successive wins in Hungary and then the Netherlands, but he finished a distant fourth last time out in Monza to leave him 96 points adrift of Antonelli – the equivalent of nearly four wins – with 10 rounds to play.

Norris was then fifth in Q1, sixth in Q2, and sixth again after his opening lap in the decisive Q3 qualifying session. But he sensationally rose to the top of the order with his final throw of the dice.

To illustrate his speed, Norris was almost half-a-second faster than Oscar Piastri, who, in the other McLaren, had to settle for seventh. McLaren team principal Andrea Stella described the lap as a “masterpiece”.

“I’m shocked and a little bit surprised to be here now, but my God, it was probably one of the best laps I’ve done in my career,” said a jubilant Norris after he shared an embrace with his mother, Cisca.

“It was one of those laps where everything came together. I had a good idea of what I wanted to do, but it was just whether my brain allowed me to do it, and in the end it was perfect.

open image in gallery Norris celebrate his pole lap with his mother, Cisca in Madrid (David Davies/PA) ( PA Wire )

“I looked at the time at the end of my lap and I was like, ‘oh s***, that feels pretty good’.

“The adrenaline was high, and at one moment through the final corner I thought I was in the wall and that the boys were going to have to repair the car tonight.

“But nonetheless it was one of the best laps I’ve done, just everything that I wanted to achieve, and it puts a big smile on my face.”

Hamilton crashed out of final practice earlier on Saturday at a street track described by Russell as “mental” and Verstappen as a “car killer” in the build-up to this week’s event on the outskirts of the Spanish capital.

open image in gallery Lewis Hamilton crashed out of final practice prior to qualifying (David Davies/PA) ( PA Wire )

However, qualifying passed by without any accidents, although Russell grazed the wall in Q1 and team-mate Antonelli locked up and ran off the track but avoided an unwanted date with the barriers.

Hamilton’s car had been repaired in time for qualifying, and he was 0.061secs ahead of Antonelli and almost two tenths clear of Russell after the first laps in Q3 to leave him dreaming of ending a three-year wait for pole only to be toppled by Norris, Antonelli and Verstappen at the death.

Russell finished three tenths off the pace, and faces losing further championship ground to Antonelli in what is becoming a one-sided title race. Russell will start Sunday’s race 66 points behind his Mercedes team-mate.

News.title: Waymo pulls over robotaxi after detecting riders were carrying assault rifle
News.content:

Two minors were arrested last week in San Francisco after a Waymo allegedly detected they were carrying a gun and alerted the police.

On September 3, a Waymo employee was alerted that a gun had been detected in one of its driverless cars in the Outer Richmond neighborhood of San Francisco. The company pulled the driverless car over and alerted police to the presence of the weapon.

Police were dispatched to 40th Avenue just before 4 a.m. and engaged in what SFPD spokesperson Allison Maxie described as a "high-risk vehicle stop," according to SFGATE.

She said that police searched the car and found an "AR-styled assault rifle also known as a ghost gun," and also found "suspected marijuana and mace spray" on the minors.

Both suspects, one male and one female, were arrested and booked into the Juvenile Justice Center, according to SFPD. They will face charges related to the illegal possession of a firearm.

Waymo employees called police and parked one of its driverless vehicles after discovering a minor had allegedly brought a firearm into the vehicle ( Getty/iStock )

Police have chosen not to release the suspects' identities due to their ages.

Waymo's Rider Rules prohibit carrying a weapon of any type inside its driverless cars. It's not clear exactly how the Waymo detected the firearm, especially one described as a "ghost gun" by the SFPD.

Ghost guns are typically homemade guns, often created using partially 3D-printed parts. They are not registered weapons and don't have serial numbers, and are thus more difficult for law enforcement to track.

The incident wasn't the first time Waymo employees called the cops on their customers. In July, company employees called the San Mateo Police Department to report that two 15-year-old boys were allegedly drinking alcohol and shooting water beads while cruising around in the car, according to SFGATE.

In that case, Waymo reportedly did not alert the riders that the police had been called, and allegedly fed them a false story to explain why the car was pulling over.

The teens "were told the vehicle had issues" before it pulled over, according to San Matteo Police Department spokesperson Jeanine Luna, who spoke to Business Insider about the incident earlier this year.

She impressed that the vehicle's doors were never locked, so the teens could have exited the car at any time before police arrived.

It's unclear if Waymo used a similar tactic to keep the juveniles with the ghost gun from exiting the vehicle.

The Independent has requested comment from the company.

Waymo has been in operation since 2009, when it was launched by Google, and eventually broke off to become its own company in 2016. It began operating in San Diego, Denver, and Tampa earlier this month.

England recovered from a poor first-half to storm to a 48-15 victory over Australia with Abi Burton emerging as the star at CorpAcq Stadium.

Trailing 10-5 at the interval, the Red Roses burst into life with their set-piece initially turning the tables before they cut loose to finish the WXV Global Series opener with eight tries and a 39th consecutive Test win.

In their first outing since being crowned grand slam champions by beating France in May and first with the new smaller 4.5 ball being trialled in the women’s game, they took time to blow away the cobwebs with their high error count before the break leading to frustration.

Australia deserved to be ahead after controlling the breakdown and showing resilience in defence and they even played 10 minutes of the first-half with 14 players after Samantha Wood was sent to the sin bin for a deliberate knock-on.

But in the 47th minute England’s pack took charge with May Campbell finishing a line-out drive before they made an ominous statement with a dominant scrum.

It ignited their attacking game with captain Meg Jones then dotting down a low kick through by Holly Aitchison, who was winning her 50th cap, to begin the stampede of tries.

Wings Mia Venner and Claudia Moloney-MacDonald were among those to breach the Australian whitewash but the world champions’ standout figure was Burton, the blindside flanker who bagged their first try as part of an impressive all-round display.

Mississippi police said Saturday they were still investigating the death of Tasia Fortune, a Black woman found hanging from a tree last month, a day after a man was arrested in connection with the killing.

Loved ones also painted a picture of Fortune as a mother, athlete and woman of faith who they hoped would not solely be remembered for her horrific death.

Police sought and found Jarques Ratliff, 51, who is Black, and arrested him when they encountered him walking on the street, authorities said Friday. Jackson Police Chief RaShall Brackney also said Friday that additional arrests are expected in the case. Ratliff should appear in Jackson Municipal Court no later than Monday morning, said André de Gruy, Mississippi's state defender.

Brackney said Ratliff had an “association” with Fortune but would not elaborate on their relationship. She said police arrested Ratliff on a homicide charge and called that “an important development” in the investigation.

“But it is not the conclusion. This case remains active, and additional arrests will be pending as our investigators continue to follow the evidence wherever it leads,” Brackney said Friday. “We understand that this case has received media attention from across the globe, and across this community.”

Police provide little new information on Saturday

The state medical examiner’s office determined Thursday evening that the death was a homicide, Brackney said, allowing police to execute the warrants they already had on hand.

Police did not respond to calls and messages from The Associated Press on Saturday about potential updates to the investigation beyond confirming it was still going on.

Ratliff also did not appear in Hinds County jail records on Saturday. It couldn’t immediately be determined if he had a lawyer, and a message was left for the public defender's office. If represented by a public defender, it would be the Hinds County public defender, de Gruy said.

Fortune's mother said she is grateful to police

Christy Spivey, Fortune’s mother, said Friday after police told her of the arrest that “I just started crying and told them ‘thank you, thank you, thank you.’”

Spivey said police did not share a motive or whether DNA led them to the arrest. Spivey said she did not know the man who had been arrested, but she was asking her daughter's friends if they knew him. Spivey described the family as “in disbelief” and “shock.”

“We still don’t have a lot of answers,” Spivey said.

Police discovered Fortune’s body hanging in the backyard of an abandoned home in Jackson on Aug. 3.

Spivey said she was certain that her daughter, 29, would not have killed herself.

“Absolutely not. Even if she could climb that tree, no, no, she would never, ever, ever,” Spivey said.

Fortune was a mother, an athlete and deeply religious, and had a troubled life

An obituary about Fortune posted on the website of Tucker Funeral Home in Central City, Kentucky, in August stated that Fortune's “path was not always easy, and there were highs and lows.” It also stated that she skipped her junior year of high school, was a star cross-country runner, and had a strong faith in God. Services were held last month in Kentucky.

“She leaves behind a powerful legacy of resilience, rooted deeply in her unwavering faith. Even in her darkest hours, she never stopped believing in her Savior,” the obituary stated.

Fortune was also the mother of four children, but she rarely saw two of them, Spivey said. The last time Spivey saw her daughter was in late July for a planned family reunion in Kentucky that was canceled, but her daughter came to see her anyway.

“When she was there, there was this pull, like a spiritual pull to her. I needed her. I guess God knew that was going to be it,” Spivey said.

Spivey said she and Fortune's father faced racism and violence as a mixed-race couple in Crittenden County, Kentucky, before Fortune was born.

Fortune was taken from her parents and placed in foster care as a child. During her high school years, she moved around among group homes and eventually ran away to Mississippi. The obituary stated that she had lived in Jackson for 10 years.

Spivey wasn’t sure where Fortune was living at the time of her death but said her daughter had been struggling with homelessness in recent years. Fortune had two sisters and was close with them. The father of one of her children was verbally and physically abusive to Fortune, Spivey said.

Before she died, Fortune had talked about starting a cleaning business and was trying to get her life in order.

“Say her name. Keep it going,” Spivey said. “Because I’m not going to stop until I get answers.”

___

Associated Press writer Josh Kelety contributed to this report.
