MaSU President Eastman K. Toe: 0887558129

Head Coach Edwin Lawal: 0880855529

World.title: U.S. Embassy Marks 25 Years Since 9/11 With Memorial Walk in Monrovia
World.content:
At 9:03 a.m., marking the moment United Airlines Flight 175 struck the South Tower of the World Trade Center, participants began a symbolic 2,977-step memorial walk.

Monrovia — The United States Embassy in Monrovia on Friday commemorated the 25th anniversary of the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks on the United States, honoring the 2,977 people who lost their lives in one of the deadliest attacks in U.S. history.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

The commemoration began with the lowering of the U.S. flag at the embassy, followed by a moment of silence led by U.S. Chargé d’Affaires Joe Zadrozny at 8:46 a.m.—the exact time American Airlines Flight 11 crashed into the North Tower of the World Trade Center in New York.

A member of the United States Marine Corps then did a beautiful rendition of the U.S. national anthem, before Zadrozny delivered remarks reflecting on the lives lost, the bravery of first responders and the international solidarity that followed the attacks.

Chargé d’Affaires Zadrozny said the anniversary was an opportunity to remember the 2,977 innocent civilians, first responders and service members killed at the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania.

“At 8:46 AM, the world shifted in an instant,” Zadrozny said. “What began as a bright September morning transformed into a day of unprecedented tragedy.”

He said the anniversary was an opportunity to remember the 2,977 innocent civilians, first responders and service members killed at the World Trade Center, the Pentagon and in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania.

The Chargé d’Affaires also paid tribute to firefighters, police officers and paramedics who rushed toward danger, as well as passengers aboard United Airlines Flight 93 who resisted the hijackers before the aircraft crashed in Pennsylvania.

“We remember the courage of the firefighters, police officers, and paramedics who ran toward danger so that others might live,” Zadrozny said. “We remember the ordinary citizens on Flight 93, who performed extraordinary acts of bravery.”

Liberia’s Solidarity Remembered

Zadrozny also recalled Liberia’s response to the tragedy, noting that the Liberian government organized an intercessory service and declared three days of national mourning for the victims, including at least one Liberian.

The commemoration began with the lowering of the U.S. flag at the embassy, followed by a moment of silence at 8:46 a.m.—the exact time American Airlines Flight 11 crashed into the North Tower of the World Trade Center in New York. “As our flag flies at half-staff, we carry a duty not only to remember the past, but to live out the values of resilience, public service, and unity that defined the days after 9/11,” he said. 2,977 Steps in Memory of 2,977 Lives At 9:03 a.m., marking the moment United Airlines Flight 175 struck the South Tower of the World Trade Center, participants began a symbolic 2,977-step memorial walk. The walk started at the embassy flagpole, proceeded through the main gate and around the embassy compound along UN Drive and Benson Street. Each step represented one of the 2,977 people who died in the September 11 attacks. Despite a heavy downpour, Zadrozny joined the walk alongside Liberian government officials, U.S. Embassy staff and members of the press. The memorial concluded with participants returning to the embassy grounds, where they gathered for coffee and refreshments. The 9/11 attacks killed 2,977 people after four hijacked commercial aircraft were used in coordinated attacks against the World Trade Center in New York, the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, and a target that was not reached after Flight 93 crashed in Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Zadrozny said the anniversary should serve not only as a moment to remember the past but also as a reminder of the values of resilience, public service and unity. He described Liberia’s solidarity with the United States following the attacks as an enduring element of the two countries’ relationship. “Our Liberian hosts and international partners stood together with the United States in our grief, reminding us that we do not stand alone,” he said. “That solidarity remains a cornerstone of our work together today.”

World.title: Liberia: Boakai Shuffles Cabinet: New Acting Defense, Commerce Ministers; Gender Deputy Suspended
World.content:
Monrovia – President Joseph Nyuma Boakai Sr. has shaken up several government ministries and agencies, announcing a wave of new appointments this week.

Cllr. Oswald Natu Tweh takes over as Acting Minister of National Defense, stepping in for Geraldine J. George. Over at Commerce and Industry, Stephen Marka Yekeson Jr. steps into the acting minister role, replacing Magdalene E. Dagoseh. Both George and Dagoseh will be reassigned to other government positions.

The president also tapped Christopher Ben Bailey to serve as Acting Superintendent of Grand Gedeh County. At the National Food Assistance Agency, Mike Khailelu B. Jabateh moves into the role of Acting Deputy Director General for Publicity.

In another appointment, Daniel Frank Gould II has been named to the Board of Commissioners of the Public Procurement and Concessions Commission, though his nomination still needs Senate confirmation.

On the disciplinary side, Frederick S. Cooper, Deputy Minister for Administration at the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, has been suspended for 60 days without pay. The Executive Mansion says the move stems from conduct it considers incompatible with Cooper’s role as a public official.

Boakai used the moment to send a broader message to his administration, warning officials that public office comes with real accountability — and that conduct undermining government integrity or public trust won’t be tolerated.

World.title: Liberia: A Mystery Vessel, a Prison, and a Warning Nobody Answered
World.content:
MONROVIA — There is a version of this story in which the boat behind the Monrovia Central Prison is nothing more than a stray vessel, pushed toward shore by the tide and forgotten within days.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected] and Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

But Thursday’s discovery is difficult to view in isolation.

Five weeks ago, the prison’s Deputy Superintendent for Operations, Jackson K. Kolako, publicly warned that he believed a plan was being developed to facilitate a mass jailbreak—potentially freeing foreign nationals detained in connection with Liberia’s largest cocaine investigation.

Now, before dawn on Thursday, a vessel of disputed ownership and unexplained movements was found at the beach behind the same prison.

Coincidence is possible. But the timing has raised questions that authorities have yet to fully answer.

What Kolako Actually Said

Kolako’s account dates to August 1, when, according to him, two men arrived at the prison claiming to be National Security Agency officers. He said the men were dressed in a manner inconsistent with prison security rules and sought access to one of the foreign nationals detained in connection with the drug case.

Kolako said he questioned whether the prison’s chief superintendent and the Assistant Minister of Justice for Corrections had authorized the visit.

He says he was arrested later that day, in front of his officers, on the orders of a senior Justice Ministry official.

According to Kolako, he spent six days in custody without giving a statement and was pressured to surrender his phones and passwords. Following his release, he publicly raised his concerns and appealed to President Joseph Boakai to consider moving detainees connected to the drug investigation to a more secure facility outside Liberia, suggesting Morocco as one possible destination.

Kolako’s account, however, remains contested.

He has not publicly produced evidence establishing that an actual jailbreak plot was underway, while officials he implicated have not publicly addressed all of his allegations. Ministry of Justice records have reportedly presented a different explanation for his suspension, saying he was sanctioned over alleged obstruction of a lawful operation rather than for raising security concerns.

The competing accounts have yet to be reconciled.

On Thursday, Kolako again took to social media, emphasizing the need for heightened coordination among the Liberia National Police, Armed Forces of Liberia and corrections authorities.

Kolako, using the name Gertrude’s Pap on Facebook, said the detention of people connected to sensitive and high-profile cases requires preparedness, coordination and vigilance.

“Security is stronger when institutions work together,” Kolako wrote.

Mystery Vessel Sparks Calls for Independent Probe

The vessel’s appearance has now triggered calls for an independent investigation.

Liberian activist Martin K. N. Kollie, whose network first reported the boat, is calling for an independent inquiry into how the unidentified vessel came to be at the beach behind the Monrovia Central Prison, commonly known as South Beach.

Kollie has described the vessel as a “ghost boat” and questioned conflicting accounts surrounding its ownership, origin and movements.

He has specifically called for an investigation outside the Liberia National Police, including Inspector General Gregory Coleman, arguing that the circumstances require investigators viewed as independent by the public.

The vessel was later moved toward the Miami Beach area, according to accounts surrounding the incident, further raising questions about who controlled it and why it had initially been positioned near the prison.

The Question of the Boat

Kollie has also challenged claims that the vessel found at South Beach belongs to a person identified publicly only as “Charlie,” who reportedly described himself during a radio interview as a Canadian miner.

Kollie maintains that images circulated by people claiming ownership show a different vessel from the one found behind the prison.

That claim has not been independently verified by FrontPage Africa.

The unresolved questions are nevertheless straightforward: Who owns the vessel? Where did it come from? Who was operating it? When did it leave the St. Paul River? How did it reach South Beach? And was anyone aboard at any point during the journey?

Those questions become more consequential because of the vessel’s location.

The beach behind the prison sits within a highly sensitive security environment, particularly as the facility houses detainees linked to Liberia’s ongoing drug-trafficking investigation.

A Country That Has Seen This Boat Before

The episode comes against a backdrop of growing scrutiny over Liberia’s maritime security.

In June, a vessel identified as the IB Atlantic IV remained off the coast of Grand Cape Mount County for several days as Liberian authorities considered how to respond before the vessel eventually moved away and was later intercepted and seized in Ivorian waters.

No drugs were officially reported recovered from the vessel.

The episode nevertheless became another example of the challenges facing Liberia in monitoring and securing its coastline.

The latest vessel presents a different but related set of questions.

Despite competing ownership claims, authorities have not publicly established who owns the boat, how it reached South Beach or whether it was carrying anything when it arrived.

Nor has any official investigation publicly established a connection between the vessel and the ongoing drug-trafficking cases.

What Remains Unanswered

For now, the boat remains less an answer than a question.

There is no publicly established evidence that the vessel was part of a jailbreak attempt. There is also no publicly established evidence that it was connected to the drug investigation.

But the combination of its location, the conflicting accounts surrounding its ownership and movement, and the prison security warnings raised weeks earlier has created a legitimate public-interest question.

An independent investigation could establish the facts without relying on competing narratives—determining the vessel’s ownership, registration, route, occupants, cargo, movements and circumstances surrounding its arrival at South Beach.

Until those questions are answered, the vessel behind the prison wall will remain what it became Thursday morning: a mystery sitting in plain sight.

World.title: Liberia: Expert Warns of Security Risks if Legislature Fails to Approve War Crimes Court Before U.N. Security Council Presidency
World.content:
Summary

Transitional justice expert Aaron Weah warns that failure to approve legislation establishing Liberia’s long-delayed War and Economic Crimes Court could create new security risks, particularly among a young generation raised on memories of the civil wars.

Liberia is preparing to assume the rotating presidency of the U.N. Security Council in December, putting a renewed international spotlight on the country’s unfinished transitional justice process.

Weah says Liberia must address how the wars are remembered and taught, warning that the absence of an agreed historical narrative, public memorials and museums has left younger Liberians exposed to disinformation about the conflict.

By Anthony Stephens, senior justice correspondent with New Narratives

Aaron Weah, the leading historian and transitional justice expert, has warned of security risks if the country fails to approve legislation establishing a War and Economic Crimes Court before it assumes the rotating presidency of the United Nations Security Council in December.

Despite years of advocacy, the push for a long-delayed court to prosecute those accused of “bearing the greatest responsibility” for atrocities committed during Liberia’s two civil wars, which the United Nations estimates left about 250,000 people dead, remains unfinished as the Legislature has so far failed to overcome opposition to the courts among lawmakers.

A recent poll by FrontPage Africa/New Narratives found 89 percent of survey respondents in 11 counties wanted to see the worst perpetrators tried in a war crimes court for atrocities committed during the war.

“You don’t want to raise expectations of people and let them down. I think it has a lot of security risk because we have a youthful population,” Weah, director of the Ducor Institute for Social and Economic Research, said in a FrontPage Africa/New Narratives interview.

Weah’s warning comes at a pivotal moment for Liberia’s unfinished transitional justice process. The country is preparing to preside over the Security Council for the first time while lawmakers consider competing proposals for the long-promised court. At the same time, a population dominated by young people who did not directly experience the wars is confronting unresolved questions about justice, reparations and how the conflict should be remembered and taught.

Weah said establishing the court is about more than prosecuting alleged perpetrators. He argued that it could help clarify Liberia’s wartime history and said abandoning the process after years of promises could create new resentment and security concerns.

His warning echoes concerns raised by the Liberian government and the United Nations. In an October 2025, statement to the U.N. General Assembly’s Sixth Committee, which deals with international legal issues, the government warned that “the absence of justice perpetuates the cycle of conflict.”

Liberia’s civil wars claimed an estimated 250,000 lives. Credit: Chris Hondros / Getty Images.

The United Nations has also linked the proposed court to preventing recurrence. Christian Mukosa, its top human rights official in Liberia, said that operationalizing a victim-centered court could “contribute to reconciliation and prevent recurrence.”

According to Liberia’s 2022 Population and Housing Census , three in every four of the country’s 5.25 million people were 35 or younger. Forty four percent of the population was born after the civil wars ended in 2003. Weah said many young Liberians have instead grown up with memories of the wars passed down by their parents. After taking the court process this far, he warned, abandoning it could have consequences beyond the justice debate.

Liberia’s official campaign graphic for its successful bid for a non-permanent seat on the United Nations Security Council for 2026–2027. Credit: Government of Liberia

Liberia previously served on the Security Council in 1961, but the December presidency will be its first time chairing the body. The 81st United Nations General Assembly began September 8, with President Joseph Boakai expected to deliver his third address during the General Debate, which begins September 22.

Jallah Barbu, executive director of the Office for the Establishment of the War and Economic Crimes Court, recently urged Boakai to recall lawmakers from their annual constituency break to act on the legislation.

Six proposals involving a War and Economic Crimes Court and a National Anti-Corruption Court are before the Legislature. They include proposals from the Liberian National Bar Association and a civil society coalition led by the Independent National Commission on Human Rights ; separate proposals from Senate President Pro Tempore Nyonblee Karnga-Lawrence and Senator Joseph Jallah; and two bills from the government’s court office.

Boakai reenergized the process when he renewed the Office’s mandate in May and later submitted its bills to the Legislature. But lawmakers went on their annual constituency break in July without approving legislation.

Before the recess, the Senate Judiciary Committee began consultations aimed at harmonizing the proposals, while more than 40 House members participated in a two-day technical session in Buchanan in June.

Some proposals have raised concerns among justice advocates over issues including the role of international experts and the appeals process. Senator Jallah has suggested international lawyers could serve as “consultants to Liberians” , rather than take direct roles.

“The final bill should include all benchmarks of fair, independent, meaningful and credible trials: crimes and modes of liability in line with international standards,” Michelle Reyes Milk, senior international justice counsel at Human Rights Watch, wrote in Just Security, a nonpartisan law and policy journal based at New York University School of Law. She also called for “full guarantees of due process for defendants” and “genuine participation and protection for victims and witnesses.”

Weah said Liberia’s Security Council role could showcase the country’s progress since the wars. He pointed to the success of international peacekeeping and the peaceful resolution of the closely fought 2023 presidential election as signs of the country’s resilience.

But he warned that sustaining that progress requires Liberia to confront how its wars are remembered and taught to younger generations.

“We have no public memorials. We have not agreed on a historical text on the war to teach kids in school,” Weah said. “And so much of what the children learn that’s passed for history is mostly the opinions of history teachers, is the opinions of civic teachers in school, and that’s dangerous.”

Weah said museums, memorials and other forms of public education could give younger Liberians a more structured understanding of the country’s past and help address violent memories transmitted from one generation to another.

Liberia has made some steps up efforts to address memorialization. A high-level government delegation has returned from a United Nations Development Program-supported study mission to Rwanda and South Africa in late August and early September, where it examined approaches to reconciliation, memorialization, peacebuilding and preserving national history. The lessons are expected to inform President Boakai’s proposed Liberia Peace, Reconciliation and Memorial Museum, envisioned as a national institution to preserve the country’s history, promote reconciliation and strengthen civic education.

TRC’s Controversial Decision to Sanction President Johnson Sirleaf Remains a Point of Debate

But Liberia’s efforts to establish an authoritative account of the wars have themselves generated controversy. More than 15 years after the Truth and Reconciliation Commission issued its final report, parts of its findings remain contested.

The commission recommended a 30-year public-office ban for a number of people, including then-President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, because it said they had been associated with former warring factions. In 2011, Liberia’s Supreme Court struck down the sanction as unconstitutional , finding that it had been imposed without due process.

Liberian civilians flee Paynesville amid fighting between rebel forces and the Armed Forces of Liberia on Aug. 10, 1990, during the country’s first civil war. Credit: Pascal Guyot/AFP via Getty Images.

In testimony to the U.S. Congress in June 1990 , as Taylor’s rebellion was terrorizing people across the country, Sirleaf portrayed Taylor’s uprising as a broad-based struggle, saying people, “many of them children,” had joined what she called a “struggle for freedom,” and describing the rebellion as an opportunity to transform Liberia’s political system. (Taylor’s alleged use of child soldiers was seen as a particularly egregious act that was copied by other warring factions in years to come.)

Weah argued that the commission’s treatment of Sirleaf contributed to her reluctance to champion implementation of its recommendations and questioned whether the report sufficiently established the extent of her involvement in the conflict.

“I think she felt embarrassed. She felt stigmatized,” Weah said. “Before you mention the names of people in report, there has to be a duty of care to make sure that your work is thorough, is rigorous. It can stand up to basic scrutiny.”

John Stewart, a commissioner who chaired the committee that wrote the TRC report, rejected Weah’s criticism. He said Sirleaf was sanctioned because commissioners concluded that her testimony about when she distanced herself from Charles Taylor conflicted with evidence they had obtained.

“We did not do so because we wanted to embarrass Sirleaf,” Stewart said. “We did so because we wanted to be fair to all others. And her being president was no exception to the rule.”

The disagreement underscores the difficulty Liberia still faces in establishing a broadly accepted account of its violent past — the problem Weah says younger generations should not be left to navigate alone.

Against that backdrop, Weah recently co-launched Liberia: Remembering the Future with British journalist Gerry Naughton. The podcast, airing on 10 radio stations across Liberia, examines the country’s history, its transition from war to peace and its election to the Security Council.

Weah said the project aims to provide historical context and clarification for Liberians, particularly younger people, as well as international audiences seeking to understand the country as its global profile rises.

This story was a collaboration with New Narratives as part of the Investigating Liberia project. Funding was provided by the U.N. Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights and the European Union. The funders had no say in the story’s content.

World.title: SpoonTV CEO Details Cooperation With U.S. Investigators That Led to Reduced Sentence and Early Release
World.content:
Monrovia — SpoonTV CEO Stanton Witherspoon has offered a detailed account of how his decision to cooperate with U.S. federal investigators ultimately helped secure his release from prison after he was convicted in a multimillion-dollar scheme involving fraudulent nursing diplomas and transcripts.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

Witherspoon, who pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud, was sentenced in November 2023 to 41 months in prison and three years of supervised release.

But on September 9, 2026, U.S. District Judge Rodney Smith granted a motion by federal prosecutors to reduce the sentence to time served, eliminating the supervised-release requirement and dismissing the remaining counts against him.

The reduction was granted under Rule 35(b) of the Federal Rules of Criminal Procedure, which allows prosecutors to seek a reduced sentence for a defendant who provides substantial assistance to the government after sentencing.

Witherspoon said Thursday that his cooperation was not simply a strategy to obtain a shorter sentence, but a decision he made after his lawyer and one of his Spoon Talk colleagues advised him that cooperating early could benefit his case and help investigators pursue others involved in the alleged fraud.

‘Cooperate’

Recounting the events on Spoon Talk, Witherspoon said panelist Abdullah Kiatamba advised him in 2023 to consider cooperating with investigators.

According to Witherspoon, Kiatamba told him that he was not making a judgment about his guilt or innocence but was speaking from his understanding of the U.S. legal system.

“He said, no matter what you do, I’m going to talk to you from experience. Cooperate,” Witherspoon recalled.

Witherspoon said he initially questioned the advice.

“I said, what are you talking about? He said, Stanton, I’m not saying you are guilty. I’m not saying you are not guilty. But I know the system. Talk to your lawyer.”

He said he followed the advice and consulted his attorney, who also recommended that he cooperate with investigators at an early stage.

According to Witherspoon, his lawyer warned that delaying cooperation could diminish its value if other defendants cooperated first.

“Every other day, the lawyer would say, Stanton, if you’re the last to cooperate, you are not needed. If you must cooperate, cooperate now,” he recalled.

Witherspoon said his lawyer subsequently explained the cooperation process and its potential implications to him step by step.

What Prosecutors Say He Provided

The government’s court filings indicate that Witherspoon’s cooperation went beyond simply providing information about his own conduct.

According to prosecutors, he was interviewed by agents from the FBI and the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General about individuals involved in nursing-school fraud schemes.

Prosecutors said his cooperation contributed to cases against several defendants, including Carleen Noreus, Cimoyne Alves, Lemuel Pierre and Cleophat Tanis.

Witherspoon testified against Noreus, who operated a separate fraudulent nursing program known as Carleen Health Institute. Following his testimony, prosecutors said Noreus pleaded guilty to wire fraud and money-laundering conspiracy charges and is awaiting sentencing.

Witherspoon also signed an affidavit identifying nursing students who received fraudulent degrees and transcripts. That information was provided to the National Council of State Boards of Nursing so state licensing authorities could take remedial action.

‘I Was a Star Witness’

Witherspoon described himself as a key witness for the government, saying investigators needed information and supporting documents that he possessed because of his involvement in the nursing-school business.

He said he had recruited students for multiple schools and therefore had knowledge of people involved in the operation.

“Now they have so many big, big people that were involved in this thing. And a lot of them came to me to recruit students for them,” Witherspoon said.

He said investigators already knew some of the individuals but needed additional evidence.

“The government knew them, but the government needed supporting documents from me.”

According to Witherspoon, one of the principal defendants initially refused to cooperate, leading prosecutors to call him to testify.

“I had to take the stand for the government. For four months, the woman couldn’t break. And the government called a star witness. And I was a star witness.”

Witherspoon said that after he testified, the defendant subsequently agreed to plead guilty.

“After I testified, the next day, the woman begged for the plea. She’s scheduled to be sentenced. It’s a public record.”

The account corresponds with prosecutors’ description of Witherspoon’s cooperation in the case involving Noreus.

A $5.17 Million Fraud

Federal prosecutors said Witherspoon was a 50% owner of Siena Education Center LLC and Siena College of Health II LLC and was also the founder and president of Nursing Education Resource Center LLC.

Prosecutors alleged that Witherspoon, working with Rene Bernadel, Alfred Sellu and Cimoyne Alves, used NERC to recruit and fraudulently train aspiring nurses.

He later worked with Eunide Sanon and Siena to provide fake nursing diplomas and transcripts, which students allegedly used to obtain fraudulent certification as registered nurses or licensed practical nurses.

Witherspoon was held responsible for approximately $5.17 million in losses.

His total offense level was calculated at 26, with a criminal history category of I, producing a federal sentencing guideline range of 63 to 78 months. He ultimately received a 41-month sentence.

‘I Wanted This to Stop’

Witherspoon said his decision to cooperate was motivated by more than his own legal circumstances.

He said he wanted to expose the broader operation and help prevent others from being harmed by fraudulent nursing credentials.

“I had to do it not because I was fighting for myself. I had to do it because I wanted this to stop,” he said.

“I had to do it because I want the system to be right.”

Witherspoon said the information he possessed was extensive and involved conversations with professionals and others connected to the business.

He also thanked his attorney for guiding him through the cooperation process.

Prosecutors Backed Sentence Reduction

The government’s motion to reduce Witherspoon’s sentence was supported by prosecutors and investigators from the FBI and HHS-OIG, who cited the scope of his cooperation.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Christopher J. Clark filed the motion on behalf of the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of Florida.

Judge Rodney Smith subsequently ordered Witherspoon released on time served and removed the three-year supervised-release component of his original sentence.

The remaining counts against him—Counts 2 through 6 and Count 8—were dismissed.

For Witherspoon, the sequence of events—from advice to cooperate, through interviews and testimony, to the government’s Rule 35(b) motion—ultimately culminated in his release.

“Yes, indeed, I cooperated with the government. And that’s why I took a plea. And today, the result of the plea is that Stanton is a free man,” he said.

He ended his account by thanking his lawyer and those who supported him during his legal battle.

World.title: Liberia: Ngafuan Highlights Gains in Health, Education and Energy, Admits More Work Remains
World.content:
Monrovia – In an appearance on the state-owned Liberia Broadcasting System, Liberia’s Minister of Finance and Development Planning, Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, walked Liberians through progress in social delivery, especially in roads, education, health, and energy.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

Minister Ngafuan told the audience how the government has been able to make life-touching progress over a little over two years, though he admitted that the government is still confronted with huge challenges amid competing priorities.

US$1.2 Billion Domestic Revenue On Course

He disclosed that, through the collaboration of the MFDP and the Liberia Revenue Authority, the country is nearing a US$1B revenue collection within days.

Health And Education

The Minister asserted that drug supply in public hospitals has improved compared to the past.

“There are more drugs in the hospitals today than there were yesterday. There could be one or two issues, but I am saying that, in comparison with the past, the situation is better,” he stated.

He announced the ongoing total construction of the C.H. Rennie Hospital in Kakata, Margibi County.

It could be recalled that the hospital was gutted by fire during the latter days of the last administration.

As it stands, he revealed that the work has advanced to the roof level.

In the educational sector, Ngafuan announced the ongoing renovations of several public high schools across the country, including the famous Williams V.S. Tubman High, Newport High, Botsweins High, G.W. Gibson, among others, as well as the total renovation of the state-run University of Liberia (UL).

In addition to the rehabilitation works, he disclosed the government’s efforts for the construction and equipping of more than 100 schools for foundational learning across the country.

“Myself, I am a product of public schools, or what we referred to as government schools; I’m a product of Botsweins, BWI and the University of Liberia. We are producing and reproducing our young people through these schools. We are creating excellence in those schools,” he points out.

“Sometimes people make the mistake of trying to grade the government as if it has been in office for five or six years. We have not even reached the halfway point. January 22, 2027, will mark the halfway point of this government. If you grade a two-year and eight-month government as if it has been there for six years, that tells us that we are strong and that we are on course.”

Economy And Budget Procurement

Ngafuan disclosed that President Joseph Boakai will chair an Economic Management Team meeting with the Central Bank governor to review the economy and the new budget.

He indicated that implementation of the US$1.2 billion FY2026 budget is on course and that allocations are increasing for key sectors.

“We are giving more money to Public Works. We are giving more money to education. We are giving more money to almost all the sectors,” the Minister indicated, adding that LBS has also received increased subsidy.

The Minister also announced upcoming procurement reforms.

“We are on an e-procurement platform, but as good as technology is, it has brought some challenges, which we are going to address. In the next week or two, there are going to be some announcements on practical measures that we are going to take to expedite procurement,” he said.

Salary And Pension

Addressing civil servant concerns, Ngafuan asserted that the government is approaching salary increment holistically rather than through individual interventions.

“President Boakai has established a Salary Structure Review Committee chaired by the Civil Service Agency Director General, with MFDP and the Ministry of State as members. The numbers, based on the revenue situation, will determine what will be done at the appropriate time.

He said there have been some top-ups in 2025 for the health sector, where some workers received more than double their salaries, and interventions in the security sector, integrity institutions, and the judiciary.

“With the Supreme Court judges and magistrates, we are almost there,” he added.

On pensions, Ngafuan explained the budget will tackle uncertainty around NASSCORP remittances, stressing that: ” Individuals retiring to some places drag retirement. We intend to change that. We want a situation where people will look forward to retirement.”

Accordingly, touching on minimum wage, the Minister argued Liberia compares favorably regionally.

“A minimum wage, especially in Liberia… Do you know that the minimum wage in Liberia is better than Ghana’s? It is better than Sierra Leone’s. It is better than Nigeria’s. I think we need to do more, but we also have to appreciate where we are as a country.” he

Energy Projects

Speaking further,

Ngafuan narrated that the government, with support from partners including the World Bank and the EU, is funding electrification in several counties.

He named River Gee, Grand Kru and Sinoe, and cited ongoing work in Greenville, River Cess and Gbarnga.

“The Rural Renewable Energy Agency, headed by Samuel Nagbe, is working on that. Lights will soon be available,” declared.

The Minister’s comments come amid public debate over the pace of service delivery and the impact of the $1.2 billion budget.

He urged patience, stating that Boakai’s administration deserves credit for methodical reforms.

“For someone to say that this is not progress and that the minister is just talking is unfair. I don’t talk just because I want to talk. We have been working. I agree that we are not there yet completely. But if we were traveling the road from here to Gbarnga, Bong County, I would say that we are somewhere there in Totota,” added the Finance Ministry boss.

World.title: Zambia-Mozambique JPC concludes
World.content:
The 14th Session of the Mozambique–Zambia Joint Permanent Commission (JPC) on Defence and Security, which commenced on September 9 in Maputo, Mozambique, concluded yesterday, September 11, 2026.

The Commission expressed deep appreciation to Presidents Daniel Chapo of Mozambique and Hakainde Hichilema of Zambia for their support in convening this important session, noting that it underscores the strong and historic relations between the two nations.

The Commission also reviewed political, socio‑economic, and security developments since the 13th Session in Chilanga, Zambia, noting with satisfaction that the political situation in both countries has remained relatively stable.

The Zambian delegation, which was led by Ministry of Defence Permanent Secretary Maambo Haamaundu, thanked the Mozambican government and its people for their warm hospitality.

As the session closed, Zambia extended an invitation to Mozambique to participate in the 15th Session, scheduled to be held in Zambia in 2027, with details to be communicated through diplomatic channels.

This was contained in a joint press statement issued to the media by the Republic of Mozambique and Zambia Joint Permanent Commission on Defence and Security.

World.title: Government commits to mobilise funds to complete Matumbo Boarding Secondary School
World.content:
Government is set to mobilise funds to facilitate the completion of the construction of Matumbo Boarding Secondary School in Shiwang’andu District in Muchinga Province.

Muchinga Province Permanent Secretary Tuesday Bwalya says government is committed to ensuring that the project, which commenced in 2012, is completed and becomes operational in due course.

Dr Bwalya noted that construction works at the school have been progressing at a slow pace over the years due to inadequate funding, adding that the government has now prioritised the completion of the project as part of its agenda to improve the education sector in the area.

He said works at the site have continued despite the delays and that efforts to mobilise the required resources are und He said works at the site have continued despite the delays, and that efforts to mobilise the required resources are underway.erway.

“We are very delighted and appreciative of such efforts by the New Dawn Government and our colleagues from the Ministry of Education, but I just want to appeal to them to see how we can expedite these works by ensuring that we give enough resources to our contractor,” he said.

Dr Bwalya also commended the quality of work being undertaken at the project, saying once the school completed it will provide modern infrastructure for learners in the area.

And Shanghai Contractors Site Foreman Alex Sitolo, disclosed that the project is currently at 70 percent completion stage.

Mr Sitolo mentioned that the project was initially scheduled for completion in September this year but erratic funding had affected the planned completion date.

He said timely availability of resources would enable the contractor to complete the remaining works.

“We are grateful that with the government’s intervention now, we will be able to finish this project when funds are quickly mobilised,” he said.

Meanwhile, Acting Matumbo Secondary School Headteacher, Lesa Bwalya has thanked the government for prioritising the completion of the project which had stalled for several years.

Mr Bwalya said the completion of the school will help accommodate the increasing number of learners returning to school following the introduction of the free education Law.

He highlighted that the strategic location of the school would also enable it to attract learners from surrounding areas where education infrastructure remains limited.

World.title: Proposed Multi-use logistics facility to boost rail transport business
World.content:
Zambia Railways Limited Acting Manager for the Central Region, Misheck Banda, says the proposed construction and operation of a multi‑use logistics facility in Lusaka’s Lilayi area by AGL Zambia Limited will help boost rail transport business opportunities in the country.

Mr Banda noted that most of the bulk cargo that AGL Zambia Limited will be handling is expected to move by rail.

He was speaking during a stakeholder scoping meeting on the proposed construction and operation of a multi‑use logistics facility in Lusaka’s Lilayi area by AGL Zambia Limited.

Mr Banda explained that his organisation is partnering with AGL Zambia Limited to transport bulk cargo using the rail line.

“AGL Limited will be dealing with bulk cargo, some of it will be transported by road but most of it will be going by rail, hence the partnering with AGL,” he said.

Meanwhile, Mr Banda has bemoaned increased encroachments by developers on the Zambia Railways Limited reserve lands.

He explained that the organization’s reserve land is meant for future developments and has since appealed to would be developers to desist from buying land meant for the organization’s future development.

“You all agree with me that no one has ever bought land from Zambia Railways Limited and the idea of Zambia Railways not selling land is for future projects like what AGL is bringing on board,” he explained.

A local resident, Zimba Lickson, has appealed to the Zambia Railways Limited, to find ways of helping him and other affected families with the issue of encroachments on the Zambia Railways Limited reserved land.

And Lusaka District Commissioner Rosa Kayuni said government remains committed to working with the private sector in delivering development.

Ms Kayuni said this in a speech read for her by Lusaka District Administrative officer, O’Neill Chiiya.

She explained that the proposed project will help bring massive development in the district and the country at large.

“This development will not only provide employment for our local people but produce revenue for the Government through taxes as well,” she appreciated.

World.title: Three arrested for repacking and selling underweight fertiliser in Nchelenge
World.content:
Police in Nchelenge District have arrested three people for allegedly repacking and selling underweight fertilizer meant for the Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP).

‎ The trio were apprehended around 02:00 hours on September 11, 2026, following a tip‑off from a member of the public that some individuals were repacking and selling suspected underweight fertilizer in the Kafimbwa area of Chief Kambwali in Nchelenge District.

‎ Luapula Province Commanding Officer Lucky Munkondya has confirmed the development, identifying the suspects as Japhet Biala, 26, a Depot Manager at Champion Agro World’s Nchelenge Depot; Kabeke Darius, 22, a motorbike rider of Dyson Village; and Mubanga Gregory, 23, also a motorbike rider from Kabosha Village.

‎ Ms Munkondya stated that police recovered more than 100 bags of Compound D fertilizer and over 200 bags of Urea fertilizer, all suspected to have been repacked into underweight bags.

‎ She said the fertilizer, which belongs to United Capital Fertilizer, was seized and taken to Nchelenge Police Station for further investigations.

‎”On August 28, 2026, Biala received a consignment of 797 bags of 50-kilogramme Urea fertilizer intended for FISP. It is alleged that Biala, together with his accomplices, subsequently unpacked the fertilizer and repacked it into additional bags of reduced weight, which were sold to local farmers for cash,” Ms Munkondya said.

‎ The Police Commissioner said the suspects are in police custody while investigations into the matter are ongoing.

World.title: The President Holds the key, as one Before him did
World.content:
“Healing will not come from the police, the gazette or the courts. It comes from State House. President Hichilema has walked out of this exact situation once before. He is the only person in Zambia who knows what it costs from the inside, and the only one who can end it from the outside”

Six Zambians lost their passports on Friday. The gazette gave the same reason for all of them, national security, and nothing else. No conduct named, no provision of the law cited, no chance to answer first.

They are Emmanuel Mwamba, a former ambassador; Dr Sishuwa Sishuwa, a historian; Binwell Mpundu and Emmanuel Jay Banda, former Members of Parliament; Kaizer Zulu, a former State House aide; and Lillian Mutambo, a blogger. A passport is not only for travel. It is how a person proves who they are at a bank, at a border, at any counter that matters, which is why Amnesty International says taking it leaves someone effectively stateless. What the six share is not a conviction. It is a habit of criticising the Government.

That same day, Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu were charged with sedition at Kabwe. Their lawyer Sakwiba Sikota explained the charge. Mundubile posted a video saying his party had won on its own count and asked the Electoral Commission of Zambia to release the results. Zulu called him president. For that, a seven-year maximum.

Every losing candidate believes for a fortnight that he was robbed. Mature democracies answer with figures, not with a charge sheet.

Why a second charge

Both men were already in Mukobeko on treason, which is non-bailable and tried only in the High Court. They could not be held more tightly. Sedition changes nothing about their detention today. It changes what happens tomorrow.

Treason is the hardest charge in our law to prove. It needs an overt act, a conspiracy, evidence that survives cross-examination. Sedition needs a video, and the video exists.

So this column will say plainly what many Zambians have already worked out. The State does not expect the treason case to stand. The second charge is there so the first does not have to. Whichever way the evidence falls, the two men who came closest to power in August stay out of public life for years, and 2031 arrives without them.

Acting Attorney-General Marshal Muchende rejects that framing. “Zambia has no prisoners of conscience or political prisoners,” he said, answering UN Special Rapporteur Gina Romero, who called the charges concocted. He argues the accused face treason and terrorism offences over alleged sponsorship of unlawful paramilitary training, that the Constitution grants no immunity on grounds of political status, and that Government treats the arrests as matters of national security.

Every one of those propositions is sound. Not one answers the question the public is asking, which is when the evidence will be tested. Two weeks on, neither matter has a court date.

A death, and three accounts of it

Former Cabinet Minister Mutotwe Kafwaya was shot during the Kabulonga operation. Government first rejected reports that he had been shot at all, Defence Permanent Secretary Maambo Haamaundu saying hospital checks showed no record of him at Maina Soko. His family had no official word for five days. His wife Dinis Ng’andu Kafwaya went to the High Court for habeas corpus to force the authorities to produce him.

On 19 August, Inspector General Graphel Musamba confirmed Kafwaya was the unidentified man fatally wounded in an exchange of gunfire, police saying a Joint Task Force came under fire and returned it. Mundubile says he was present and that Kafwaya was shot inside his bedroom beside him.

The Law Association of Zambia said it was gravely concerned and called for an independent probe, pointing to inconsistencies between what emerged later and earlier statements by three permanent secretaries. A complaint has since gone to The Hague seeking an investigation into the chain of command behind the use of lethal force. Chief Mpepo asked something simpler: show the nation the weapons, as has always been the practice when such a find is made.

A man is dead, three senior officials gave accounts that do not sit together, and a widow had to sue to learn where her husband was. A month has passed without an explanation.

The count, honestly stated

Hichilema was declared winner with 60.49 per cent against Mundubile’s 37.87, a gap of more than a million ballots. Trouble in a handful of constituencies does not close a margin that size and nobody should pretend it does.

But a vote must also deliver a process the loser can see was clean, and process failures poison confidence whether or not they change a result.

On 14 August the ECZ suspended counting nationwide, saying staff were being attacked and ballot papers stolen in some instances, without saying by whom. Halting an entire national count was never properly explained.

In Mandevu, Chief Electoral Officer Brown Kasaro confirmed that unknown individuals attacked the totalling centre, destroyed the transmission kits and fled with all documentation, leaving the returning officer unable to declare the result. A fresh election was ordered. Videos afterwards appeared to show ballots in drainages and others burnt, and police recovered a stolen ECZ laptop.

The former ambassador among the six goes further, alleging that UPND cadres led by a man he names as Kalufyanya attacked polling stations in Chaisa, Lilanda and Chawama and destroyed thousands of votes, with similar scenes at Bwacha North in Kabwe. Those are his allegations. Nobody has been charged and the man he names has not answered them, which is why they need investigating rather than leaving to circulate. Citizens First’s Steven Mwale made a related point, that the commission should have pursued those responsible instead of making a whole constituency vote again.

Note the sequence. A man alleges ballot destruction, names names, calls for a fresh national poll. Weeks later his passport is cancelled on grounds nobody will explain. Those events may be unconnected. Government has said nothing to establish that they are.

Observers did not find the election unfree, and the record should be given whole. One regional mission led by former Botswana President Mokgweetsi Masisi found the process transparent, fair, legal and peaceful on the whole. Others found it free and transparent but not fair, citing misuse of state resources and restrictions on opposition campaigning. Reuters reported that two independent observer reports flagged indications the winning count may have been inflated. Hichilema denies any fraud.

None of that settles much. Missions watch polling stations for a day. They do not audit a count or follow the chain of custody of a ballot box, and they are guests of the state they assess. Their word is useful, never final. Nor is a telegram: the congratulations from UN Secretary-General António Guterres are a courtesy extended to every re-elected head of state on earth, and treating that as an audit is a generosity nobody in State House would extend to a critic.

The courthouse door

There is one proper place to settle all of this. Article 105 gives a losing candidate seven days from the declaration to petition the Constitutional Court. Hichilema was declared on 18 August. The window ran to the 24th.

On 24 August the courts were closed.

The High Court in Lusaka was sealed, and the Supreme Court building that houses the Constitutional Court, and several local courts, and High Court premises in Ndola, Chipata and Livingstone. In Chipata armed officers let nobody in. A memorandum from the judiciary’s chief administrator, seen by Human Rights Watch and Reuters, told staff not to report “for security reasons” and promised guidance once the situation was contained. Police called it an intelligence-led preventive measure and said no more.

Human Rights Watch said the closure came without credible explanation and blocked any challenge to the result. LAZ recorded concern at heavily armed military personnel around court premises. One lawyer told the BBC that three armed men stopped his vehicle and ordered him from the area.

No petition was lodged across a counter, because the counters were shut. An attempt was made to transmit one electronically, and whether that counts as a valid filing is now itself before the Constitutional Court. The inauguration went ahead on 1 September.

State House denies the President ordered the closure and points out that the judiciary is independent. That denial should be taken seriously, because there is no evidence he ordered it. It also sharpens the question rather than answering it. If the judiciary is independent, then an independent judiciary shut its own doors on the single day in five years when they were required to be open, and has still not said why.

Professor Cephas Lumina argues the arithmetic was wrong anyway, that seven days from 18 August runs to the 25th, and points to the Constitutional Court Rules of 2026, which require the Registry to open for an election petition from half past eight until six, including on days the courts are otherwise shut. Those rules exist so that this cannot happen.

The judge who advised

Then came the part that should trouble every lawyer in this country.

Former Constitutional Court judge Anne Mwewa Sitali was taken from her home at night, held at Richard Kachingwe Police Post and accused of conspiring to commit a felony. The alleged felony was the legal advice she gave to lawyers preparing the petition. She applied for habeas corpus and has since been granted bail.

Read that slowly. A former judge of the Constitutional Court was arrested over advice about how to approach the Constitutional Court. If that stands, no lawyer here can safely advise on a presidential petition again, and Article 105 becomes a right nobody will help you exercise. A right you cannot get advice about is not a right. It is an ornament.

Her history with that bench gives it an edge no columnist could invent. In 2016 she was one of three judges who dismissed Hichilema’s own presidential petition on the ground that time to hear it had lapsed. In October 2024 he removed her from the court along with the other two in that majority, Mungeni Mulenga and Palan Mulonda. In September 2026 she was arrested for helping someone else petition against him.

Three events across ten years, and this column does not claim one hand joined them. It records that they happened, in that order, to that woman.

She is not alone. Opposition sources and rights monitors put the number arrested since 13 August above three hundred, a figure Government has not confirmed and has not answered with one of its own.

A man may be wrong about an election. Thousands may think he is wrong. He is still entitled to be wrong in a courtroom, on the record, with the figures before a judge, advised by a lawyer who is not afraid of the cells. Close that door and you do not silence the allegation. You guarantee it outlives you.

Zambia has done this better

In April 2017 an opposition leader was arrested for treason after his convoy failed to give way to the presidential motorcade. He spent four months inside and his case was never heard.

Catholic bishops led by Archbishop Telesphore Mpundu pushed for talks. When that stalled, Commonwealth Secretary-General Patricia Scotland came to Lusaka, met both men and secured a commitment to dialogue. It began with the opposition leader walking out of prison. Days later the State dropped the case.

The man released was Hakainde Hichilema. The President who released him was Edgar Lungu, under no obligation to do it. Nine years later Hichilema decorated Scotland and called that charge politically motivated. He was right, and he knows better than any man alive what a treason count is worth when the State has no intention of trying it.

The cases are not identical and pretending otherwise would be dishonest. A motorcade on a rural road is not a raid where weapons are alleged and a man died. The 2026 allegations are far graver and, if proved, deserve the full weight of the law. That is the point. Neither was ever tried, and an untried charge proves nothing, grave or trivial.

Healing is his to give

None of this establishes that the count was falsified, and this column does not claim it. It establishes that serious questions were raised, that the commission confirmed ballots were stolen, that the courts shut on the day those questions could have been filed, that the judge who advised on the filing was arrested, and that Government has answered with prosecutions instead of evidence.

Confidence is not built by a count alone. It is built by what a government does in the weeks after. Ours has cancelled passports without reasons, charged speech as sedition, left eighteen people in a maximum security prison with no trial date, and let the one constitutional avenue for challenging a result close without explanation.

In 2017 a president opened a prison door and dropped a case he could have pursued. He gained nothing by it. The country calmed, and the man he released went on to lead it. That door is now on the other side of the corridor.

The charges can be tested in open court or discontinued in the public interest, and either is lawful and honourable. The Kafwaya shooting can be independently investigated, the inconsistent statements explained and the weapons shown. The court closure can be explained by whoever ordered it. The case against Justice Sitali can be dropped. The figures can be published constituency by constituency.

What cannot hold is silence.

Healing will not come from the police, the gazette or the courts. It comes from State House. President Hichilema has walked out of this exact situation once before. He is the only person in Zambia who knows what it costs from the inside, and the only one who can end it from the outside

By Clement Haanzunga

World.title: Anglican Diocese launches malaria prevention, control initiative in Rufunsa
World.content:
The Anglican Diocese of Lusaka has launched a cross-border malaria initiative in Munyeta area of Rufunsa district in Lusaka Province which is aimed at reducing malaria incidences and strengthening community participation in the fight against the disease.

The initiative, which was launched at Munyeta Rural Health Centre, brought together government officials, traditional leaders, health workers, the church and community members in a renewed effort to prevent malaria and control it.

Rufunsa District Commissioner, Richard Mabena, who officiated at the event, commended the Anglican Diocese of Lusaka and its partners for complementing government efforts in the fight against malaria.

“Government appreciates the role being played by the church and other stakeholders in supporting efforts to end malaria as it cannot achieve this role alone,” Mr Mabena said.

He said malaria has for a long time cast a heavy shadow over communities by affecting economic productivity and keeping children away from school.

Mr Mabena added that the initiative is particularly important as local people play a critical role in the implementation of programmes and policies at household level.

And Chief Bunda Bunda, Chimapepe II, welcomed the initiative, stressing that the involvement of community members would strengthen the fight against malaria.

The traditional leader said initiatives that empower communities with knowledge and practical measures to prevent malaria can contribute significantly to reducing the disease.

Meanwhile, the Provincial and District Health Offices have also welcomed the programme, noting that Rufunsa has recorded high incidences of malaria in the province.

Chief Environmental Health Officer Kelvin Mwakapushi, who represented the Provincial Health Director, said the launch was more than a ceremony as it was an initiative of strengthening community-level malaria prevention, early identification of fever and referral of severe cases.

Mr Mwakapushi disclosed that in 2025, Lusaka Province recorded 69,868 confirmed malaria cases, making the disease the seventh leading cause of morbidity in the region with incidences increasing from 17.29 percent in 2024 to 21.1 percent in 2025.

“Rufunsa recorded the highest confirmed malaria incidences among the districts in the province and also recorded an inpatient malaria case fatality rate of 29.85 percent,” he said.

And Rufunsa District Health Director, Peter Kakonde, welcomed the initiative and support of the Anglican Diocese of Lusaka and pledged unwavering institutional support to the partnership.

Programme Coordinator, Constance Njovu, said the initiative is aimed at strengthening community participation in malaria prevention and control.

Canon Charles Thomas, who represented the Anglican Diocese of Lusaka Archbishop Albert Chama, reaffirmed the church’s commitment to complementing government efforts in the health sector.

World.title: Over 5,000 Kasenengwa farmers redeem FISP inputs
World.content:
More than 5,000 farmers in Kasenengwa district in Eastern Province have redeemed their farming inputs under the Farmer Input Support Programme (FISP) ahead of the 2026/2027 farming season.

This is out of the targeted 14,038 FISP beneficiaries.

Kasenengwa District Agriculture Coordinator, Adamson Mwale, told the media that a total of 5, 227 farmers have redeemed their inputs in readiness for the next farming season.

“Over 5,000 farmers have managed to redeem their farm inputs but we expect this number to steadily rise in the coming weeks,” he stated.

Mr Mwale revealed that out of this figure, 5, 063 farmers have fully redeemed their inputs while 214 have partially redeemed.

He also indicated that a sum of 7,994 Authority to Deposit (ATDs) have so far been issued to enable farmers to make their K400 contributions.

He disclosed that of this figure, a total of 7, 783 farmers have already made their deposits

World.title: Limulunga councillors, council chairperson urged to work for communities
World.content:
Western Province Local Government Officer, Nickson Nkwapu, has urged newly elected Councillors and the Council Chairperson to put aside personal interests and prioritise the needs and aspirations of the people they represent.

Mr Nkwapu said national development cannot be achieved if leaders fail to put the interests of their electorates first.

He said the government’s main agenda is to ensure that development reaches all parts of Western Province, hence the need for newly elected leaders to work together with communities and other stakeholders to achieve meaningful development.

Mr Nkwapu was speaking during the swearing in ceremony of the Limulunga Council Chairperson and councillors held at the Limulunga Town Council offices.

Speaking shortly after being sworn in, new Limulunga Council Chairperson, Muyunda Lubinda, assured the people in the district that improving health infrastructure would be among his priorities.

Mr Lubinda said improved health facilities would contribute to quality healthcare delivery and better the wellbeing of people in the district.

He also identified the improvement of the agricultural sector as another priority area, saying he would work closely with the Limulunga community to enhance agricultural productivity and improve the livelihoods of local people.

Meanwhile, Barotse Royal Establishment (BRE) Representative, Induna Namuyamba has expressed disappointment with some previous council leaders whom he accused of engaging in selfish activities at the expense of the people.

Induna Namuyamba has therefore urged the newly elected Councillors and the Council Chairperson to learn from the shortcomings of the previous leadership and ensure that their decisions are guided by the interests of the people.

He said the new council leadership should promote transparency, accountability and unity while working closely with the traditional leadership and communities to accelerate development in Limulunga district.

Thirteen (13) Councilors and Council Chairperson took oath in Limulunga district for them to have authority to execute their mandate.
