World.title: Kochi airport launches robot for enhanced passenger assistance and cultural promotion
World.content:
Cochin International Airport Limited (CIAL) has introduced robotic assistance as part of its efforts to enhance passenger services and convenience.

In the first phase, a passenger assistance robot has been deployed at Kalangan, the art museum located in the domestic security hold area. CIAL managing director S. Suhas inaugurated the service. The robot was developed for CIAL by Pune-based Kinetics Robotics.

The robot welcomes passengers, provides directions and real-time flight information, and guides them to boarding gates and other airport facilities. Passengers can also interact with it for travel-related assistance, including details on CIAL services, flight schedules, and gate numbers.

It will additionally promote Kerala’s cultural heritage by offering information on traditional art forms such as Kathakali and Ottanthullal, as well as the sculptures and artworks displayed at Kalangan. Passengers will be directed to the relevant exhibits.

In the next phase, CIAL plans to deploy passenger assistance robots in the airport’s check-in halls. The operator is also exploring the introduction of delivery robots that could bring food and other products directly to passengers inside the terminal, according to a statement issued by the airport.

CIAL executive director Santhosh Poovattil, head of commercial Manoj P. Joseph, and Kinetics Robotics representative Jignesh Nair were present.

World.title: Slum settlement in south Delhi veiled for BRICS Summit
World.content:
With the BRICS Summit underway in Delhi, a slum settlement located along the Nelson Mandela Marg and Munirka Marg in south Delhi’s Vasant Vihar has been covered with white-purple banners. The banners went up on Thursday night (September 10, 2026), two days ahead of the summit, to “hide the slums” from foreign dignitaries visiting Delhi during the summit, residents said.

Known as ‘Coolie Camp’, the settlement houses about 281 households, according to 2012 data from the Delhi Urban Shelter Improvement Board (DUSIB). It’s situated a few kilometres away from the DLF Promenade mall in Vasant Kunj, and is surrounded by markets, parks, and government housing. The entire stretch along the Nelson Mandela Marg and Munirka Marg has been covered by 10-ft.-high curtains, with entry and exit restricted to two points, which has led to problems for them, residents said.

“This is not the first time this area has been covered like this. Even earlier, in 2023, when the G20 Summit happened, the basti (slum) was covered with huge green curtains,” Manoj, a vendor and a resident in the area, said.

While the sanitation and beautification of the national capital is underway in full swing, the settlement housing sanitation workers has been veiled.

“Jaise kooda-kachra dhak dete hain, ese hi hamein bhi kooda samajh kar dhak diya hoga [just like we cover garbage, they must have thought of us as garbage, too],” Manisha, a resident, said.

Residents expressed exasperation with the government’s action in covering up slum settlements rather than investing in welfare programmes that uplift communities from poverty. “If the government has a problem with poverty, why isn’t anything being done to eradicate it?” Golu, a sanitation worker, said.

The ‘Coolie Camp’ comprises compact multi-storeyed huts, two-foot-wide lanes, open drains, and common water taps and washrooms. The curtains have covered the settlement, and the roads have been cleaned up, but an overflowing garbage bin continues to be kept right outside the curtain-wall, with garbage littered around it.

“We have been facing difficulty bringing in our carts and vehicles since these curtains have come up,” Mr. Manoj said. “We are not taking out our carts as we are afraid the police and MCD (Municipal Corporation of Delhi) officials might seize them. Due to this, income has dropped over the last three days,” he said.

The area houses scores of tenants who pay at least ₹3,000-4,000 per month as rent. “Our earnings are anyway less. With movement and income restricted, we have to be careful about our expenses, too,” Shivani, a domestic worker, said.

“Why do the politicians come to us asking for votes with their hands joined during elections if this is what they think of us — people who need to be hidden so that their pride doesn’t get hurt? What happened to ‘jahan jhuggi wahin makaan’ [slum rehabilitation programme]?” Reena, a sanitation worker, said.

“Despite having lived here for generations, we are not considered residents. I have no Aadhaar card, no voter card, no other document that can help me establish myself as a resident of Delhi. Tomorrow, if the government decides to demolish the slum, where will I go?” Ms. Reena said.

World.title: Over 250 video clips, including porn, found on mobile and pendrive seized from Prajwal Revanna
World.content:
The forensic analysis of the mobile phone and pen drive seized from the prison cell, where former MP Prajwal Revanna was lodged, during the CCB raid, found over 250 video clips on the mobile phone and the pen drive. These reportedly include porn clips, OTT series and movies. While the mobile phone had 147 clips, the pen drive had over 100 videos.

Prajwal has reportedly told investigators that he used the phone mainly for making calls and denied any knowledge of the videos on these devices. He reportedly claimed that since the phone was circulated among several prisoners on a rotational basis, he did not know who had downloaded the videos and other material found on the device.

Prajwal reportedly admitted to contacting his mother, but said he spoke to her through a phone used by one of her maids rather than calling her directly. He also reportedly told investigators that he had spoken to a female friend. He is said to have used the mobile phone while in jail to make both regular calls and video calls.

The police are now scrutinising the call records and are likely to issue notices to persons whose numbers were contacted from the device. Investigators will question them to establish who used the phone and the nature of the calls.

Money paid

Prajwal reportedly paid around ₹1 lakh to get the phone which was supplied to him through many people including a prison staff who are now being arrested and questioned.

The police are also examining the mobile phone data and other digital evidence to establish who used the device at different times and the circumstances under which it was operated inside the jail.

World.title: Malaysian Prime Minister’s visit: stringent traffic restrictions in Kozhikode on September 13
World.content:
Extensive traffic restrictions will be in place in Kozhikode city and adjoining areas on Sunday (September 13) in connection with the visit of Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim, the traffic police have said.

The restrictions will come into effect from 5 p.m. on Sunday. Complete traffic restrictions will be enforced on the stretch from Vaidyarangadi and Ramanattukara to Malaparamba, and from Malaparamba towards Kunnamangalam and Mavoor.

Vehicles arriving from the Wayanad side will have to enter Kozhikode city through Thamarassery, Balussery, Nanminda and Eranhipalam. Vehicles from the Koduvally side will be diverted through Padinjarathilam-Kalarikkandi-Varattiyakk-Peringalam, while those arriving from Mukkam will have to take the Chettukadavu-Peringalam route.

Vehicles from the Kannur side will be diverted through Elathur-Pavangad-Nadakkavu. Vehicles arriving from the University side will have to take the Idimuzhikkal-Ramanattukara-Feroke-Cheruvannur route to reach Kozhikode city.

Vehicles from the city heading towards Kunnamangalam will have to use the Medical College-Mundikkalthazham-Kottamparamba-Manathanath road. Vehicles from the Malaparamba side will have to proceed via Poolakkadavu-Iringadanpalli-Mundikkalthazham-Kottamparamba-Manathanath towards Kunnamangalam.

Passengers travelling to the Calicut International Airport and the railway station have been advised to leave early. No vehicle parking will be permitted on roads between Malaparamba, Kunnamangalam, and Mavoor. Traffic on the route will be completely halted during the movement of the VVIP convoy, the police said.

Mr. Anwar is scheduled to arrive at the Kozhikode International Airport at 6.30 p.m. on Sunday. He will be at the Markaz from 7.30 p.m. to 9.30 p.m., where he will receive the first ‘Excellence Award’ instituted by the Sheikh Abubacker Foundation. Kanthapuram A.P. Aboobacker Musliyar will present the award at the ceremony.

The Malaysian Prime Minister will subsequently visit the C.M. Makham at Madavoor, where he is expected to spend about 20 minutes, before leaving for his place of stay at 10 p.m.

Kozhikode city and its adjoining areas have been brought under a high security cover for the visit. Security arrangements for Mr. Anwar are being made on a scale similar to those provided for the Prime Minister and President of India. Intelligence Additional Director General of Police Dinesh Kashyap recently visited the city to hold discussions with security officials regarding the arrangements.

World.title: Eritrea accuses Ethiopia of destabilising region
World.content:
Eritrea on Saturday (September 12) accused Ethiopia of destabilising the region, in the latest war of words between the two fractious Horn of Africa neighbours.

Eritrea won independence in 1993 after decades of armed unrest. A two-year war between 1998 and 2000 then left tens of thousands dead and sent diplomatic relations into a deep freeze.

The neighbours normalised ties when Abiy Ahmed took office in Ethiopia in 2018, pushing a rapprochement which earned him a Nobel Peace Prize the following year.

Eritrean forces backed the Ethiopian federal army during the conflict in the Tigray region. But since that war ended in late 2022, relations have dived anew, with Eritrea claiming that landlocked Ethiopia has designs on its port of Assab.

An Eritrean Foreign Ministry statement accused Mr. Ahmed's Prosperity Party of "actively destabilising the Horn of Africa.

"While Eritrea has maintained strict strategic patience, Addis Ababa has been immersed in incessant escalation of its war rhetoric for more than three years now; challenged international treaties; and actively hosted, trained, and financed subversive, sectarian proxy groups with an explicit 'regime-change' agenda against Eritrea," the statement said.

Contacted by AFP, the Ethiopian premier's spokesman did not immediately comment on the allegations.

Eritrea, a country ruled with an iron fist by Isaias Afwerki since independence, also accused Addis Ababa of "harbouring, supporting and actively encouraging" the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan, a paramilitary group that has been locked in a devastating civil war with the regular army since 2023.

World.title: Mawthoh joins BJP; eight UDP MLAs may follow in Meghalaya
World.content:
Former Meghalaya MLA and United Democratic Party (UDP) leader Jemino Mawthoh joined the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Saturday, intensifying speculation that at least eight of the regional party’s 12 MLAs could also switch over, a move that may make the BJP the second-largest party in the Meghalaya Assembly.

Mr. Mawthoh, who quit the UDP in May, joined the BJP in Shillong on Saturday. His move came amid growing indications of a possible larger shift of UDP leaders to the BJP.

The speculation grew stronger after six UDP MLAs skipped the party’s Central Executive Committee meeting in Shillong on Friday (September 11, 20260), while three others admitted that they were in talks with the BJP.

The UDP leadership, including party president Metbah Lyngdoh, however, maintained that the party’s legislators remained united.

Both the UDP and the BJP are constituents of the National People’s Party (NPP)-led Meghalaya Democratic Alliance government. The NPP has 33 MLAs, two more than the simple majority mark in the 60-member Assembly, while the UDP has 12 and the BJP two.

The possible merger of eight UDP legislators—within the ambit of the anti-defection law—would increase the BJP’s seat tally to 10, making it the second-largest party in the House.

Meghalaya-based publications, citing unnamed party leaders, reported that three UDP legislators told the Central Executive Committee that their next move would depend on whether the BJP accepted their demand. These MLAs are Cabinet Minister Lakhmen Rymbui, Balajied Kupar Synrem, and Ollan Sing Suin.

The three MLAs, however, said they had no differences with the UDP leadership, and their decision to switch parties would be in the best interest of their constituencies and the State.

Senior Meghalaya BJP leader and MLA Alexander Laloo Hek declined to say how many UDP legislators would cross over and when. “With two seats, the BJP has one Cabinet berth. The party should demand more berths after the possible increase in its numbers,” he said.

World.title: Russians cast votes for Duma polls in Keralam capital
World.content:
Russian nationals residing in Keralam and tourists cast their votes in the State capital ahead of the elections to the Russian Parliament on Saturday.

Elections are being held to the State Duma, the lower house of the Russian Parliament, from September 18 to 20.

As part of arrangements by embassies and consulates around the world to allow Russians around the world to cast their votes, a polling station was arranged at the Russia’s Honorary Consulate here too.

Aleksandr Fomin, Deputy Consul General, Chennai; Ratheesh Nair, Honorary Consul of Russia; and Anastasiia Pismennaia and Sergei Kliukin of the Chennai Consulate led the arrangements.

On Sunday, voting will be organised for Russian nationals working at the Kudankulam nuclear plant.

Mr. Ratheesh Nair said that since opening in Thiruvananthapuram in 2008, Russia’s Honorary Consulate had made arrangements for casting of votes for both Presidential and Parliamentary elections. Usually, the number of voters for Presidential elections was more. Moreover, as these were held in March, the voters included a number of tourists. The conflict in West Asia, however, had led to a dip in the number of visitors from Russia. Opportunities for online voting too are available. Despite this, around 10 voters turned up to cast their votes, Mr. Ratheesh Nair said.

World.title: A taste of Odisha at BRICS Summit: Koraput coffee given to global delegates
World.content:
Odisha’s Koraput coffee was given to delegates and journalists at the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, putting the tribal farmers-grown Arabica brand in the international spotlight, officials said on Saturday (September 12, 2026).

Tiger Bright, a brand of Koraput coffee, was included in the kits distributed to media personnel and delegates at the summit by the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA). A 250-gram packet of the coffee was distributed as part of the kits, officials said.

Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi welcomed the recognition for the State’s home-grown coffee and said it provided a platform to showcase Odisha’s local produce.

‘Vocal for local’

“Over the past few days, I have been speaking about #Odisha on global platforms, inviting the world to see the opportunities, strength and potential of our State. Today, it is especially heartening to see Koraput coffee telling another side of Odisha’s story at the BRICS India 2026 Summit,” Mr. Majhi said in a post on X.

He said the initiative reflected the spirit of ‘Vocal for Local’ promoted by Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

“For me, it is a moment of immense pride to see the hard work of our people and the richness of our land being recognised beyond the State. This is the Odisha I want the world to know, rooted in its soil, proud of its identity and confident in sharing its story with the world,” he said.

Deputy Chief Minister Pravati Parida also described the inclusion of Koraput coffee at the summit as a proud moment for Odisha.

The Odisha government said the presence of the coffee at the BRICS Summit highlighted the work of tribal farming families and the potential of products originating in rural and tribal areas to access wider markets.

Koraput coffee is cultivated mainly in Nandapur and Machhkund areas of Koraput district, at elevations of around 920-950 metres. The coffee is predominantly 100% Arabica and is grown under the shade of trees such as mango, jackfruit and citrus, officials said.

Handpicked cherries

The coffee cherries are handpicked at peak ripeness and processed before being procured, dried, graded, processed and marketed with support from the Tribal Development Co-operative Corporation of Odisha Ltd (TDCCOL).

The ‘Koraput Coffee’ brand was launched on September 11, 2019, to create a structured market for coffee produced by tribal farmers and strengthen the value chain, officials said.

Under the end-to-end support of TDCCOL, the coffee passes through procurement, drying, grading, processing and marketing before reaching consumers.

During the 2025-26 season, TDCCOL procured a record 102.54 metric tonnes of coffee fruit, compared with 34.68 tonne in 2022-23 and 34.41 tonne in 2024-25, officials said.

The growth has benefited around 360 tribal families, they said.

Tiger Bright is marketed as a premium Arabica coffee, with officials describing its flavour profile as having tropical citrus notes along with caramel, chocolate and cocoa undertones.

The coffee is sun-dried on raised wooden beds and subjected to processing and hygiene standards before being marketed.

World.title: PML-N's Rana Sanaullah says Parliament to decide on more provinces
World.content:
Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah said on Saturday that Parliament will decide on the matter of creating new provinces.

The recent debate regarding new provinces began in late July when Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi called for new provinces as part of reforms to the current governance system, drawing strong reactions from government ministers.

During a press conference in Lahore, Sanaullah was asked about Naqvi’s recent remarks where he said that “new administrative units will eventually have to be created as Pakistan’s growing population and changing needs can no longer be effectively managed through the existing administrative structure”.

The PML-N leader replied that making such statements at business seminars or conferences had not resulted in any “improvement” in the situation.

“In my humble opinion, this debate should have been started in Parliament,” he said, adding that issues of such magnitude should not be reduced to speeches, social media, seminars or business forums.

“The outcome will also emerge in Parliament,” the PM’s adviser said, adding that the “matter will be resolved in a better direction” when all political parties and the leadership of all provinces discuss it.

“In any circumstance, the decision of whether any province will be created or not will be made in Parliament, and by Parliament,” Sanaullah reiterated.

He also stressed that Naqvi, in his remarks, had said the creation of new provinces depended on whether the public wanted it. “If the public wants, then no one can stop it. The decision of whether the public wants it or not can only be made in Parliament,” the PML-N leader said.

Sanaullah said his party was deliberating upon the matter and will issue a policy statement after participating in the debate and once it “comes to a proper place where a result could emerge”.

The PM’s aide further said that no minister had raised the matter before the federal cabinet so far, adding that Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif would issue the appropriate directives once the topic is discussed.

He emphasised that even if a referendum were to be held to gauge public opinion, it would require approval by the parliament.

He remarked that the PML-N was not “bound” to issue a statement on the topic of new provinces merely based on economic forums. Referring to the Sindh Assembly’s adoption of a resolution against dividing the province, Sanaullah said the PPP had “overreacted”.

Coalition partners to resolve differences

Speaking on the recent rift between the PPP and the PML-N, the minister said differences between the two parties had, by and large, been resolved.

Sanaullah, who is also a member of the core committees formed to resolve differences between the two major coalition partners, said after attending a meeting at Governor House that any remaining issues would be settled amicably, as both sides were committed to resolving them.

“Ideally, the core committees should meet every month, but this could not happen due to the elections in GB and AJK. Meetings will now hopefully be held more regularly to smooth over any old or new rough patches,” he said.

He attributed the tensions mainly to emotionally charged election campaigns in Gilgit-Baltistan and Azad Kashmir, saying the campaigns were now over and so were the frictions.

The PPP, which rules Sindh and is also an ally of the PML-N government at the Centre, has strongly opposed the suggested move to carve out Karachi as a separate province.

PML-N’s Khawaja Asif, who had earlier noted that the appropriate forum for such a discussion was the parliament, said last week that devolution of power was “inevitable”.

The opposition parties, including the PTI, have said they will hold consultations to call an all-parties conference to discuss several issues, including the creation of new provinces, law and order and the economy.

PTI, JI marches to Islamabad

Asked about the plans of the Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) and the PTI to march towards Islamabad on September 20 and 27, respectively, Sanaullah remarked that the JI’s past political activities had been peaceful while the same could not be expected from the PTI.

“Everyone knows that JI is a political party and it has always carried out its activities according to the Constitutional and legal requirements,” he said.

He affirmed that the government “respected” political protests and therefore had held negotiations with the JI during which its representatives “carefully and seriously listened to their demands”.

The PM’s adviser urged JI leaders not to “overwork themselves needlessly” as the PML-N and PM Shehbaz also wanted a reduction in the fuel prices and electricity bills “as much as and even more than JI did”.

On the other hand, Sanaullah said the government had “no expectation” that the PTI’s long march would remain peaceful and referred to remarks made by its leaders.

“If they are coming to Islamabad to overthrow the government and if this is their intention and thinking, then it is obvious that they will carry out violence after coming there,” he asserted.

“Based on these reports, our assessment is that it could be a replay of May 9. If it takes that route and assumes a similar proportion, it would be very unfortunate. Since the matter is also before the courts, the government is awaiting their decisions before finalising its strategy. But one thing is certain: violence cannot be allowed,” he said.

Additional input from Ahmed Faraz

World.title: England survive scare to seal 3-0 sweep against Pakistan
World.content:
Joe Root led from the front as England survived a major wobble to beat Pakistan by eight wickets in the third Test at Edgbaston on Saturday, sealing a 3-0 series whitewash.

The home team, chasing just 130 to win, were in deep trouble when openers Ben Duckett and Emilio Gay were dismissed in the first over, bowled by Mohammad Abbas.

Root, England’s record run-scorer, edged his first ball, bowled by Razaullah, through the slips for four in a nervy start but settled and scored quickly to take the sting out of the situation.

The captain was given a huge reprieve when he chopped onto the stumps off Mohammad Ali, only for the umpire to signal a no ball, leaving the bowler distraught.

Root, with Jordan Cox at the other end, had another let-off when he edged an Abbas delivery between first and second slip, with neither fielder moving.

But he reached his half-century off 57 balls with a cut for four and Cox reached the landmark shortly afterwards.

England reached their target in the 25th over, with Root unbeaten on 62 and Cox 59 not out.

Root, in his second spell as England skipper after the departure of Ben Stokes, admitted his team were not the finished article but said he was delighted with their series win.

“The amount of uncertainty, noise and I guess chaos there was coming into the series, the way the guys have dealt with that – being so clinical with what we’ve had in front of us – and be stood here with a 3-0 win is really pleasing,” he told Sky Sports.

“It sets us up nicely looking ahead to the start of a new era with (new head coach) Stephen Fleming coming in.”

Pakistan woes

England celebrated their first Test series win since 2024 while Pakistan have now lost 16 of their past 21 games and are rooted at the bottom of the World Test Championship table.

Root’s men had appeared set for a quickfire win inside three days on Friday before debutant fast bowler Razaullah launched an audacious assault with the bat, clubbing nine sixes as he raced to 81 off 63 balls.

The 21-year-old number nine, who also took four wickets in England’s first innings, put on 121 for the ninth wicket with fellow paceman Abbas (42) as England floundered.

“We had a little bit of pushback yesterday which, in a strange way, was quite a good thing for the group,” said Root.

“Fair play to Razaullah, he made things difficult for us. He played some wonderful shots and made it very difficult to set fields to. He struck the ball nicely – I don’t know how he didn’t pull a muscle, swinging the bat that hard.”

Razaullah’s heroics have changed the mood music but they came too little, too late for Pakistan, who have endured a miserable series, losing the first Test by an innings and 103 runs and the second by 194 runs.

The tourists sent seven players home after their crushing defeat in the second Test at Lord’s and brought in seven replacements, with Razaullah among them.

They also sacked head coach Sarfaraz Ahmed and assistant Umar Gul as their tour plunged into chaos.

Pakistan made four changes to their side for the third Test in Birmingham and they put up a fight despite being dismissed for a paltry 133 in their first innings.

Captain Babar Azam admitted his team would have to take stock after a one-sided series.

“Before we came here we had to think about different things and to decide our team,” he said.

“We had a couple of changes after losing two matches. Playing in England is very difficult. We were trying to do our best in the third match.

“We need to sit down and look hard at our mistakes, decide our playing XI.”

The 3-0 win is a huge tonic for England, who were in turmoil just weeks ago following a series loss to New Zealand and the exits of head coach Brendon McCullum and Stokes.

But tougher challenges lie ahead, starting with a Test series in South Africa in December and January, while a home Ashes looms next year.

World.title: Coalition partners PPP, PML-N seek to bridge differences amid strained ties
World.content:
LAHORE: Differences continued to mar the working relationship between the PPP and PML-N as the coalition partners’ coordination committees met on Saturday to resolve outstanding issues and iron out their differences.

The PML-N-led government enjoys a two-thirds majority in the National Asse­mbly with the PPP’s support.

The meeting, held after months of strained relations during the acrimonious election campaigns in Azad Jammu and Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan, did not go smoothly, according to insiders.

The PPP delegation included former prime minister Raja Pervaiz Ashraf, Punjab Governor Sardar Saleem Haider Khan, Hassan Murtaza, Qamar Zaman Kaira and Ali Qasim Gilani.

Representing the PML-N were Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, National Assembly Speaker Sardar Ayaz Sadiq, Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah and Khawaja Saad Rafique.

The PPP protested that, as a coalition partner, it was paying a heavy political price for the PML-N government’s failure on multiple fronts, including runaway inflation, rising petroleum prices, the unresolved farming crisis, load-shedding and delays in local government elections.

The PML-N, on the other hand, maintained that instead of acting as a coalition partner and sharing responsibility, the PPP was behaving more like an opposition party and exploiting public issues for political gains, despite knowing that the government had little control over factors such as petroleum prices and inflation.

“There were moments of heated debate, but tempers soon cooled as both sides knew that they had no option but to work together as political guarantors of the system,” one of the participants told Dawn.

The PML-N also invited Punjab Inspector General of Police Rao Abdul Karim to address the PPP’s concerns relating to police matters and assured the party of its share in development schemes.

The PPP, however, recalled that previous decisions taken on both matters had not been implemented and had effectively been forgotten.

However, the bad blood and trust deficit that had built up over months of acrimonious relations between the two coalition partners may take several more meetings and confidence-building measures to overcome, the participant said, adding: “Both sides agreed to implement decisions taken previously, meet more regularly and work together to improve governance.”

The two sides also agreed to maintain the consultation process and continue working together to resolve differences and address coalition-related matters through mutual understanding and in the national interest.

The PPP and PML-N were engaged in a war of words following the PML-N’s emergence as the winner of the first phase of elections in AJK.

Last week, the PPP questioned Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s silence over the debate on creating new provinces and sought his stance on the matter.

The PPP had earlier maintained that any move to create additional federating units must follow the procedure laid down in the Constitution. However, the PPP-led Sindh government on Wednesday got a resolution passed by the provincial assembly opposing any further division of the country’s existing four provinces.

World.title: Nadra-linked vaccination certificate mandatory for pilgrims from Sept 14
World.content:
All pilgrims travelling for Hajj and Umrah from September 14 will be required to carry a vaccination certificate linked to the National Database and Registration Authority (Nadra), it emerged on Saturday.

The requirement was announced by Border Health Services-Pakistan (BHS-P) in a notice issued on September 7, which laid down vaccination requirements for Umrah and Hajj pilgrims.

The directives issued to all chief operating officers cover pre-departure vaccinations against polio, meningitis, yellow fever and influenza.

The BHS-P said that from September 14, no passenger would be allowed to travel without “Nadra-integrated” proof of vaccination.

It noted that, as per the health minister’s directives, the federal Government Civil Dispensary was the only authorised centre for vaccinating international travellers going for Hajj or Umrah.

To avoid any inconvenience for pilgrims, all airlines were requested to “strictly inform their travel agents that from now on, only proof of vaccination linked to Nadra will be acceptable for travel”.

The BHS-P also requested station managers of all airlines to inform travel agents that Umrah pilgrims must obtain a “digital vaccine card linked to Nadra from an authorised vaccination centre” before their departure.

Vaccination and online registration facilities will also be available at the airport in the next few days so passengers must reach six hours before their flight if they require vaccination at the airport.

The vaccination fee will be paid through Nadra’s e-Sahulat platform.

In January, Pakistan decided to enforce “strict and enhanced health surveillance” at all entry points in the country to prevent the cross-border transmission of Nipah virus.

World.title: Islamabad IG Ali Nasir Rizvi transferred, appointed NCCIA director general
World.content:
The federal government on Saturday transferred BS-20 officer Syed Ali Nasir Rizvi from his post as inspector general of Islamabad Capital Territory (ICT) Police and appointed him director general of the National Cyber Crime Investigation Agency (NCCIA), according to a notification issued by the Establishment Division.

The notification said the transfer and appointment had been made with the approval of the federal government under Section 29(3) of the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act, 2016, as amended by the Prevention of Electronic Crimes (Amendment) Act, 2025, and Section 10 of the Civil Servants Act, 1973. The order takes “immediate effect and until further orders”.

Under Section 29(3), the government can appoint the NCCIA chief for a non-extendable term of three years.

Meanwhile, the outgoing Rizvi’s post will be filled by Captain (retd) Muhammad Sohail Chaudhry, who is currently serving “under the Government of Punjab”, according to a separate notification.

Syed Ali Nasir Rizvi was appointed Islamabad IG on March 29, 2024, after having served in Punjab.

World.title: CM Bugti says 'no dialogue' with those taking up arms against state
World.content:
Balochistan Chief Minister Sarfraz Bugti said on Saturday there would be “no dialogue in any case” with those who took up arms against the state.

He made the remarks while speaking via video link to the country’s media anchors, senior journalists and other representatives at the Chief Minister’s Secretariat on Saturday, according to a statement issued by his office.

CM Bugti said the war against terrorism would continue in Balochistan until the “last terrorist” was eliminated, adding that it was not possible to control the entire province while sitting in Quetta.

He affirmed that the civil and military leadership were united against terrorism and there was “no ambiguity or confusion” on the matter.

The chief minister noted that security forces were performing their duties in difficult circumstances in Balochistan, adding that state institutions were working in complete coordination in the fight against terrorism.

Before the talk with journalists, CM Bugti was also provided multiple briefings covering the provincial government’s strategy for social and economic development, governance and service delivery, effective use of development funds, and measures to ensure that development projects benefited the people.

A briefing on minerals and mining highlighted the sector’s potential, ongoing projects and measures being taken to develop it and better utilise the province’s mineral resources, the statement said.

The Ministry of Interior and Tribal Affairs also briefed the chief minister on the law and order situation, the Provincial Action Plan, police reforms and progress on the integration of the Levies Force into the police, the statement added.

Bugti was also briefed on the Safe City project, legislation and coordination among law-enforcement agencies.

During the interaction with journalists, CM Bugti also expressed his views on the creation of new administrative units, saying, “If new provinces are to be created in Balochistan, they should be on administrative rather than linguistic grounds.”

On Thursday, Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said the Parliament was expected to debate the issue of new provinces next month.

Speaking to mediapersons, Bugti said he had no knowledge of any “two-and-a-half-year government agreement” for Balochistan, according to the statement.

The decision to change the government had to be taken by the political leadership, he said, adding that his cabinet would continue to serve the people as long as they were in office.

The chief minister was quoted as saying that although he could not claim that corruption across the province had been completely eliminated, it had decreased compared to the past. Measures were being taken to ensure merit in all government departments, including educational institutions, he added.

He said development projects in Balochistan had been completed in record time compared to the past, adding that the provincial government was focused on making the development process effective, result-oriented and aligned with public needs.

Referring to the return of foreign nationals, Bugti said that 1.1 million Afghan refugees, along with other foreigners, had been sent back to their homeland from Balochistan.

On the issue of missing persons, he said the matter was sometimes presented on national media and other forums without proper context, which did not reflect the true picture of the situation.

“Terrorism was not an issue of one province but of the entire country and required joint efforts at the national level for its elimination”, Bugti was quoted as saying.

World.title: Trump says Houthis have asked US not to intervene in Yemen
World.content:
United States President Donald Trump said on Saturday that Yemen’s Iran-allied Houthi fighters, who have seized a vital shipping corridor linking Europe and Asia, have asked Washington not to intervene.

The Houthis have taken control of Yemen’s entire Red Sea coast after capturing three strategic islands in a lightning offensive.

Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest oil exporter, has relied on the area ever since Iran’s Hormuz blockade choked off its shipments via the Gulf.

“The Houthis called us and they don’t want to fight with us,” Trump told reporters on a visit to Dublin, Ireland.

“They don’t want us to go after them.”

He added that “everything’s gonna work out fine and dandy,” in the region.

Trump also mentioned having spoken to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, whom he described as a “friend”.

According to US outlet Axios, the Saudi crown prince called Trump twice on Thursday to request US strikes on the Houthis, but the American president declined.

The Houthis also targeted Saudi Arabian oil facilities this week with a massive drone and missile attack.

Yemeni govt forces hit Houthis in Mocha

In Yemen, the government forces said on Saturday they have struck Houthi fighters in the strategic Red Sea city of Mocha.

Men gesture in a screen grab from a video released on Sept 11, 2026 and said to show Khaled bin Walid camp after Houthis captured the city of Mocha in Taiz Province. — Al-Masirah TV/Handout via Reuters

Following a week-long offensive, the Houthis on Friday captured Yemen’s Red Sea coast, cementing their hold on the Bab al-Mandab strait, a vital artery for Saudi Arabian oil exports as the Strait of Hormuz remains closed amid the US-Iran war.

“The armed forces destroyed vehicles and weapons and killed members of the Houthi terrorist militia backed by the Iranian regime,” near the port of the city of Mocha, the government news agency Saba reported.

The spokesman for the Yemeni government forces, Majed Abdullah al-Nazili, said they have also struck the Houthis’ “vehicles and members” on the Mocha-Dhubab road, 11 kilometres from the city, according to Saba.

Nazili said on Friday they had begun shelling areas in Mocha, and called on citizens not to use the Taiz-Mocha and Mocha-Dhubab roads.

The Houthis seized control of Mocha on Thursday, with their attack driving many to flee to Aden, where the internationally recognised government is based.

On Friday, Houthi media said two Saudi strikes hit Mocha’s airport, while a local official said the city’s seaport was hit by six missiles of unknown origin.

The Houthi offensive, which started last week, has killed more than 500 people, according to sources on both sides.

It has also displaced about 46,000 people, the UN migration agency said on Friday.

It is part of renewed hostilities in Yemen’s civil war that began with the group’s takeover of the capital Sanaa in 2014.

World.title: Govt approves ‘extraordinary security allowance’ for police, civil service officers in 26 KP districts
World.content:
PESHAWAR: The federal government has designated 26 districts in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa (KP) as “terror-affected”, declaring that all Pakistan Administrative Service (PAS) and Police Service of Pakistan (PSP) officers posted therein are eligible for an ‘extraordinary law and order and security risk allowance’, effective from July 1 this year, it emerged on Saturday.

According to a notification issued by the Establishment Division to the KP chief secretary and seen by Dawn, the allowance for 26 of the 35 districts will be 250 per cent of the running basic pay and paid retroactively.

It read that the ‘KP Extraordinary Law, Order and Security Risk Allowance’ would be admissible to PAS and PSP officers posted in Peshawar, Khyber, Mardan, Charsadda, Nowshera, Mohmand, Kohat, Hangu, Karak, Kurram, Orakzai, Bannu, Lakki Marwat, North Waziristan, Dera Ismail Khan, Tank, Upper and Lower South Waziristan, Swat, Buner, Shangla, Bajaur, Upper and Lower Dir, besides Upper and Lower Chitral.

Citing an August 18 letter from the Establishment Division to the KP chief secretary, the notification stated that Swabi and the entirety of Hazara Division, comprising Abbottabad, Haripur, Mansehra, Battagram, Torghar, Kolai-Palas and the Upper and Lower Kohistan districts, were “excluded for the purpose of admissibility of subject allowance”.

The federal government requested the KP government to proceed with payment of the allowance with effect from July 1, 2026.

In the August letter seen by Dawn, the Establishment Division said the government approved the grant for PAS and PSP officers serving in the “seriously disturbed KP districts”, due to the law and order situation and the danger to officers and personnel.

It added that the allowance would be admissible only to PAS and PSP officers in districts categorised as seriously disturbed, which would be identified by the Interior and Narcotics Control Division at the start of each financial year.

“Establishment Division will notify the districts where this allowance will be admissible, on [an] annual basis, at the start of each financial year,” the letter read. “The allowance shall be discontinued upon transfer of the officers from the notified districts.”

It further stated that the allowance would be provided during sanctioned leave of any kind, except extraordinary leave, and would not be available during suspension, appointment as an officer on special duty, or training of any kind.

Furthermore, it would not be treated as part of emoluments for the purpose of calculating pension and gratuity, and the cost of the allowance would be borne by the federal government.

KP has seen a rise in terrorist attacks over the past year.

According to the Annual Security Report 2025 from the Centre for Research and Security Studies (CRSS), KP recorded a significant surge in violence last year as “fatalities rose from 1,620 in 2024 to 2,331 in 2025”.

Due to a resurgence of terrorism, especially in KP and Balochistan, where attacks often target security personnel and LEAs , the state has intensified counter-terrorism operations.

According to monthly data compiled by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS), mainland KP recorded 54 terrorist attacks last month, marking a 50 per cent increase compared to July.

Meanwhile, the merged districts recorded 54 terrorist attacks in August, marking a 126pc increase.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.

This makes me think of the "Lost Tribes" and a piece by Premendra Mitra about the Patuas (traditional scroll painters). Premendra once had a great desire to find the lost Patuas of Kalighat. Briefly, the story goes like this—a young boy walking the streets of Kalighat would watch with wonder a specific style of indigenous painting. Ordinary men in dirty clothes sat cross-legged on mats in small roadside shops, painting those pictures. Yet, the walls of the shops were adorned with framed, colourful photographs of gods and goddesses. People coming to the temple preferred to buy the framed photos. Even so, the Patuas would sit down to paint whenever they found a moment’s respite between sales.

Then came a day when not only the scroll paintings but even the expensive printed pictures of deities vanished from those shops. The Patuas disappeared too. I don't know if that young boy was Premendra himself—since his childhood was spent in North India, having been born in Varanasi. But for a creative man like him to imagine that boy while thinking of the Patuas is not far-fetched. When a kind soul eventually went looking for those Patuas, he was utterly disappointed. He learned that they had been pushed out of the city. Their descendants had not become "useless" painters; some took jobs as labourers in jute mills or chose other professions. At most, unable to ignore the "blood connection," some practised their hand at painting the chalchitra (background canopy) of idols. Premendra tracked down a few of these "unfortunate" descendants and asked to see old scroll paintings. He was shocked to find they had almost nothing left. One or two pulled down a bundle of papers tucked into the thatch of their huts. Premendra saw the pathetic state of those soot-stained, discoloured papers—they were ready to crumble at any moment. Calling the insects "connoisseurs of art," a somber Premendra described how those paintings were being destroyed.

The author was accompanied by an art collector. His friend bought some paintings that were in good condition from the descendants for an unexpectedly high price. Later, he and others wrote about them. Premendra noted how his "self-satisfaction" was bruised. He commented that while many were becoming famous artists by adopting the Patua style, and those paintings were selling at major exhibitions to decorate drawing rooms—even impressing Pablo Picasso—the Patua sitting on a dirty mat in a narrow shop and the ordinary customer buying them for a pittance are nowhere to be found today.

Thinking of the early artists of Bengali advertising, I am reminded of Premendra Mitra's essay "Barbar Yuger Pore" (After the Barbaric Age), just as I was of The Lost Tribes of Israel. In it, I found no real difference between the forgotten Patuas and the nameless illustrators from the dawn of Bengali advertising.

The artists whose work I later came to know and appreciate were giants like Annada Munshi—whose ideas and illustrations revolutionised the look and feel of Bengali advertising. But I wanted to see what kind of "ugly and tasteless" creations (as labelled by later critics) Annada and his peers had replaced. Without seeing those, how could I understand the evolution of style?

Here, I must mention the artist Hemen Majumdar. He is never known to have drawn for s. Everyone knows that when art lovers discuss him, his paintings of "drip-wet Bengali women" inevitably come up. Who that woman was, was once a subject of intense speculation. A few know that he often painted while keeping a photograph by his side. Hemen had taken photos of his wife, Sudharani, in various poses as she returned from bathing in the family pond. His wife was his model. When giving the picture its final form, he would simply change Sudharani’s face and paint the face of a relative instead—much like modern-day Photoshop!

Essentially a romantic artist, Hemen Mazumdar never illustrated s himself. Yet, his signature style of depicting women was extensively adapted by other advertising artists.

Though Hemen was skilled at copying photographs, he knew the magic of glorifying them with colour. But that wasn't all. This was a man who was invited to design the gateway for King George V’s visit to India, who was a pioneer in publishing art journals, who painted the landscapes of Kashmir at the invitation of the Maharaja, who was the "Court Artist" of the Maharaja of Patiala, and who gave an artistic form to Mahatma Gandhi at the spinning wheel. He didn't just paint wet clothes!

At the same time, it is true that his skill at painting beautiful women was so popular that other artists, while drawing women for s, often mimicked Hemen’s postures—or those of the women painted by Raja Ravi Varma. Thus, even without drawing for ads himself, Hemen was "present" in this branch of art through the figures of women drawn in his style. Of course, bringing out the "wet-clothed" look or suggestive sensuality in black-and-white newspaper ads was a difficult task!

It’s worth mentioning that Hemen’s own work was occasionally used in advertising. An organisation called "Bengal Autotype" used to run ads featuring a sketch of Rabindranath Tagore by Hemen, accompanied by the Poet’s message. The advertisers even sold prints of that picture. The ad read: "A Wonderful Picture of Poet." Each print cost one rupee, with an additional 50 paise for postage. This ad appeared in the Visva-Bharati journal in the late 1930s, detailing the paper quality and dimensions.

In the eyes of some critics, the work of the "erotic painter" Hemen began to gain popularity in 1926 after a commercial firm in Mumbai bought his paintings to make calendars. The "forbidden" sword of the Hemen-style became a weapon for advertising illustrators too. One could easily call them followers of Hemen’s "voyeuristic" work. However, no matter how they were drawn, it's not as if the artists of the Battala press or the Patuas hadn't used such "swords" long before! Based on the consumer's mindset, this tradition seems never-ending—at home, abroad, and everywhere else.

Sandip Dasgupta has spent nearly three decades working in the editorial offices of newspapers and news portals. He has authored several history-based books, and a subject particularly close to his heart is the illustrations created by Bengali artists.
