World.title: Brisbane Lions v Adelaide player ratings: Fagan’s men who stood tallest after embarrassment against Swans
World.content:
SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion Brisbane Lions v Adelaide player ratings: Fagan’s men who stood tallest after embarrassment against Swans

Scott Spits and Steve Barrett Updated September 12, 2026 — 11:38pm , first published 11:03pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

The Brisbane Lions lost their first final last year. What happened next? A barnstorming run through their semi-final and preliminary final, back to the big dance, and another premiership to top it all off. They’re on track for a repeat dose this year after obliterating the Crows at the Gabba in what became Adelaide favourite son Taylor Walker’s farewell game. Scott Spits (Brisbane Lions) and Steve Barrett (Adelaide) run their eye over every player in from the semi-final. What a return to form for Charlie Cameron and the Lions. AFL Photos



Brisbane Lions (1) Kai Lohmann: He was creative for most of the match, kicking the opening goal after only 30 seconds. Just as importantly, he put a block on and allowed Zac Bailey to kick his opener after four minutes. 8/10 (2) Sam Draper: Tried and tried but was not among Brisbane’s best as the club’s second ruck. Had close to 60 per cent game time. 4.5/10 (3) Jaspa Fletcher: A good game by the 22-year-old, who is fast approaching 100 matches. He got plenty of early touches (seven in the first quarter) as Brisbane set up their impressive victory. 6/10 View post on X



(4) Oscar Allen: There could be a “watch” on the former Eagle after tonight. He had just five touches by the final break and two behinds. The Lions will want a bit more out of him in their flag push. 4/10 (5) Josh Dunkley: One of the Lions’ best and typically strong at the coalface. He did the one-percenters regularly (no surprise there), and spent time on Izak Rankine and nullified his influence. He got plenty of the ball himself, too. 8/10 (6) Hugh McCluggage: Yet again, he didn’t get a lot of the ball for a player of his class. It was notable that Chris Fagan came to his defence during the week. McCluggage has had his injury woes this year, but importantly he was up and going early when the Lions stoned the Crows with five goals in eight minutes. 7/10 (7) Jarrod Berry: He finished with 19 touches and was a solid contributor. Unfortunately, Berry was off-line with an early shot at goal when the Lions were heaving. By that stage, Brisbane had 10 forward entries to Adelaide’s zero. 6/10 Will Ashcroft fires off a handball. AFL Photos



(8) Will Ashcroft: Despite their qualifying final loss, the Lions have again set themselves up perfectly for another flag push, and Ashcroft’s form reflects that. He got better and better as the match wore on, as the Lions found their groove ahead of next week’s preliminary final against the Hawks. The two-time Norm Smith medallist finished with 30 touches. 8.5/10 (9) Lachie Neale: The veteran star was not among Brisbane’s match-winners, but he still picked up 21 possessions as others lifted around him. That’s probably a good sign for the Lions as they eye off a hat-trick of flags, and needing a multitude of contributors 6.5/10 (10) Levi Ashcroft: Quiet by his standards, he spent time on star Crows skipper Jordan Dawson and was probably shaded by him. 5.5/10 (13) Logan Morris: He slotted a brilliant snap goal after eight minutes in the third quarter when he finally got on the board. It gave the Lions a 50-point lead – basically snuffing out any Adelaide hopes. He left the game in the final quarter with injury. 5.5/10 The fired up Oscar Allen and Dayne Zorko. AFL Photos



(15) Dayne Zorko: It was a strong game from the super-veteran. Zorko was the other Lion (aside from Zac Bailey) to re-sign during the week, and he showed why they still want him in the side. The 37-year-old kicked a ripping goal in the third quarter and led the Lions for metres gained. 7/10 (16) Cam Rayner: He was oozing with confidence throughout and was involved in plenty of key moments. By midway through the second quarter Rayner already had five score involvements. Go back and witness his goal – Brisbane’s fifth – when he took Alex Neal-Bullen on and kicked beautifully. It gave the Lions a 31-point lead and the tone was set. 9/10 (22) Ty Gallop: He came into the side to replace the injured Noah Answerth. He did his bit with at least 10 touches. 5/10 (23) Charlie Cameron: A non-factor in the Lions’ qualifying final loss to the Swans, in this sudden-death clash he proved his worth and much more. He had his first goal after 90 seconds (Brisbane’s second) and his second after 23 minutes. Cameron is clearly an “energy” player, and with a return of 5.3 against his former side, the Lions and coach Fagan will be rapt. 8/10 View post on X



(26) Conor McKenna: He had a real crack but was in and out of the game. He finished with 13 touches and 1.2. Look back to his early “toe-poke” pass to Lohmann for a goal. 5.5/10 (27) Darcy Gardiner: The big man was largely quiet but typically handy for Brisbane’s team defence. 5/10 (30) Eric Hipwood: I quite liked his game. He regularly gave the Lions something to kick to and played an important role with Morris and Allen both a bit hot and cold. He kicked a goal in the last quarter and finished with 2.1. 7/10 (31) Harris Andrews: He played an intriguing game. The star defender didn’t hit his usual heights, but with so many teammates in hot form against the Crows, that mattered less. He manned Riley Thilthorpe for much of the game and won. Strangely, Andrews picked up a shot at goal in the first quarter after a double 50-metre penalty. His rare chance to score was offline. 6/10 (32) Darcy Fort: Solid and dependable as Brisbane’s first ruck. He split the points with Adelaide’s Lachlan McAndrew. 5.5/10



View post on X (33) Zac Bailey: What a game by the newly re-signed gun. Ever classy by foot, he was nothing short of brilliant – ironically against the club that desperately wanted him. He had a stack of score involvements and was one of the five Lions to get on the board in the first eight minutes. He finished with 23 touches and kicked 3.3. 8.5/10 (35) Ryan Lester: A quality contributor, Lester was heavily involved in the win from the start. Witness a strong defensive effort on the wing (a punch from behind) that helped set the mood. Quirkily, like Andrews, Lester had a rare shot at goal in the first term, but missed. 8/10 (44) Darcy Wilmot: He did his bit. He got enough of the ball and was more than solid in defence and playing as a link player. Thumbs up for an important player in Fagan’s all-conquering side. 6.5/10



Adelaide (2) Ben Keays: Two consolation goals in the first half almost masked a forgettable night for the defensive forward. Normally such a spark plug in attack, Keays was unsighted when the whips were cracking and was soundly trumped by Zorko. 4/10 (3) Sam Berry: The hardworking onballer was one Adelaide player who could hold his head high. Berry did his best to stem Brisbane’s early onslaught, chalking up five first-quarter clearances by himself. He finished with a game-high 31 disposals. 7.5/10 (4) Callum Ah Chee: Other than a sprayed shot out on the full early, Ah Chee struggled to get involved early doors at his old stomping ground. He had just three touches in the first half before spending time on the wing in the third term and getting more involved. 5/10 (6) Daniel Curtin: A big second half saw him finish with 22 disposals and seven clearances. Curtin booted the Crows’ first goal and played predominantly on the ball, but he – like many of his mates – wasn’t able to stop Brisbane’s game-breaking mids. 7/10



Daniel Curtin celebrates a goal with Taylor Walker. AFL Photos (7) Riley Thilthorpe: Had his hands full with Andrews in the first half before playing much better footy after the main break, booting two goals and using his body well against the Lions’ skipper. Thilthorpe’s contest was strong, but his ball use wasn’t quite up to scratch. 5/10 (8) Josh Rachele: Enjoyed a second-quarter purple patch when he slotted a major and then handed another one off to Darcy Fogarty. But otherwise, Rachele – fresh off a three-goal haul against the Bulldogs – had a poor evening. He conceded an early 50-metre penalty and was thrashed in the air by Lester. 2/10 (12) Jordan Dawson: He gave it everything he had with 30 touches and 512m gained, but his normally pristine ball use was missing, going at 50 per cent disposal efficiency. Dawson’s six first-quarter tackles said as much about the Lions’ dominance as it did about his own never-say-die approach. 7.5/10 (13) Taylor Walker: Ended his AFL journey with two fourth-quarter goals – to finish with 715 for his career – after being frustrated throughout the first three terms. Not an ending he wanted in his 319th and last top-flight game, but what a star he has been. 4/10



Walker leaves an AFL playing field for the final time with his children. AFL Photos (14) Jake Soligo: Adelaide needed more from him – for much of the home-and-away campaign and in both finals. Soligo was part of the midfield rotation, but struggled to get his hands on the footy. 3.5/10 (15) Brayden Cook: The crafty wingman’s usually clean ball use was a touch ragged and, aside from one neat goal assist early, he struggled to influence the match. 4/10 (16) Max Michalanney: There’s no lonelier place on an AFL field than one-out against Cameron in the mood he was in. Michalanney, normally a reliable stopper, was absolutely torched by the Lions’ brilliant goalsneak in the first half, before being mercifully moved to the wing. 1/10 (19) Zac Taylor: After missing the elimination final with a hamstring injury, Taylor ratified his recall instant by providing pressure and contest, while splitting minutes between half-forward and the centre-square. All up, 10 of his 17 possessions were contested. 6.5/10



(23) Izak Rankine: The highest-rated player in the AFL since round 17 was due a downer – and a downer he had, thanks chiefly to the disciplined, iron-fisted glove of Dunkley. Rankine was kickless at quarter-time and still had just two at the half. He was given more room to roam after half-time, but it just wasn’t his night. 5/10 Izak Rankine had his hands full all night against the Lions. AFL Photos (24) Josh Worrell: After enjoying the game of his life against the Bulldogs, when he racked up an AFL finals record 19 intercept possessions, Worrell wasn’t allowed anywhere near the same the influence to make plays. Although he still finished with 18 touches, he had just four of them by half-time. 5/10 (27) Luke Nankervis: He played major minutes on the wing before taking on the Cameron job late. Nankervis snared a magnificent mark over Levi Ashcroft and goaled to give the Crows a glimmer late in the first period, but otherwise was quiet. 4.5/10 (28) Alex Neal-Bullen: Splitting time between wing and half-forward, the experienced ex-Demon didn’t have a great impact in the first half but was serviceable after the interval. 5.5/10



(29) Rory Laird: The experienced half-back flanker never waved the white flag, but didn’t give the Lions too many major headaches either. 6/10 (30) Wayne Milera: The dashing All-Australian half-back wasn’t afforded the same time and space that he enjoyed a week earlier against the Bulldogs. Normally so calm and creative, his disposal was hurried thanks to the Lions’ pressure. Kicked a neat late goal. 6/10 (32) Darcy Fogarty: Conceded a horror 100m penalty in a forgettable opening term before springing to life in the second quarter, spearheading Adelaide’s revival by booting two goals and assisting another one to Rachele. But he was unsighted too often. 4.5/10 Darcy Fogarty had a frustrating night for the Crows. AFL Photos (35) James Borlase: Quiet for four quarters, he rarely intercepted and struggled to have much involvement, despite how much time the Sherrin spent in Brisbane’s attacking area. 3/10



(40) Hugo Hall-Kahan: The unsung half-back has barely put a foot wrong since being picked up in the mid-season draft. He wasted very few of his 27 disposals, racked up plenty of metres of rebound and contested well in the air and on the ground. A real find. 7.5/10 (42) Lachlan McAndrew: After shading Tim English last week, the towering ruckman had his hands full with Draper and Fort. McAndrew matched them both in the air, but it was harder for him on the deck. 6/10 (48) Mark Keane: He struggled all night with an aggressive Hipwood, finishing with four kicks and virtually no impact. 2/10 Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Fans stay home but Sharks turn up to end Cowboys’ season
World.content:
If you build it, they won’t come.

It may be the one of the best stadiums in the southern hemisphere, a mere 25.2 kilometres from the Sharks’ spiritual home in the Shire. But many Cronulla fans refuse to leave Cronulla.

Not even the siren song of their Mermaids cheerleaders, free public transport for ticket holders, or the chance to witness their team in a finals fixture was enough to bring them to Allianz Stadium.

Loading

An official crowd of 17,429 was posted. That’s only about 2,500 more than the capacity of Shark Park, otherwise known as Ocean Protect Stadium. Understandably, only a handful of hearty Cowboys souls made the long commute from Townsville.

The decision to shift the game here was a controversial one. Head office will hope the extra corporate cash it pockets from playing at Allianz offsets the broadcast images of a stadium less than half full.

The reasons for non-attendance remain unclear. Is it because rugby league is such a good television product? The fatigue of watching the seventh North Queensland-Cronulla post-season clash since 2013? Or just a preference for “Portaloo Park”?

Nicho Hynes celebrates a try. Getty Images

Whatever the case, the Sharks got the job done without the vocal support they would normally get at their regular home.

“It’s not our decision,” Cronulla coach Craig Fitzgibbon said. “I felt like this last year - obviously the amount of sulking that went on about playing at Shark Park, I thought we weren’t any chance of getting it this year. They should have just told us earlier.

“But also, for us, we’re happy to play here. We’re in semi-finals; we want to play in a big stadium. But our members and fans pay their money all year to be able to watch their team make semi-finals and play at home, and we earned that. We didn’t get it … but that’s not up to me. I would imagine it’s a financial decision or viewing optics for the game. I’m not sure.”

A 26-16 win against their old sparring partners was achieved despite their returning maestro playing with the use of only one shoulder. Braydon Trindall took his place after three weeks on the sidelines. Despite being clearly hampered, he passed, tackled and kicked his side to a scrappy victory.

At one point in the second half, “Tricky” gave his shoulder an unnecessary test when he tried to retrieve the football from his own short kick-off. The pivot couldn’t be accused of playing in a dinner suit. When he produced a season-high 31st try assist with a pass to fullback Will Kennedy – not even Nathan Cleary comes near that figure – it was due reward for playing through the pain.

Loading

The Cowboys have been the most curious side in the NRL. They qualified for the top eight despite conceding more points than any other finalist in history. Their devil-may-care attitude is best exemplified by Scott Drinkwater. The Dragons-bound fullback is the ultimate gunslinger. One errant cut-out pass resulted in an intercept that gifted Sione Katoa his 100th NRL try. Undeterred, he threw another one that hit Zac Laybutt on the chest from 25 metres away to give his side hope.

However, it was always going to come down to the Cowboys’ application without the football. They defended stoutly when starved off possession for much of the opening half, particularly when their tryline was peppered. However, those exertions eventually took their toll. When Nico Hynes shaped to kick, but instead stepped off his left foot, their fate was sealed.

There is every chance that the Sharks could be required to return to Allianz next week. Asked whether he hoped more of their fans will follow them there, captain Cameron McInnes deadpanned: “I don’t know. If you can afford it, come. If you can’t, watch it on TV. I couldn’t care less, really.”

World.title: Liberal chivalry lost at Griffin door
World.content:
James Griffin’s reflections on his time in the NSW legislature as a Liberal member present a neat encapsulation of the dilemma now facing the Liberals at the local, state and national levels (“Retiring MP slams Liberal hacks as moderates wane”, September 6). For some reason, they seem unable to accept the world (electorate) as it is, instead focusing on niche issues that frequently appeal to a particular audience, rather than the general one of the electorate. Which, in turn, continues to make them broadly unelectable in the macro sense. Issues around renewables, climate, women, gender, internal politics/governance or global impacts on our economy. They seem to think that much of our current situation is linked to what is happening now, without considering previous policies of theirs. Examples include removing carbon tax, negative gearing (a government subsidy to reduce tax on high incomes at the expense of those on low incomes buying a home), privatisation/outsourcing, robo-debt, aged care reforms and various others. None of these are “nation building” policies, but rather divisive ones that set us against each other. What One Nation is doing is effectively doubling down on this approach, effectively cannibalising them. Until Liberals realise that they are pushing policies that aren’t dealing with the world as it is, rather than some halcyon time of the past, they will continue to flail about and continue to lose ground. Bernard Stever, Richmond

Manly MP James Griffin has decided that he has had enough. Sitthixay Ditthavong

Retiring Manly MP James Griffin stands out as one of the rare figures in politics who appear genuinely decent – not a retail politician who dodges accountability or hides behind the usual excuses when things go wrong. He took his responsibilities so seriously that it affected him when he couldn’t assist one of his constituents. He is young, capable, and possibly a future NSW premier. But he clearly sees what many moderates in the Liberal Party have been feeling for years: the endless culture war battles offer nothing to the voters they are meant to serve. It has become increasingly difficult for politicians with principles, empathy and a moral compass to survive in that environment – let alone thrive. Griffin’s departure is a loss for Manly, for the Liberal Party, and for moderates generally. It is challenging for values-driven MPs to stay the course in a party increasingly defined by internal conflict rather than public purpose. Voters are forgotten. Mukul Desai, Hunters Hill

I recently met James Griffin, and I was left with the strong impression that if the Liberal Party could nurture people of his calibre, there was still some hope left, not only for his party, but for politics in general. His intelligence, capacity to listen and desire to make a positive contribution were clear. It leaves me with immense sadness to hear of his retirement. This is everyone’s loss. Elizabeth Darton, Lane Cove West

Patients deserve better

World.title: Child dead after fire rips through Central West home
World.content:

A four-year-old child has died after a fire tore through a home in the state’s Central West on Saturday.

Emergency services were called to the home in Woodstock, about 22 kilometres north-east of Cowra, just before 3pm. Officers arrived to find the house well alight.

A woman and two children were able to escape, but the four-year-old remained unaccounted for. The woman was taken to Cowra Hospital in a stable condition, suffering from smoke inhalation.

Fire and Rescue NSW firefighters extinguished the blaze before locating the body of the child inside the home.

“A crime scene has been established, and inquiries into the circumstances surrounding the fire are ongoing,” NSW Police said in a statement.

World.title: Fagan got ‘nasty’ at four players for the first time this year. It sparked carnage for the Crows
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 Fagan got ‘nasty’ at four players for the first time this year. It sparked carnage for the Crows Nick Wright September 13, 2026 — 12:53am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Loading

Brisbane: For the first time this year, Chris Fagan felt he needed to target one group of players and ensure they knew their performances hadn’t been up to scratch. The Brisbane Lions’ small forwards were in the firing line, and needed to respond. Cam Rayner went as far as to describe the two-time premiership coach’s week as “nasty” on Kayo Sports, and after last week’s capitulation against an undermanned Swans still hurting from the Pullman Hotel saga, it was probably warranted. Kai Lohman was lethal against the Crows. AFL Photos The quartet of Rayner, Charlie Cameron, Kai Lohmann and the newly re-signed Zac Bailey all went goalless that night. But in the 53-point semi-final thrashing of the Crows at the Gabba, they responded emphatically. “They’re proud performers, they’ve been pretty good for us all year, [but] it was pointed out to them during the week that they let us down against Sydney,” Fagan lamented.



“They hardly contributed in that game, our talls were actually all OK, and our small forwards didn’t get on the scoreboard. I reminded them of how good they were when we played Adelaide in round seven … and probed and prodded them a bit on the performance last week. Charlie Cameron celebrates with the fans. AFL Photos “This is the first time this year [I’ve had to pull that lever]. I know there’s been some games this year where we haven’t played all that well, but this was the first time this year where it was a pretty fierce week.” It took just 29 seconds in the contest for Lohmann to kick the first goal of the night – triggering a procession of five unanswered goals in the opening seven-and-a-bit minutes – with his second coming less than 50 seconds into the third term to ensure the Lions stayed on the front foot. His 18 disposals on Saturday night were the equal-second most of his career, bettered only by his five goals and 24 touches in round 22 against Hawthorn – their preliminary final opponents. Loading



“It was an extraordinary start – I was standing there with my mouth open going, ‘This is unbelievable’. It was a very prompt response to a disappointing game last week. We needed to make a statement,” Fagan said. Cameron had the crowd screaming their most vocal renditions of Take Me Home, Country Roads, kicking a bag of five for the first time since round 10, 2024, while Rayner’s two goals and three goal assists were only bettered by his frequent tackle busts. Related Article AFL 2026 Walker makes tearful exit as Lions respond to ‘nasty’ Fagan’s tough love; preliminary final times confirmed But it was the performance of Bailey, fresh off inking an eight-year extension to remain in Brisbane until the end of 2034 – turning down a reported $10 million offer from the Crows in the process – that was perhaps the most poetic. During the week, it was almost with disbelief that Dayne Zorko gushed about the retention of Bailey, such was the kind of lucrative rival offer he was attracting. But the Lions, as they did with Hugh McCluggage, all but ensured the 26-year-old would remain a one-club man.



The livewire had one moment to forget – a complete shank for goal off the side of his boot when under no pressure – but aside from that, he was electric; finishing with three goals, 23 disposals, three clearances and three goal assists,as he roamed around contests hunting for loose-ball opportunities. Ironically, it was against the Crows in round seven when he best showcased his all-round skill set with another three goals and 29 touches. The Lions faithful would have been forgiven for fearing the lack of defensive intent which plagued them at the SCG was showing signs of reappearing as their rivals kicked the next four goals – two in quick succession off Darcy Fogarty’s boot – as an early 31-point lead was cut to less than two goals. Loading But either side of the main break, the Lions would kick the next seven, and managed the momentum of the contest – timing their opportunities to attack with precision and showing a willingness to slow the tempo after a frantic start.





“It’ll be one step at a time for us.” On an otherwise forgettable night for the Crows, the retiring Taylor Walker kicked his final two goals before drawing the curtain on his career – an effort in vain, but something for the visitors to savour. “He was saying to our group we’re not getting rid of him, so he’s sticking around in some capacity – I don’t know what that is, but it’s just been an absolute pleasure to coach him,” Crows coach Matthew Nicks said of the former skipper. Matthew Nicks and his Crows were taught a lesson on Saturday night. AFL Photos “We’ve had our challenges along the way, that’s what brings an even higher respect when you go through challenges and share your thoughts and ideas on life. He’s been like having another coach.”



There had been speculation before their elimination final win over the Bulldogs that that Nicks’ future at the Crows was on thin ice – his record since taking the reins in 2020 featuring five campaigns in the finals wilderness before bowing out in straight-sets after clinching the minor premiership last year. But Nicks insisted he was the coach to spearhead the club to the promised land. “There are no guarantees in footy, but I’m confident of where we’re at and the conversations that are ongoing with the leaders of our football club and my colleagues,” Nicks said. “We have great forward momentum as a football club – we’re building something quite special. We’re not there yet, we know we still have a far way to go, but no doubt we’re heading in the right direction, and we’ve got the right people around the club. “I do [think I can take us to a premiership], and I think I’ve got the right support around [me].”

The Brisbane Lions lost their first final last year. What happened next? A barnstorming run through their semi-final and preliminary final, back to the big dance, and another premiership to top it all off. They’re on track for a repeat dose this year after obliterating the Crows at the Gabba in what became Adelaide favourite son Taylor Walker’s farewell game. Scott Spits (Brisbane Lions) and Steve Barrett (Adelaide) run their eye over every player in from the semi-final. What a return to form for Charlie Cameron and the Lions. AFL Photos

Just as importantly, he put a block on and allowed Zac Bailey to kick his opener after four minutes. 8/10 (2) Sam Draper: Tried and tried but was not among Brisbane’s best as the club’s second ruck. Had close to 60 per cent game time. 4.5/10 (3) Jaspa Fletcher: A good game by the 22-year-old, who is fast approaching 100 matches. He got plenty of early touches (seven in the first quarter) as Brisbane set up their impressive victory. 6/10 View post on X



(4) Oscar Allen: There could be a “watch” on the former Eagle after tonight. He had just five touches by the final break and two behinds. He did the one-percenters regularly (no surprise there), and spent time on Izak Rankine and nullified his influence. He got plenty of the ball himself, too. 8/10 (6) Hugh McCluggage: Yet again, he didn’t get a lot of the ball for a player of his class. It was notable that Chris Fagan came to his defence during the week. AFL Photos



(8) Will Ashcroft: Despite their qualifying final loss, the Lions have again set themselves up perfectly for another flag push, and Ashcroft’s form reflects that. He got better and better as the match wore on, as the Lions found their groove ahead of next week’s preliminary final against the Hawks. The two-time Norm Smith medallist finished with 30 touches. 8.5/10 (9) Lachie Neale: The veteran star was not among Brisbane’s match-winners, but he still picked up 21 possessions as others lifted around him. That’s probably a good sign for the Lions as they eye off a hat-trick of flags, and needing a multitude of contributors 6.5/10 (10) Levi Ashcroft: Quiet by his standards, he spent time on star Crows skipper Jordan Dawson and was probably shaded by him. 5.5/10 (13) Logan Morris: He slotted a brilliant snap goal after eight minutes in the third quarter when he finally got on the board. It gave the Lions a 50-point lead – basically snuffing out any Adelaide hopes. He left the game in the final quarter with injury. 5.5/10 The fired up Oscar Allen and Dayne Zorko. AFL Photos



(15) Dayne Zorko: It was a strong game from the super-veteran. Zorko was the other Lion (aside from Zac Bailey) to re-sign during the week, and he showed why they still want him in the side. The 37-year-old kicked a ripping goal in the third quarter and led the Lions for metres gained. 7/10 (16) Cam Rayner: He was oozing with confidence throughout and was involved in plenty of key moments. By midway through the second quarter Rayner already had five score involvements. Go back and witness his goal – Brisbane’s fifth – when he took Alex Neal-Bullen on and kicked beautifully. It gave the Lions a 31-point lead and the tone was set. 9/10 (22) Ty Gallop: He came into the side to replace the injured Noah Answerth. He did his bit with at least 10 touches. 5/10 (23) Charlie Cameron: A non-factor in the Lions’ qualifying final loss to the Swans, in this sudden-death clash he proved his worth and much more. He had his first goal after 90 seconds (Brisbane’s second) and his second after 23 minutes. Cameron is clearly an “energy” player, and with a return of 5.3 against his former side, the Lions and coach Fagan will be rapt. 8/10 View post on X



(26) Conor McKenna: He had a real crack but was in and out of the game. He finished with 13 touches and 1.2. Look back to his early “toe-poke” pass to Lohmann for a goal. 5.5/10 (27) Darcy Gardiner: The big man was largely quiet but typically handy for Brisbane’s team defence. 5/10 (30) Eric Hipwood: I quite liked his game. He regularly gave the Lions something to kick to and played an important role with Morris and Allen both a bit hot and cold. He kicked a goal in the last quarter and finished with 2.1. 7/10 (31) Harris Andrews: He played an intriguing game. The star defender didn’t hit his usual heights, but with so many teammates in hot form against the Crows, that mattered less. He manned Riley Thilthorpe for much of the game and won. Strangely, Andrews picked up a shot at goal in the first quarter after a double 50-metre penalty. His rare chance to score was offline. 6/10 (32) Darcy Fort: Solid and dependable as Brisbane’s first ruck. He split the points with Adelaide’s Lachlan McAndrew. 5.5/10



View post on X (33) Zac Bailey: What a game by the newly re-signed gun. Ever classy by foot, he was nothing short of brilliant – ironically against the club that desperately wanted him. He had a stack of score involvements and was one of the five Lions to get on the board in the first eight minutes. He finished with 23 touches and kicked 3.3. 8.5/10 (35) Ryan Lester: A quality contributor, Lester was heavily involved in the win from the start. Witness a strong defensive effort on the wing (a punch from behind) that helped set the mood. Quirkily, like Andrews, Lester had a rare shot at goal in the first term, but missed. 8/10 (44) Darcy Wilmot: He did his bit. He got enough of the ball and was more than solid in defence and playing as a link player. Thumbs up for an important player in Fagan’s all-conquering side. 6.5/10



Adelaide (2) Ben Keays: Two consolation goals in the first half almost masked a forgettable night for the defensive forward. Normally such a spark plug in attack, Keays was unsighted when the whips were cracking and was soundly trumped by Zorko. 4/10 (3) Sam Berry: The hardworking onballer was one Adelaide player who could hold his head high. Berry did his best to stem Brisbane’s early onslaught, chalking up five first-quarter clearances by himself. He finished with a game-high 31 disposals. 7.5/10 (4) Callum Ah Chee: Other than a sprayed shot out on the full early, Ah Chee struggled to get involved early doors at his old stomping ground. He had just three touches in the first half before spending time on the wing in the third term and getting more involved. 5/10 (6) Daniel Curtin: A big second half saw him finish with 22 disposals and seven clearances. Curtin booted the Crows’ first goal and played predominantly on the ball, but he – like many of his mates – wasn’t able to stop Brisbane’s game-breaking mids. 7/10



Daniel Curtin celebrates a goal with Taylor Walker. AFL Photos (7) Riley Thilthorpe: Had his hands full with Andrews in the first half before playing much better footy after the main break, booting two goals and using his body well against the Lions’ skipper. Thilthorpe’s contest was strong, but his ball use wasn’t quite up to scratch. 5/10 (8) Josh Rachele: Enjoyed a second-quarter purple patch when he slotted a major and then handed another one off to Darcy Fogarty. But otherwise, Rachele – fresh off a three-goal haul against the Bulldogs – had a poor evening. He conceded an early 50-metre penalty and was thrashed in the air by Lester. 2/10 (12) Jordan Dawson: He gave it everything he had with 30 touches and 512m gained, but his normally pristine ball use was missing, going at 50 per cent disposal efficiency. Dawson’s six first-quarter tackles said as much about the Lions’ dominance as it did about his own never-say-die approach. 7.5/10 (13) Taylor Walker: Ended his AFL journey with two fourth-quarter goals – to finish with 715 for his career – after being frustrated throughout the first three terms. Not an ending he wanted in his 319th and last top-flight game, but what a star he has been. 4/10



Walker leaves an AFL playing field for the final time with his children. AFL Photos (14) Jake Soligo: Adelaide needed more from him – for much of the home-and-away campaign and in both finals. Soligo was part of the midfield rotation, but struggled to get his hands on the footy. 3.5/10 (15) Brayden Cook: The crafty wingman’s usually clean ball use was a touch ragged and, aside from one neat goal assist early, he struggled to influence the match. 4/10 (16) Max Michalanney: There’s no lonelier place on an AFL field than one-out against Cameron in the mood he was in. Michalanney, normally a reliable stopper, was absolutely torched by the Lions’ brilliant goalsneak in the first half, before being mercifully moved to the wing. 1/10 (19) Zac Taylor: After missing the elimination final with a hamstring injury, Taylor ratified his recall instant by providing pressure and contest, while splitting minutes between half-forward and the centre-square. All up, 10 of his 17 possessions were contested. 6.5/10



(23) Izak Rankine: The highest-rated player in the AFL since round 17 was due a downer – and a downer he had, thanks chiefly to the disciplined, iron-fisted glove of Dunkley. Rankine was kickless at quarter-time and still had just two at the half. He was given more room to roam after half-time, but it just wasn’t his night. 5/10 Izak Rankine had his hands full all night against the Lions. AFL Photos (24) Josh Worrell: After enjoying the game of his life against the Bulldogs, when he racked up an AFL finals record 19 intercept possessions, Worrell wasn’t allowed anywhere near the same the influence to make plays. Although he still finished with 18 touches, he had just four of them by half-time. 5/10 (27) Luke Nankervis: He played major minutes on the wing before taking on the Cameron job late. Nankervis snared a magnificent mark over Levi Ashcroft and goaled to give the Crows a glimmer late in the first period, but otherwise was quiet. 4.5/10 (28) Alex Neal-Bullen: Splitting time between wing and half-forward, the experienced ex-Demon didn’t have a great impact in the first half but was serviceable after the interval. 5.5/10



(29) Rory Laird: The experienced half-back flanker never waved the white flag, but didn’t give the Lions too many major headaches either. 6/10 (30) Wayne Milera: The dashing All-Australian half-back wasn’t afforded the same time and space that he enjoyed a week earlier against the Bulldogs. Normally so calm and creative, his disposal was hurried thanks to the Lions’ pressure. Kicked a neat late goal. 6/10 (32) Darcy Fogarty: Conceded a horror 100m penalty in a forgettable opening term before springing to life in the second quarter, spearheading Adelaide’s revival by booting two goals and assisting another one to Rachele. But he was unsighted too often. 4.5/10 Darcy Fogarty had a frustrating night for the Crows. AFL Photos (35) James Borlase: Quiet for four quarters, he rarely intercepted and struggled to have much involvement, despite how much time the Sherrin spent in Brisbane’s attacking area. 3/10



(40) Hugo Hall-Kahan: The unsung half-back has barely put a foot wrong since being picked up in the mid-season draft. He wasted very few of his 27 disposals, racked up plenty of metres of rebound and contested well in the air and on the ground. A real find. 7.5/10 (42) Lachlan McAndrew: After shading Tim English last week, the towering ruckman had his hands full with Draper and Fort. McAndrew matched them both in the air, but it was harder for him on the deck. 6/10 (48) Mark Keane: He struggled all night with an aggressive Hipwood, finishing with four kicks and virtually no impact. 2/10 Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: NRL Highlights: Sharks v Cowboys - Finals Week 1
World.content:
NRL Highlights: Sharks v Cowboys - Finals Week 1

See all of the scoring plays, big hits and highlight moments from the Sharks vs Cowboys Elimination Final at Allianz Stadium! Find out who survived and made it to Week 2!

World.title: Fans stay home but Sharks turn up to end Cowboys’ season
World.content:
If you build it, they won’t come.

It may be the one of the best stadiums in the southern hemisphere, a mere 25.2 kilometres from the Sharks’ spiritual home in the Shire. But many Cronulla fans refuse to leave Cronulla.

Not even the siren song of their Mermaids cheerleaders, free public transport for ticket holders, or the chance to witness their team in a finals fixture was enough to bring them to Allianz Stadium.

Loading

An official crowd of 17,429 was posted. That’s only about 2,500 more than the capacity of Shark Park, otherwise known as Ocean Protect Stadium. Understandably, only a handful of hearty Cowboys souls made the long commute from Townsville.

The decision to shift the game here was a controversial one. Head office will hope the extra corporate cash it pockets from playing at Allianz offsets the broadcast images of a stadium less than half full.

The reasons for non-attendance remain unclear. Is it because rugby league is such a good television product? The fatigue of watching the seventh North Queensland-Cronulla post-season clash since 2013? Or just a preference for “Portaloo Park”?

Nicho Hynes celebrates a try. Getty Images

Whatever the case, the Sharks got the job done without the vocal support they would normally get at their regular home.

“It’s not our decision,” Cronulla coach Craig Fitzgibbon said. “I felt like this last year - obviously the amount of sulking that went on about playing at Shark Park, I thought we weren’t any chance of getting it this year. They should have just told us earlier.

“But also, for us, we’re happy to play here. We’re in semi-finals; we want to play in a big stadium. But our members and fans pay their money all year to be able to watch their team make semi-finals and play at home, and we earned that. We didn’t get it … but that’s not up to me. I would imagine it’s a financial decision or viewing optics for the game. I’m not sure.”

A 26-16 win against their old sparring partners was achieved despite their returning maestro playing with the use of only one shoulder. Braydon Trindall took his place after three weeks on the sidelines. Despite being clearly hampered, he passed, tackled and kicked his side to a scrappy victory.

At one point in the second half, “Tricky” gave his shoulder an unnecessary test when he tried to retrieve the football from his own short kick-off. The pivot couldn’t be accused of playing in a dinner suit. When he produced a season-high 31st try assist with a pass to fullback Will Kennedy – not even Nathan Cleary comes near that figure – it was due reward for playing through the pain.

Loading

The Cowboys have been the most curious side in the NRL. They qualified for the top eight despite conceding more points than any other finalist in history. Their devil-may-care attitude is best exemplified by Scott Drinkwater. The Dragons-bound fullback is the ultimate gunslinger. One errant cut-out pass resulted in an intercept that gifted Sione Katoa his 100th NRL try. Undeterred, he threw another one that hit Zac Laybutt on the chest from 25 metres away to give his side hope.

However, it was always going to come down to the Cowboys’ application without the football. They defended stoutly when starved off possession for much of the opening half, particularly when their tryline was peppered. However, those exertions eventually took their toll. When Nico Hynes shaped to kick, but instead stepped off his left foot, their fate was sealed.

There is every chance that the Sharks could be required to return to Allianz next week. Asked whether he hoped more of their fans will follow them there, captain Cameron McInnes deadpanned: “I don’t know. If you can afford it, come. If you can’t, watch it on TV. I couldn’t care less, really.”

World.title: Child dead after fire rips through Central West home
World.content:
Remove items from your saved list to add more.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

A four-year-old child has died after a fire tore through a home in the state’s Central West on Saturday.

Emergency services were called to the home in Woodstock, about 22 kilometres north-east of Cowra, just before 3pm. Officers arrived to find the house well alight.

A woman and two children were able to escape, but the four-year-old remained unaccounted for. The woman was taken to Cowra Hospital in a stable condition, suffering from smoke inhalation.

Fire and Rescue NSW firefighters extinguished the blaze before locating the body of the child inside the home.

“A crime scene has been established, and inquiries into the circumstances surrounding the fire are ongoing,” NSW Police said in a statement.

World.title: Warriors toppled by Dolphins in NRL qualifying final
World.content:
The NZ Warriors have been defeated by the Dolphins in their NRL qualifying final, at Go Media Stadium in Auckland.

The Warriors will now have to take the scenic route to the NRL grand final, after bowing to the Dolphins 26-16 on Saturday night.

After finishing second, to earn homefield advantage for the opening round of the playoffs, the Warriors could not take advantage of their fan support and a penalty advantage that had them 12-8 ahead at halftime.

Their only try of the game came when fullback Taine Tuaupiki spun out of a tackle near the line and scooted clear to score. Tuaupiki scored all the Warriors' points, adding a conversion and five penalties, as his team chose to kick for goal, instead of push for tries in the redzone.

They probably should have led by more at the break, but Tuaupiki stretched the margin beyond a converted try, with two more penalties in the second half, before the Dolphins piled on three unanswered converted tries in the final 20 minutes.

The Warriors' cause was not helped by ill-discipline, as centre Adam Pompey was sin-binned for a no-arms shoulder tackle and then second-rower Kurt Capewell was matched for sparking a melee just before halftime.

Dolphins wing Selwyn Cobbo was also sent to the bin in the same incident, after Jackson Ford was dumped in a tipping tackle and the teams came together.

The Warriors lost centre Leka Halasima to injury during the warm-up, with Pompey promoted to the starting line-up in his place.

The Dolphins were good for their win, scoring four tries to the Warriors' one, all converted by wing Jamayne Isaako, and they will now take a rest next week, as they await their opponents for a preliminary final in two weeks.

Meanwhile, the Warriors will host Newcastle Knights next week.

The result broke a six-game winning streak and marked the first time this season they have lost, after leading at halftime.

World.title: Two-thirds of middle-aged adults delay eye tests despite problems - survey
World.content:
More than two-thirds of middle-aged adults are delaying their eye tests despite having problems.

A survey by YouGov commissioned by Specsavers showed that 70 percent of adults between 40 and 59 put off getting their sight checked by more than a month when having trouble with their vision.

Longer delays weren't uncommon with almost half waiting for more than six months to get help, and one in five stalling for more than two years.

Chair of Ophthalmology NZ Dr Sonya Bennett told RNZ it was "probably human nature" to avoid confronting health problems.

"It's not uncommon for us to hear the story that they've put off getting seen until they've got quite significant issues."

She said people would find ways to cope before seeing an optometrist "because they actually don't want to wear glasses" out of vanity or perceived impracticality.

And YouGov's survey found one in five avoided wearing glasses despite needing them because of social perception.

It found half of respondents simply increased texts and display settings on their devices to cope - with a third simply missing out on certain activities because of their eyesight.

Dr Bennett explained that "presbyopia" was the most common age-related cause of eyesight loss, often setting in around middle age.

"It gradually affects your ability to read at near [distance]. Distance vision is usually in most cases okay, but you just lose the ability to see things up close.

"And that's because what we call 'accommodation' - which is the ability to focus - reduces with ageing due to changes in the lens, inside the eye and changes in the muscle that moves the lens."

The survey found nine in 10 had never heard the medical term for this common condition.

She said the only real danger of delaying getting help was if there were another underlying disease, such as glaucoma, where vision could not be regained once lost.

World.title: Man charged after election hoardings damaged in "vandalism spree", police say
World.content:
Charges have been laid against a Tauranga man after what police called a "vandalism spree", damaging political hoardings in Papamoa.

About 30 hoardings were attacked in a two hour period, from about 6:30am on Thursday, police said.

The first damaged were in Parton Road, then more were damaged throughout the suburb of Papamoa.

Senior Sergeant Shannon Clifford thanked the people who had provided information about the damage, which led to an arrest on the same day.

A 43-year-old man faces charges of wilful damage and is scheduled to appear in court again next month.

Ahead of November's general election, the case was a warning that damaging political hoardings is not okay, Senior Sergeant Clifford said:

"The damage in some cases is significant and unfortunately that's an unnecessary cost for the people who own them.

"We won't tolerate this illegal and destructive behaviour in our community."

World.title: Fiji government announces death of a Cabinet Minister
World.content:
Fiji's Government has annouced the death of its Minister for Employment, Productivity and Workplace Relations, Agni Deo Singh.

A government statement said that "It is with great sadness that the Office of the Prime Minister announces the passing of the Minister for Employment, Productivity and Workplace Relations, Agni Deo Singh."

He died in Brisbane.

Prime Minister and chair of the Coalition Cabinet Sitiveni Rabuka extends his deepest condolences to the family, loved ones, colleagues, and friends of the late Minister during this difficult time.

Prime Minister Rabuka acknowledges Singh's dedicated service to the workers and people of Fiji and his invaluable contribution to the Government and the nation.

World.title: Ranfurly Shield stays in Whangārei, after Northland crush Waikato
World.content:
Northland have just one more defence before they can tuck the Ranfurly Shield away for the summer, after seeing off Waikato in Whangārei.

The Taniwha's magic season continued on Saturday as they defended the log o' wood in dominant fashion, hammering the moo-loos 34-17.

Australian import Lachlan Hooper opened the scoring for Northland, before Waikato flyer Dan Sinkinson responded for the Mooloos.

Taha Kemara pushed the conversion wide in trying kicking conditions, to leave Northland in front, a lead they stretched courtesy of a contentious try to halfback Sam Nock.

After a Northland maul splintered, Nock weaved through the mess to dot down as the Waikato players pleaded for an obstruction call which never came.

Rivez Reihana nailed a penalty on the siren, to send his side to half-time with a 15-5 lead.

The Tani's extended their advantage shortly after oranges through James Ramm, but Waikato weren't done, Tepaea Cook-Savage keeping his side in touch with a spectacular finish in the corner.

A second for Hooper put Northland 17 points in front with 15 to play, before Brady Rush sealed the result after Corey Evans stabbed through a grubber, which sat up perfectly for his winger.

Waikato would pick up a late consolation through replacement hooker Sean Ralph.

The win marks the first time Northland have ever beaten Waikato in a shield match, and extends their tenure to two successful defences.

Northland's one remaining shield defence will come against Counties Manukau, on 26 September.

World.title: Medicine company bids to get pseudoephedrine out from behind pharmacy counters
World.content:
A pharmaceutical company wants the cold and flu drug pseudoephedrine out from behind the counter and back on pharmacy shelves.

Reckitt Benckiser has put in an application with drug regulator Medsafe to make the medicine easier to purchase.

The medicine - a precursor for manufacturing methamphetamine or P - was no longer a threat in its retail form because criminal gangs imported their raw ingredients in bulk, Reckitt said in its application.

Currently, pseudoephedrine was available as a restricted medicine from pharmacies, meaning it was not stocked on open shelves.

People who wanted to buy it must instead ask a pharmacist who would decide if it was suitable for them before providing it.

Under the new proposal, small packets of the pill form, effectively one day's worth, would be available for people to select themselves, alongside medicines like panadol and ibuprofen.

It would still only be sold in pharmacies.

Pseudoephedrine was made a prescription-only drug in 2011 because of its use in the manufacture of P.

But in 2024, it was reclassified to its current status after ACT's David Seymour pushed for the change on the back of an election campaign promise.

ACT's David Seymour. RNZ / Nathan McKinnon

Reckitt's application said the proposed change would give New Zealanders better access to a very effective nasal decongestant and lessen the workload of stretched pharmacists.

Heavily restricting pseudoephedrine in 2011 did not effectively control the supply and use of meth in New Zealand, it said.

"The supply and manufacture of methamphetamine use in New Zealand has shifted from small scale production, where pharmacy sourced pseudoephedrine was the main precursor used," it said.

Instead it there was "large scale clandestine manufacture" with ingredients brought in from overseas or bulk importation of methamphetamine, the application said.

When pseudoephedrine was banned from shelves in 2011, many cold and flu remedies changed to the drug phenylephrine.

That was now the subject of a class action lawsuit after evidence it was ineffective.

Medsafe's Medicines Classification Committee would discuss Reckitt's application at its meeting next month.

World.title: Wellington Airport evacuated after burnt cooking triggers smoke alarm
World.content:
Wellington Airport has been evacuated after a smoke alarm went off.

Fire and Emergency responded with one crew from Kilbirnie, and another from Newtown, at 4.19pm on Saturday.

It found the alarm had been triggered by burnt cooking.

Wellington Airport said the southwest pier had been briefly evacuated, with the area quickly cleared for re-entry.

World.title: Why officials are 'reasonably confident' of avoiding fuel supply shocks
World.content:
Regardless of the uncertainties surrounding the Iran war and the US administration, New Zealand officials six months on are hopeful - confident, even - that supply chains will hold. In the first of this two-part series RNZ political reporter Russell Palmer sits down with MBIE's Iain Cossar.

"Reasonably confident" is how New Zealand's top fuel official rates the country's chances of avoiding fuel shortages.

It's a remarkable shift considering the level of exposure for New Zealand which Iain Cossar says is among the highest in the world.

"As far as markets go, we couldn't be probably more. We were probably one of the most exposed to a Hormuz closure and were rightly quite worried about what that might mean for actual supply."

After the US and Israel launched attacks against Iran in February, resulting in the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet set up an all-of-government response group including 11 agencies.

Treasury leads the price response, and the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) leads the supply response. At the height of the crisis they were meeting daily at 7.30am.

At the time, the world was producing about 106 million barrels of oil a day, and consumed about 104 million a day in 2025. Nearly 20 percent transits the Hormuz Strait - mostly from Middle-East states to Asia.

A fine line between too much and not enough

Cossar took over in early April as the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment's deputy secretary for the fuel supply response, which has drawn on expertise from 180 ministry staff and secondees.

He says with New Zealand no longer refining onshore, it is largely reliant on Asian markets with Korea, Singapore, Malaysia and Japan supplying more than 90 percent of the fuel Kiwis used in 2025.

"We are highly dependent on them getting the raw product to refine and then send to us. We're about three weeks shipping away, give or take," he says.

New Zealand runs on a "just-in-time" model where about 50 days of fuel - with about 20 days' of that being offshore - are booked on shipments up to three months in advance.

So far, only one shipment has been delayed, because the ship diverted to another destination.

"It's literally the equivalent of you driving to one petrol station and then deciding you can get a better price at another one," Cossar says.

"The fuel that was on that consignment ... was sought and bought from another supplier to come to New Zealand within six hours," Cossar says.

New Zealand's top fuel official Iain Cossar. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

New Zealand also needed to worry about the opposite problem: ullage, a term from the wine industry meaning the space left in the tank. With the just-in-time model relying on stable fuel consumption, people buying less to save money could disrupt things.

"We can only hold so much fuel in the country and if people reduce their consumption of that fuel, what could happen is that a ship arrives with ... jet or petrol and it can't offload," Cossar says.

"They are then waiting in harbour and because you've got a large tanker sitting at dock doing nothing, you're actually paying quite a price for that."

Cossar says the Strait's closure had an impact on the world economy "consistent with, and I think slightly higher maybe, than the supply shock of the '70s", but several factors helped:

markets adjusted very quickly, with oil and refined product flows around the globe going to those countries that could afford it

more product was coming out of the Middle East than anticipated, including through other channels and some through the "closed" strait

Southeast Asian markets and poorer countries were affected and responded by reducing consumption

China reduced its demand considerably, easing global demand (about 5 million barrels per day)

more oil production came online in other countries, particularly the US, Kazakhstan and Brazil (about 1.2 million barrels per day)

the International Energy Agency ordered 400 million barrels of global oil reserves to be released to market over the course of the crisis (about 300 million were released by early August).

Going dark, or over land

Cossar says markets have always been optimistic the conflict in Iran would be resolved eventually "so they priced that in, but you do see continuing variability with the ever-changing geopolitics".

Oil continued to leave the Middle East through various methods: dark transits, ship-to-ship transfers, US military night corridors and alternative land pipelines.

In August, the pre-conflict rate of 55 ships a day had dropped to about 10, largely through dark transits where ships "go dark" by shutting off their identification transponders to avoid detection.

Sometimes these were small ships that could run the Strait, then transfer oil to larger tankers in the open Arabian sea. Other times, the US military would run convoys at night in coordinated groups.

Ways oil was leaving the Strait of Hormuz. Supplied / International Energy Agency

Overland pipelines also played a part, with the East-West pipline across Saudi Arabia and the UAE taking up to 7 million barrels a day; the Habshan-Fujairah Pipeline carrying up to 1.8 million barrels a day from Abu Dhabi to Fujairah; and Saudi Arabia increasingly diverting Yanbu exports via the SUMED pipeline and the Suez Canal.

China a big player in supply and demand

China - as one of the world's biggest importers of crude - "played and continues to play quite a critical role" by cutting imports by a third to half.

"They solved a third of our problem right there, globally. Now, we don't know exactly why they've done that - the price would have been an impact and perhaps they just chose to not import, as they had quite extensive reserves."

Beijing did impose export controls on refined fuel for a time but released those again in July, and Cossar says a return would not necessarily mean a shortage.

The size of China's reserves is a mystery - particularly below ground - but Cossar says they are believed to be "significant" and demand remains below pre-conflict levels.

He says despite the uncertainty, and although New Zealand is prepared in case a supply shock should emerge, he is not expecting that to happen.

"We're reasonably optimistic we won't face a supply shock because we have seen world markets adjust, new supply has become available, and there is supply getting out of the Middle East that we weren't actually aware of.

"Some countries will continue to buy for those who can afford it, and those who can't, won't. Put bluntly, New Zealand is in the countries who could probably afford it. We won't like it [when prices are higher] and it will have impacts on us, but we'll still be able to afford fuel."

A graph of global fuel reserves. Supplied / International Energy Agency

Further reassurances come from New Zealand's "robust" regulatory system, the additional reserves loaded up at Marsden Point, continued shipments finding ways out of the Hormuz Strait and out of the Red Sea.

By the end of May, the number of staff dedicated to the response had dropped to 110, and today fewer than 12 people remain involved, many splitting their time with other work.

In the long term, although global reserves have fallen below 7.9 billion barrels, they are still above 2022 levels "so it's not like we are in uncharted territory", Cossar says.

World.title: Trindall returns from shoulder dislocation to lead Sharks in finals win
World.content:
One month after dislocating his shoulder, Braydon Trindall has returned to lead the Cronulla Sharks to a 26-16 win, advancing to the second week of the NRL finals while knocking out the North Queensland Cowboys.

Trindall missed the final four matches of the NRL regular season after suffering the shoulder dislocation in round 24 against the Canberra Raiders, with the Sharks losing three of those games.

With a heavily strapped shoulder, Trindall looked uncomfortable throughout the match but remained strong in defence.

Trindall's kicking game put North Queensland's back-three under pressure, with two drops from Cowboys fullback Scott Drinkwater, with one leading to a first-half try.

He set up the match-sealing try late in the second half, with his 31st assist of the season putting fullback Will Kennedy over for his side's fifth try.

The Sharks will meet the loser of Sunday's qualifying final between the Penrith Panthers and Sydney Roosters.

Meanwhile, the Dolphins scored three tries in the final 20 minutes of the club's maiden NRL finals match to stun the Warriors in Auckland.

Herbie Farnworth scores for the Dolphins during their qualifying final win over the Warriors. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

In a fiery contest which had three players sent to the sin bin in the first half, the Dolphins were hampered by indiscipline.

Both sides had one try each after 60 minutes, but five penalty goals from Warriors fullback Taine Tuaupiki gave the Auckland-based side a 16-6 lead with a quarter to play.

But the Dolphins ran in three tries, including a length-of-the-field effort started and finished by Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow to take the lead in the 66th minute.

The Dolphins have earned the right to host a preliminary final at Lang Park in Brisbane in a fortnight, while the Warriors will host the Newcastle Knights next week in a knock-out semifinal.

"It is big. It is massive for everyone involved at the club," Dolphins coach Kristian Woolf said.

"The club has done such a good job over the last four years in every department, but the blokes that deserve the credit are the players with the way they played tonight and the bravery they showed under pressure.

"They are in this position for a reason and that's because they want to work hard for each other."

Relive all of Saturday's NRL finals action in the blog below.

World.title: Newcastle's finals win is proof the future has come
World.content:
If Newcastle were going to pull off a classic finals ambush on South Sydney they were going to need some new heroes to be born under the bright lights of the Sydney Football Stadium.

The Knights went into the game light up front, not in size, strength or willingness, but certainly in experience and definitely in recognition. After their 20-10 win over South Sydney, however, they will never have the luxury of being underestimated again.

Across 80 minutes of a classic blood-and-thunder final, fresh faces and young legs won the day as the star-studded Rabbitohs outfit fought on despite being busted until they were finally beaten.

NRL Finals live Newcastle holds on for a 20-10 victory over South Sydney to kick-off the 2026 finals series, but Rabbitohs coach Wayne Bennett fumes at more Bunker confusion after a contentious call.

Perhaps it could have all been different were it not for Cody Walker falling to a sniper's shot early in the second half, suffering a calf injury that ended his night early.

The ageless Walker is what binds the Rabbitohs left edge together and takes it from a series of talented individuals to the closest thing rugby league has to a hammer of the gods.

But you'll find little sympathy for an injury up Newcastle way. They were without Dylan Brown, Dylan Lucas, Trey Mooney and Jacob Saifiti heading into this and while plenty expected them to fight few expected them to win.

After their first finals win away from home in 13 years, expectations be damned. They defied them all over the park, perhaps no more than down their right, where backrower Jermaine McEwan had the game of his young life.

It was always going to be a big night for the 21-year old, one way or the other. It was he who would be tasked with setting up Newcastle's defences against the Rabbitohs knockout left.

He did that with aplomb, even before Walker went down, from setting the tone with driving hits from the inside to holding his width and his nerve when Souths gave their chainsaw a rip.

Throw in two tries and it's the last time McEwan will catch anybody by surprise.

Together that Knights edge put together some of the best defensive plays of the night, but it wasn't the biggest — that honour must belong to McEwan's backrow partner, Francis Manuleleua.

They call him "Big Frisco" and people were put in Alcatraz for the type of violence he dropped on Cameron Murray late in the first half as he raced out of the line to dish out one of the hits of the season.

Technically it was illegal — the shot was clean, but Manuleleua was half a metre offside. The red and blue hordes at the southern end of the ground didn't seem to care, even though Souths scored off the field position, because sometimes it's worth it.

Paying the blood price for a little bit of rough stuff is something Dane Gagai and Latrell Mitchell know well.

The two centres fought like demons after a scuffle midway through the first half and while both won their share of battles it was Gagai who won the war.

Gagai is one of the few older heads in this side — you can call him older but don't call him old, whatever you do — and only a player as sure as himself as the 35-year old would risk poking a bear like Mitchell.

It's something few have done while surviving to tell the tale but Gagai didn't just weather the might and power, he fought like a far younger man, with nothing held back and no regard for his own safety.

His try in the 25th minute was a snapshot the endless love of competition that keeps him young even as the years keep passing and his roar of triumph after he was first to a Sandon Smith kick was among the first harbingers of what was unfolding.

There were other fine battles and contributors — Bradman Best and Jack Wighton, who was close to his side's best, went hell for leather on the other side of the field to Gagai and Mitchell.

Tyson Frizell had a game up front that puts the war back into warhorse and Keaon Koloamatangi left everything out there in his final game as a Rabbitoh.

Kalyn Ponga, once the sun around which everything in Newcastle orbited, was prominent throughout but the class of Smith and Fletcher Sharpe meant the whole game was not on his shoulders and the Knights fullback thrived as a result.

It meant he was able to access the best parts of his game, something the Rabbitohs found difficult throughout even as a torrid defensive effort and several last gasp saves by Campbell Graham kept their heads above water.

They will be haunted by the hypothetical over the summer after their first trip to the finals in four years fell at the first hurdle.

Walker cut a forlorn figure on the South Sydney bench. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

If only Walker didn't get injured, or at least had made it through more of the game.

If only Bud Sullivan's circus act of a try wasn't chalked off for a knock on from Alex Johnston that could have easily been called a strip, just as Dom Young's try could have easily been rubbed off the board.

If only Brandon Smith's last desperate effort with three minutes left — which would have forced a big finish at the very least — didn't come up a blade of grass short.

If only, on a night where they played something resembling their top side for one of the first times all season, they were able to tap into the tried and true talent that lurks somewhere within and rises to the surface enough to tantalise and tease.

They are a team built for the present with stars who made their reputation on tearing down what came before them. That's the law of the jungle and the nature of the game.

The Rabbitohs will fancy their chances of returning to the mix next year but this time around were served a reminder there comes a time when the young feed on the old.

This night was such a time and with nothing to lose and everything to prove, Newcastle was ravenous.

World.title: Shelton through to US Open final as he looks to end 23-year drought
World.content:
American eighth seed Ben Shelton has the chance to end his country's long wait for another men's US Open champion after beating compatriot Frances Tiafoe to reach the final.

Shelton posted a 4-6, 6-3, 6-3, 7-5 victory over Tiafoe in the second semi-final and will play top seed Alexander Zverev in the final on Monday morning, AEST.

He showed plenty of energy after ousting defending champion Carlos Alcaraz in a quarterfinal match that ended at 3:33 am Wednesday, local time.

It was the latest finish to a match in US Open history.

Andy Roddick was the most recent American to win the men's US Open title, in 2003.

Zverev will play for his second major title this year after beating Karen Khachanov 6-3, 7-6 (9/7), 7-6 (8/6) in the first semi.

Zverev, who had long been considered the best men's player without a major, finally broke through at the French Open this year. The German followed by reaching the Wimbledon final, which he lost to Jannik Sinner, and is 24-2 in grand slam matches this season.

"Sometimes just things go your way and I feel like I've had a lot of struggles at the major level. I was so close so many times and maybe this year God has said that this is going to be your year and just enjoy the time on the court," Zverev said.

Alexander Zverev on his way to a straight-sets win against Karen Khachanov. (Getty Images: Manuela Davies/USTA)

Now he will try to win the title that he still can't believe he let get away in 2020. Zverev won the first two sets against Dominic Thiem but then lost in a fifth-set tiebreaker, as Thiem became the first man to win the US Open title after dropping the first two sets since 1949.

Zverev was solid after going up two sets this time, and has won 13 consecutive sets after becoming the first number one-seeded man to play five-setters in each of the first two rounds of a major.

Khachanov was trying to reach his first major final after a surprising run in New York. He arrived with a losing record for the season but went on to reach his third grand slam semifinal, including second at the US Open.

He started playing better after dropping the first set and then falling behind 2-0 in the second. He finally broke Zverev's serve to tie it and it stayed even until they went to the tiebreaker. The Russian erased Zverev's first two set points in it before Zverev finished it off by winning a 34-shot rally.

Khachanov then had leads of 3-0 and 5-2 in the third-set tiebreaker before Zverev battled back.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: Aussie athletics star shocked at massive pay packet for coming second
World.content:
Nicola Olyslagers has had the best bad night of her career after missing out on becoming a new 'Ultimate' athletics high jump champion, only to learn to her surprise that she had still leapt to the biggest payday of her life.

Australia's world champion only managed to clear 1.95m on the first night of World Athletics' inaugural Ultimate Championship in Budapest this morning (AEST).

She struggled with her approach on a difficult surface on a cold night as Ukraine's Olympic champ Yaroslava Mahuchikh beat her to the title with a 1.99m leap.

Olyslagers' runner-up spot earned her $US75,000 ($105,000) — $5,000 more than she pocketed for winning the world title last year — as part of the record $US10 million ($14 million) prize pot for the streamlined new event that World Athletics hopes will attract a host of new fans.

Only when speaking to reporters afterwards did Olyslagers realise just what she would be taking home.

Nicola Olyslagers clears the bar on her way to second in the high jump. (Getty Images: Christel Saneh/World Athletics)

"What? Really? I genuinely thought it was just first prize got the 150k and second was like 10,000," she said.

"You are the bearer of good news. That's fantastic."

Olyslagers, wrapped in a scarf and still shivering 40 minutes after her event, said she struggled with her approach on a firm-surface run-up but, with more than half the field exiting early, she realised that after two fails at 1.95 a clearance would be enough for second place.

She duly sailed over at the final attempt, punching the air in delight.

"That's the happiest I've ever been after a 1.95. I think I celebrated as if I'd won the whole competition and it was a really good jump," she said.

"It just showed tonight that all of us were a little bit tired but I mean, that 95 jump, I'm still living off that."

Olyslagers' domestic rival Eleanor Patterson also looked uncomfortable all evening but took joint third with a modest clearance of 1.91 a week after she'd jumped 10cm higher to win the Diamond League crown.

"It's the lowest I've jumped all year. Really, really frustrating," Commonwealth champ Patterson said.

"After the best season of my life I really wanted to enjoy it but I didn't really."

Marschall fourth as Duplantis stars again

Meanwhile, triple Commonwealth pole vault champion Kurtis Marschall managed only fourth with a best of 5.95m as Swedish superstar Armand Duplantis again revelled in being the star attraction, having seen the event open with a theme song he had both co-written and performed.

With the title secure after a faultless run to 6.20m, the spellbound full house of 20,000 willed him to clear a world record 6.32, but he narrowly failed in what would have been a remarkable 16th world best in six years.

Earlier, Australia's Ky Robinson gave it a real go in the 5,000m, leading at the bell, but got swallowed up in the run for home as Norway's Jakob Ingebrigtsen roared back to his best with a superbly-judged victory charge.

Sarah Billings ran well in her 800m semi-final to qualify for tomorrow's final when there will be four more Australians in action.

Abbey Caldwell and Jess Hull will go in the women's 1,500m, Mackenzie Little in the javelin and Oceania record holder Lachlan Kennedy in the men's 100m.

World.title: England has won 38 straight Tests but Wallaroos won't die wondering
World.content:
On paper, the Wallaroos aren't given a chance of beating England in this weekend's WXV Global Series Test.

The Red Roses, as England is known, are on a 38-match winning streak, stretching back to 2022.

They're reigning Women's Rugby World Cup winners and have claimed eight straight Six Nations titles, which include a run of five consecutive Grand Slams.

Why Wallaroos are 'family' Past and present Wallaroos players reflect on the journey and challenges to reaching 100 Tests.

England has never lost to the Wallaroos, with the most recent meeting — in last year's World Cup — finishing in a 47-7 victory to the tournament hosts in Bristol.

The Australians, though, aren't intimidated ahead of the Test in Salford, which will be played on Sunday morning, AEST.

They respect the Red Roses, but possess a quiet confidence in their ability to compete with the world champions.

"I think it will be a hard challenge," said Wallaroos winger Amelia Whitaker, who will make her Test debut.

"Obviously England [is] number one, but this week I feel like we've really rallied together so I think we're up for the task."

Amelia Whitaker will make her Test debut for the Wallaroos. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

Wallaroos reserve forward Jemma Bemrose, who could debut off the bench, was similarly undaunted.

"They've [Red Roses] got a strong reputation, and they've achieved a lot as a team," Bemrose said.

"But I'm just really excited to embrace the challenge."

Wallaroos assistant coach Mike Ruthven knows England's strengths, but he believed there might be a chink in the Red Roses' armour.

"They're a pretty complete footy team," Ruthven said.

"We know what's coming, but we think we've identified a few things that we've been really able to target and have a crack at."

Rugby's 'benchmark'

The Red Roses' status as the top-ranked nation in the world did not come by chance.

England's governing body, the Rugby Football Union (RFU), made a wise investment in the women's game when it offered full-time contracts to players in 2019.

The Red Roses now have 32 full-time contracted players for the 2026/27 season, with an additional six players on transition contracts.

England won last year's Women's Rugby World Cup on home soil. (Getty Images/World Rugby: Molly Darlington)

England's pathways haven't been ignored either, with the RFU boasting it's invested 14.5 million pounds ($27 million) in the community game.

The national team also benefits from a thriving club competition, Premiership Women's Rugby (PWR), which involves nine clubs playing 16 league matches each before a finals series is contested.

The RFU announced in June it's committing 24 million pounds ($45 million) to PWR across 10 years.

The Red Roses have been embraced by the English public, with 219,439 spectators attending their World Cup matches last year, including a global record of 81,885 at Twickenham when they beat Canada 33-13 in the final.

There was also a 336 per cent increase in TV viewing hours during the tournament, helping raise the visibility of the players amid England's crowded sporting landscape.

This is reflected in the fact that star back Ellie Kildunne finished runner-up in 2025's publicly voted BBC Sports Personality of the Year Award, outpolling the likes of Formula 1 world champion Lando Norris.

Ellie Kildunne is among the most recognisable figures in English sport. (Getty Images: Ian MacNicol)

It's all food for thought for Rugby Australia (RA), which is shifting the Wallaroos to a full-time program ahead of the 2029 World Cup to be hosted on home soil.

Some positive steps have already been made, such as the appointment of successful rugby sevens coach Tim Walsh as RA's director of women's high performance.

Rugby Australia setting high standards Only three years out from hosting the Women's Rugby World Cup, Australia makes a key appointment it hopes will help deliver success on the international stage.

Australia has the playing and coaching talent to become a World Cup contender, but as Walsh recently acknowledged to ABC Sport, the Wallaroos must have the "infrastructure for them to be able to excel".

Ruthven, who is working under Walsh on the Wallaroos' staff until incoming coach Sione Fukofuka begins next year, rated England's program as the gold standard.

"The RFU have done a great job to support the women's game over here, underpinned by a really strong PWR competition," Ruthven said.

"You look at their players, and they're playing 20-odd competitive games of domestic football.
